title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Realistic Scenarios Through Representation Engineering
abstract: Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Abstract

Reward hacking is a major problem in current production machine learning systems, resulting in costly and dangerous failures. Here we study how to monitor for and mitigate reward hacking in realistic settings, including tool calls and long contexts. We apply a dynamic intervention to steering directions obtained by three different methods: difference-in-means vectors from labeled rollouts, gradient optimization-based vectors, and vectors extracted when models reference an anti-reward-hacking model spec. This dynamic intervention perturbs model representations less than uniform steering vector addition to the residual stream, allowing for more precise edits. We find that we are able to cheaply and significantly reduce reward hacking without correspondingly significant costs to model coherence or capability, and that steering vectors originally extracted from coding environments also generalize to reducing reward hacking in other domains. Our results pave the way towards latent space monitoring and control over realistic production systems.

## 1 Introduction

Reward hacking is a well known failure mode in machine learning systems, where models learn to increase reward on a proxy objective in ways that model developers don’t intend. This can lead to many safety issues when those models go into downstream production (MacDiarmid et al., 2025). This is no longer a theoretical concern. Recent events involving an agent swarm penetrating HuggingFace’s infrastructure were due in large part to misconfigured training environments which the agent hacked to increase its reward (METR, 2026). As agents continue to grow in prevalence and capability, this failure mode will correspondingly become much more important than its current state. We propose inference time techniques for monitoring and mitigating reward hacking in realistic agentic coding environments over long contexts.

Inference time interventions work well only when the behavior can be cheaply detected and mitigated against. We find that this is the case in our setting. A small number of labeled rollouts is sufficient to identify a direction that is useful not only for monitoring, but also for dynamic steering via representation engineering (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). We use activation capping from Lu et al. (2026) to suppress reward hacking by intervening only when activations exceed some threshold along the hacking direction, minimizing collateral effects on other capabilities. This allows model developers to be more confident in applying this technique, as it will minimally alter representations and only in a small, predictable fraction of a model’s rollouts.

As a baseline, we also provide a model specification (model spec), which instructs the model to act according to a list of principles opposing reward hacking. This acts as a smaller, domain-specific form of constitutional alignment (Bai et al., 2022). We find this works well, but expect that prompting baselines will likely degrade over long contexts due to compaction, context rot, and multi-agent swarm dynamics where many agents may be given contradicting instructions. Extending this, we train model spec vectors that steer towards references to the model spec and similarly are implemented dynamically.

We study these techniques on Qwen3.5-27B (Team, 2026) using agentic rollouts on ImpossibleBench (Zhong et al., 2025) from the MisTrace dataset (Meek et al., 2026). Our contributions are:

• 

Latent space monitoring for reward hacking using cheap linear probes and investigation of projection behavior during misaligned reasoning, which motivates our dynamic steering interventions.

• 

Dynamic steering across three methods to mitigate reward hacking at inference time, while minimizing negative effects on capabilities. We test difference-in-means vectors, optimization vectors, and steering vectors extracted from a model’s references to an anti-reward hacking model spec.

• 

Generalization between domains by showing that steering vectors from coding environments transfer to natural language reward hacking environments, similarly without negative effects to model capabilities.

Figure 1: We test four different interventions to reduce reward hacking in agentic coding environments. A small number of labeled rollouts is enough to provide latent space interventions that minimally perturb model representations. An anti-reward hacking model specification, or model spec, is also effective, and with a small number of rollouts we can use spec steering vectors to reduce misaligned behavior. Additionally, steering vectors from coding environments transfer to natural language domains.

## 2 Related Works

Reward Hacking is a failure mode in machine learning that occurs when a model achieves high reward on a proxy objective without achieving the actual outcome that the system designers intended for the model to pursue (Amodei et al., 2016). This is similar to goal misgeneralization, where the reward is correctly specified in distribution but the model learns a slightly different goal that is only visible under distribution shift in deployment. Unlike goal misgeneralization, reward hacking is visible in the training distribution itself. The danger comes when that hacking behavior is not caught and may also then cause the model to generalize to broader misalignment (Taylor et al., 2025; MacDiarmid et al., 2025), something which requires advances in monitoring to help catch. Earlier work treated it as a specification gaming problem (Krakovna et al., 2020) and later studies formalized it, showing that proxy reward functions are hackable except under restrictive conditions (Skalse et al., 2022; Karwowski et al., 2024). Current frontier systems exhibit this behavior in practice, including in agentic coding settings (Von Arx et al., 2025; Baker et al., 2025). Our method attempts to monitor for and mitigate this failure mode at inference time, without costly training updates or formal verification, similarly to concurrent work by Bergen et al. (2026).

Representation Engineering involves techniques that intervene on models’ latent spaces in order to achieve behavioral effects, through methods such as steering (Turner et al., 2023; Zou et al., 2023). Even if such techniques are imperfect (Tan et al., 2024), they have the advantage of being generally training-free, enabling finer and cheaper post-hoc control of models relative to the larger costs to train them more. Downstream work advances beyond applying interventions to all generated tokens uniformly, which is brittle to long contexts and distributional shifts, through scheduling or conditional approaches (Bharadwaj, 2025; Lee et al., 2024), or through activation capping (Lu et al., 2026). We provide a more detailed review in Appendix C, particularly characterizing representation engineering methods by their level of dependence on the hidden state.

Activation Monitoring research extends monitoring to the latent space, instead of relying purely on black-box monitors such as those focusing on models’ chain-of-thought (Korbak et al., 2025; Meek et al., 2025; Emmons et al., 2025) or action-only monitors (Sinha et al., 2026). Simple techniques such as building classification probes on model activations (Alain and Bengio, 2016) have been used in production systems to detect instances of misuse, such as cybercrime (Kramár et al., 2026). Similarly to other types of monitoring systems, it’s important to not expose safety monitors to optimization pressure as capable models can obfuscate their activations (McGuinness et al., 2025; Taufeeque et al., 2026). Our method does not train against latent space monitors, only using them during inference to cheaply redirect the model towards aligned behavior.

## 3 Methods

## 3.1 Data and experiment suite

We study reward hacking behavior using Qwen3.5-27B (Team, 2026) on ImpossibleBench (Zhong et al., 2025) and LiveCodeBench tasks (Jain et al., 2024), where the former is constructed of tasks from the latter but with test cases deliberately garbled such that models must reward hack to pass the test, such as by hard coding special answers for faulty test questions. Our rollout corpus consists of 103 agentic transcripts of the model, 42 of which result in a successful hack, pulled from the MisTrace dataset (Meek et al., 2026). These rollouts contain tool calls, large token allowances for thinking, and reach up to 120 turns; these rollouts take approximately 3 hours on average on an H200 GPU and reach roughly 80k tokens each, totaling 84 million tokens in total.

Text in each MisTrace rollout is grouped into segments of approximately sentence length. These segments span the model’s chain of thought, tool calls and their outputs, and normal output text. Segments in MisTrace are annotated as hacking or not by a GLM-5 judge (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026), calibrated against a human gold set of hack annotations at an F1 score of 0.784. In this work, we augment these labels by also annotating decline segments, also with a GLM-5 judge. Decline segments are instances where a model explicitly declines hacking, typically by accepting failing tests or rejecting potential workarounds. These were also labeled by a GLM-5 judge model. Full details regarding the dataset and labeling procedures, such as judge model prompts, can be found in Appendix J.3. In addition, we also augment the MisTrace dataset with action labels: a hack edit is a code-writing tool call (such as an edit to test.py or a shell command to do the same) that a GLM-5 judge labels as implementing a hack (prompt in Appendix J.2). Further information about the dataset splits can be found in Appendix A.

## 3.2 Model Spec Steering

Model specifications (specs) or constitutions, are detailed instructions describing how models should behave during deployment (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026). When narrower, custom model specs are used for specific domains, it becomes a mix of prompt engineering (Schulhoff et al., 2024) and constitutional AI approaches (Bai et al., 2022; Kundu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2024). Previously, anti-scheming model specs have been studied for reducing scheming behavior (Schoen et al., 2025). Here we study how well an anti-reward-hacking model spec reduces such behavior in the ImpossibleBench (Zhong et al., 2025) setting. Additionally, we then steer towards instances of the model referring to the spec during rollouts, and compare those against the other steering experiments.

We also use the model spec rollouts to extract model spec steering vectors. We test two methods: steering towards the mean activations over the spec itself, and steering towards references to the spec that the model makes as it reasons about the problem, over 73 sample tasks from MisTrace (Meek et al., 2026). Details about the dataset splits and labeling procedures can be found in Appendix A. The full model spec we append to the prompt and the judge prompt that we use to label spec references can be found in Appendix J.

More formally, let $\mathcal{R}$ be the set of rollouts which contain a sentence citing the spec, $S_{r}$ be the spec citing reasoning tokens, and $R_{r}$ be the remaining reasoning tokens on the same rollout. We remove the principle IDs from the vector construction, so that a model references ‘ARH1’ for ‘anti-reward-hacking principle 1’, does not cause the spec vector to collapse to that string representation. With $\mu(\cdot)$ being the mean residual stream activation from layer 35,

 $v_{\mathrm{spec}}=\frac{\bar{c}}{\|\bar{c}\|},\quad\bar{c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}}c_{r},\qquad c_{r}=\mu(C_{r})-\mu(R_{r}),$ 

(1)

We apply $v_{\mathrm{spec}}$ using the floor operator of Eq 8 in in Section 3.5, and with addition (Eq. 6) to provide a standard comparison.

## 3.3 Difference-in-Means Vectors

Construction.

We construct a difference-in-means probe for steering (Panickssery et al., 2023). We consider the two classes of segments, hack segment $S_{h}$ and decline segments $S_{d}.$ Each segment $s\in S_{h}\cup S_{d}$ is represented by the mean of its token activations, $\bar{h}_{s}$ , so all segments are given equal weight. We first contrast each class with its complement within a rollout. For a class $C\in\{h,d\}$ , let $\mu_{r}(S_{C})$ be the mean of $\bar{h}_{s}$ over the segments of rollout $r$ in $S_{C}$ , and $\mu_{r}(\neg S_{C})$ the mean over the rest of that rollout’s segments (all of them reasoning segments; see above). The class direction is the within-rollout difference, averaged over the training rollouts $R_{C}$ that contain at least one segment of $S_{C}$ :

 $v_{C}=\frac{1}{|R_{C}|}\sum_{r\in R_{C}}\big[\mu_{r}(S_{C})-\mu_{r}(\neg S_{C})\big].$ 

(2)

Each rollout is given equal weight. However, 5 of 24 training rollouts have no hack segments; these do not contribute to $v_{h}$ .
Letting $\hat{x}=x/\|x\|_{2}$ , the steering direction is

 $u=\frac{\hat{v}_{h}-\hat{v}_{d}}{\|\hat{v}_{h}-\hat{v}_{d}\|_{2}},$ 

(3)

where $u$ points in the “hacking" direction; negating it points in the “decline” direction.

Following this method, we construct a difference-in-means probe $u_{l}$ at every fourth layer $l\in\{3,7,\dots,63\}$ in our model. Probes are constructed using the train MisTrace set and evaluated for their ability to discriminate between hacking and decline segments against the validation set. For further details on probe construction and how we chose which layer to steer on, see Appendix D.

Probe as a monitor.

Before using our probe to steer, we first consider its use as a monitor by reading the per-token projections of the residual stream onto $u$ at layer 35, as in Figure 10. On inspection, one observation is that projections onto $u$ are particularly volatile in the period before hacking verbalization or hacking action. We consider the hypothesis that hacking segments are best anticipated not by the mean projection within some token window (characteristic of a sustained distributional shift along $u$ ), but rather by the maximum projection, consistent with acute spikes along our probe $u$ . We investigate this hypothesis in more detail in Appendix H.

Figure 2: Held-out reasoning in the plane of the approach-to-action axis $e$ and $u_{\perp e}$ , the component of $u$ orthogonal to $e$ . Left: segment mean activations. Right: mean path over the last 128 reasoning tokens before a tool call, for turns ending in a hacking edit (red), an honest submit (teal, ‘decline’), or neither (grey, ‘other’). Paths are smoothed with a causal EWMA (half-life $1.5\log_{2}d$ tokens, applied twice, $d$ = tokens before the call). Dots darken toward the call.

While the focus of this work is not monitoring, we encourage future activation monitoring work to study the predictive value of non-trivial activation dynamics, like volatility, or maximum activation, possibly seeking inspiration from other disciplines. However, the study of which temporal features are predictive of hacking motivates the use of particular causal interventions to mitigate hacking. In particular, in addition to more traditional activation addition, we also steer rollouts via activation capping, described in Section 3.5.

Hacking geometry.

We note that in the above construction, the hack vector $v_{h}$ and decline vector $v_{d}$ share a substantial component ( $\cos(v_{h},v_{d})=0.35$ ). Hacking and decline segments both generally mark a decision point in the model’s reasoning process, i.e., where the model has decided to complete the task by either submitting a failing solution or hacking the grader; both segment types also typically occur later in the reasoning turn, usually closely preceding a tool call. We call $s$ the component shared by $v_{h}$ and $v_{d}$ , which is orthogonal to $u$ by construction. One hypothesis is that $s$ is dominated by features related to ending the reasoning turn, pressure to complete the turn or task, and general task resolution.

This motivates the creation of an ‘approach to action’ feature $e$ , shown in Figure 2, with further details provided in Appendix G, where we also provide the top J-lens tokens for $u_{\perp e}$ , $e$ , and $s$ in Table 5 to provide a qualitative comparison.

## 3.4 Optimization Steering

Rather than constructing a steering direction directly from labeled activations, we can directly optimize a steering vector for the behavior we want to induce. Dunefsky and Cohan (2025) introduce optimization-based steering vectors, where a vector is trained to increase the likelihood of desired completions and decrease the likelihood of undesired completions.

We introduce three additions to their approach to make it better suited for our setting:

1. 

We optimize over a corpus of examples, rather than one vector per example.

2. 

We stop optimization on individual examples in the corpus when their loss reaches a set target, rather than the total loss over the corpus. This prevents a subset of examples from being optimized into incoherence.

3. 

We train through the cap from Eq. 7, so that the same operation is applied during training and inference.

Training data.

We construct training examples from reasoning segments labeled as reward hacking. For each segment, the hacking sentence serves as the suppressed completion, while the prompt consists of the most recent user message followed by the model’s reasoning in the current turn up to that sentence. Because full rollout histories can be prohibitively long for training, we omit intermediate messages, tool calls, and tool outputs, and discard examples whose resulting prompts still exceed our context-length limit. We additionally apply a second round of LLM judging to the original hacking labels (Appendix J.4). This is necessary because some segments labeled as hacking discuss or consider a potential hack without actually committing to it, including cases where the model ultimately rejects the hack. limitations: We have several limitations. First, due to computational constraints, we study reward hacking only on one model and one main testbed for agentic coding environments, even though we do test OOD generalization. Second, we use labels from an LLM judge. While the labels were calibrated against a human gold set, ultimately the number of rollouts that steering vectors were fit on was small due to the expense of collecting on-policy reward hacking behavior. Future work may elaborate on these constraints as well as our methods, as we only mitigate reward hacking along one direction in latent space, rather than ablating a more nuanced subspace.
conclusion:
Reward hacking in production systems has already proven itself to be a major issue and we expect that it will continue to increase in importance. Designing a perfect objective function during training, and monitoring for all instances that display reward hacking behavior and filtering them such that those rollouts are not trained on, is an extremely difficult problem. Here we study inference time mitigations to cheaply reduce the rate of reward hacking in deployment while reducing as much as possible any negative effects on model capabilities.

We find that we can easily monitor for reward hacking through difference-in-means probes. We can then use projections along this to steer only when it passes a specific threshold, a technique known as ‘activation capping’, to minimize perturbations to the model’s representations. This works well for steering vectors fit from a difference-in-means direction, vectors found through optimization, or the model spec steering vectors that we introduce. We also show generalization of these methods to reducing reward hacking in natural language domains, even though they were extracted from agentic coding environments. Future work can test these methods on model organisms trained for deception and probe evasion, or in settings with multi-agent swarm dynamics.

Ultimately we see our approach as a step towards better latent-space monitoring and control over production systems in realistic scenarios. Reward hacking is a fundamental issue in machine learning, and we cannot rely only on training-time safety techniques. A defense-in-depth approach across training and deployment will be very necessary.

title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven by Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence from Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul
abstract: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on tens of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries with per-leg reliability annotations through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi, the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts were measured for Baku and estimated for the other four cities, and the comparison involves a single baseline, so the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.

## 1 Introduction

Digital technology has reshaped how travelers discover, evaluate, and sequence the attractions of a destination, and the itinerary that a tourist actually follows is now, to a considerable degree, the output of an information system rather than of a guidebook. The day-trip design problem, in which a tourist arriving in an unfamiliar city must select a sequence of points of interest (POIs) and the transport options that connect them so as to balance experiential, monetary, temporal, and environmental criteria, has accordingly become one of the canonical applications of multi-criteria optimization (Gavalas et al., 2014; Vansteenwegen et al., 2011). Commercial planners such as TripAdvisor itineraries, Google Maps multi-stop routing, Sygic Travel, and Wanderlog, together with academic prototypes such as P-Tour (Maruyama et al., 2004), CT-Planner5 (Kurata et al., 2015), and PersTour (Lim et al., 2018), address this task with considerable sophistication. What they do not address is the uncertainty in the data on which every such planner relies.

That uncertainty has two sources. Routing services supply travel times that depend on the departure hour, the transport mode, and the recent traffic pattern, so that a single origin-destination-mode triple yields estimates that differ by a factor of two or more across the tourist-active day on congested corridors. Ratings carry uncertainty of a different kind: a POI with a mean of four and a half stars from five reviews carries less information than one with the same mean from five thousand, yet existing planners treat the two identically. A planner that ingests this evidence as crisp numbers discards the dimension of reliability that the evidence itself supplies. The Z-number formalism of Zadeh (2011) represents an uncertain quantity as an ordered pair of fuzzy numbers, a restriction on the value and a reliability on the assertion, and so separates by construction the magnitude of an estimate from the sufficiency of the evidence on which it rests. Z-number arithmetic and ranking have been developed in depth (Aliev et al., 2016b; Aliev et al., 2016a), but Z-numbers have rarely served as the substrate of a working trip planner whose parameters come from operational data rather than from linguistic judgments.

In the current research, we build such a planner and test it. Its travel-time Z-numbers are constructed from Google Routes observations (Google, 2026) at six departure hours, its rating Z-numbers from the platform rating and review count of each POI, and its itineraries are optimized under a hybrid loss and returned through a conversational interface with per-leg reliability annotations. The study pursues three objectives, which we state as research questions.

RQ1 

Can travel-time and rating Z-numbers be constructed from routing-service observations and review counts, without linguistic elicitation, and embedded in a working planner?

RQ2 

Under an identical optimizer, identical loss weights, and identical data, does the Z-number representation change the carbon footprint and the travel time of the selected itineraries relative to a crisp-mean representation of the same data?

RQ3 

How does any such effect vary across cities of contrasting geography, and which selection behavior accompanies it?

We answer these questions on five cities of contrasting urban form, Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, and we compare the planner, denoted ZN-Full, with a crisp-mean baseline (B1) at thirty seeds per city. Because the two methods compute their loss terms by different formulas, we do not compare them on the loss; we evaluate the itineraries they select on physical outcomes measured identically for both, namely the trip carbon footprint, the total travel time, the transport modes used, and the across-seed stability of the selected POIs.

The contributions of the paper are three. First, we specify data-driven construction operators that map routing observations and review counts to trapezoidal Z-numbers, a hybrid loss that combines them with crisp carbon and cost terms, and a two-step treatment of soft constraints, and we document a working implementation in sufficient detail for reproduction. Second, we report a seed-paired comparison on five cities with per-city tests under a Holm correction and pooled tests supplemented by a city-clustered bootstrap, as a check that the pooled conclusions do not depend on treating seeds from the same city as independent, and we document a full re-run of the experiment from the released bundle. Third, we characterize where the effect appears and where it does not, and we state plainly which parts of the evidence are measured and which are estimated. A companion study extends the comparison to five uncertainty representations on 349 POIs across the eight cities of the United Arab Emirates (Turaev et al., 2026); the present paper is the cross-national counterpart with a single baseline.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the related work. Section 3 presents the Z-number framework, and Section 4 the implemented system. Section 5 specifies the case-study design, Section 6 reports the results, Section 7 discusses them together with the limitations, and Section 8 concludes.

## 2 Related Work

## Academic trip planners.

P-Tour (Maruyama et al., 2004) allows a tourist to express preferences over time and POI categories and returns a sequenced itinerary that respects time windows. CT-Planner5 (Kurata et al., 2015) supports interactive tour planning that benefits both tourists and destinations, the team-orienteering variant is addressed by the greedy randomized adaptive search of Souffriau et al. (2008), and PersTour (Lim et al., 2018) personalizes POI recommendation from visit histories. Mobile and multimodal tour planners are surveyed and exemplified by Gavalas et al. (2014) and Gavalas et al. (2015), and the orienteering problem on which all of these systems rest is surveyed by Vansteenwegen et al. (2011). Two features of this body of work motivate the present study. Travel times are treated as crisp scalars, drawn from a static matrix or from a single routing call per leg, so the variation that routing services expose across the day is not represented; and ratings are reduced to a single mean per POI, so a POI with abundant evidence and one with sparse evidence are scored identically when their means coincide.

## Commercial planners.

TripAdvisor itineraries, Google Maps multi-stop routing, Sygic Travel, Visit-A-City, and Wanderlog operate at very large scale. Their user-facing output is crisp: a travel time is shown as a single number, and a rating as a single mean, with uncertainty acknowledged, if at all, through narrative hedges of the kind “traffic may be heavy”. Their optimization layers are undocumented, so we treat them as a reference for the user experience rather than as methodological baselines.

## Uncertainty in tourist routing.

Stochastic orienteering (Campbell et al., 2011; Evers et al., 2014) models travel and service times as random variables and optimizes an expected or chance-constrained objective, which requires a distributional assumption that a handful of routing observations does not support. Fuzzy formulations avoid that assumption: Ruiz-Meza et al. (2021) develop a multi-objective fuzzy trip-design model with sustainable itineraries, Expósito et al. (2019) propose a fuzzy GRASP for trip design with clustered POIs, and Derya et al. (2024) combine an intuitionistic fuzzy POI score with exponentially distributed travel times. None of these representations, however, holds the spread of a value apart from the amount of evidence behind it. The Z-number formalism does (Zadeh, 2011), and its continuous arithmetic (Aliev et al., 2016b), ranking (Aliev et al., 2016a), and conversion to classical fuzzy numbers (Kang et al., 2012) supply the operations a planner needs. To our knowledge, the Z-number literature on routing has relied on linguistically specified parameters, and the present work, together with its companion benchmark (Turaev et al., 2026), builds the parameters from operational data instead.

## 3 The Z-Number Framework

A Z-number is an ordered pair $\tilde{Z}=(\tilde{A},\tilde{B})$ of fuzzy numbers, in which $\tilde{A}$ is a restriction on the uncertain value and $\tilde{B}\subseteq[0,1]$ is the reliability with which the restriction is asserted (Zadeh, 2011). We work throughout with trapezoidal components $[a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}]$ , $a_{1}\leq a_{2}\leq a_{3}\leq a_{4}$ ; a triangular component is the case $a_{2}=a_{3}$ , and a crisp number the case $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}$ . Rating restrictions are triangular, reliabilities trapezoidal, and the monetary and carbon quantities crisp.

## 3.1 The travel-time construction operator

For an ordered origin-destination-mode triple, let $\mathcal{O}$ be the set of travel times returned by the routing service at the six departure hours 08:00, 10:30, 12:30, 14:30, 17:30, and 22:00, pooled over the primary and alternative routes returned at each hour. The operator $\Phi_{T}$ assigns the restriction

 $\tilde{A}_{T}(\mathcal{O})=\bigl[\,\tau_{(1)},\;Q_{0.25}(\mathcal{O}),\;Q_{0.75}(\mathcal{O}),\;\tau_{(|\mathcal{O}|)}\,\bigr],$ 

(1)

in which $\tau_{(1)}$ and $\tau_{(|\mathcal{O}|)}$ are the smallest and largest observations and $Q_{0.25}$ , $Q_{0.75}$ the empirical quartiles, and the reliability

 $\tilde{B}_{T}(N)=\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}+\frac{N-1}{N_{\max}-1}\,\bigl(\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{high}}-\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}\bigr),$ 

(2)

in which $N$ is the number of departure hours at which the triple was observed, $N_{\max}=6$ , $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}=[0.65,0.70,0.70,0.80]$ , and $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{high}}=[0.85,0.95,0.95,1.00]$ . The bounding trapezoids are design parameters of the implementation, fixed before the experiments reported here.

The restriction anchors its support at the observed extremes and its core at the inter-quartile range, so it inherits the empirical spread without a distributional assumption. The reliability reflects how consistently the triple is available across the day: a triple observed at all six hours receives $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{high}}$ , one observed at a single hour receives $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}$ , and intermediate cases interpolate linearly. Two properties follow directly from the definitions. When observations are added, the support $[\tau_{(1)},\tau_{(|\mathcal{O}|)}]$ can only widen and $N$ can only grow, so the support of the restriction and the reliability are both monotone under set inclusion; the inter-quartile core, by contrast, may move in either direction, so the restriction as a whole is not monotone.

## 3.2 The rating construction operator

For a POI with platform rating $\bar{s}\in[0,5]$ and review count $n\geq 0$ , the operator $\Phi_{R}$ assigns the triangular restriction

 $\tilde{A}_{R}(\bar{s},n)=\bigl[\,\max(0,\bar{s}-\delta(n)),\;\bar{s},\;\bar{s},\;\min(5,\bar{s}+\delta(n))\,\bigr],\qquad\delta(n)=\frac{\delta_{0}}{\sqrt{\max(1,n)}},$ 

(3)

whose spread decays with the square root of the review count in the manner of a standard error, and the reliability

 $\tilde{B}_{R}(n)=\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}^{R}+\bigl(1-e^{-n/n_{0}}\bigr)\bigl(\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{high}}^{R}-\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}^{R}\bigr),$ 

(4)

with $\delta_{0}=1.0$ , $n_{0}=100$ , $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{floor}}^{R}=[0.50,0.55,0.55,0.65]$ , and $\tilde{B}_{\mathrm{high}}^{R}=[0.85,0.95,0.95,1.00]$ . A POI with abundant evidence and one with sparse evidence are therefore no longer scored identically when their means coincide.

## 3.3 The hybrid loss functional

The planner minimizes

 $\mathcal{L}(\pi)=w_{s}L_{s}+w_{c}L_{c}+w_{t}L_{t}+w_{r}L_{r}+\lambda_{T}V_{T}+\lambda_{O}V_{O}+\lambda_{B}V_{B},$ 

(5)

in which $\pi$ is a candidate plan, that is, an ordered sequence of POIs together with the transport option chosen for each leg. The score term $L_{s}$ is a Hellinger-based distance from the trip’s aggregated rating Z-number to a reference Z-number at the rating ceiling with maximal reliability. The carbon term $L_{c}$ is crisp: the trip’s carbon footprint divided by that of the same POI sequence visited entirely by car, so that $L_{c}\in[0,1]$ . The travel-time term $L_{t}$ is a Hellinger-based distance from the trip’s aggregated total-time Z-number to the zero Z-number, normalized to the unit interval. The reliability term $L_{r}$ penalizes low reliability of the traversed legs. The terms $V_{T}$ , $V_{O}$ , and $V_{B}$ penalize violations of the total-time, opening-hours, and budget soft constraints. In all experiments $w_{s}=0.70$ , $w_{c}=0.20$ , $w_{t}=0.10$ , $w_{r}=0.10$ , and $\lambda_{T}=\lambda_{O}=\lambda_{B}=1$ . The carbon and budget terms use ordinary arithmetic, since emission factors and prices are calibrated values rather than observed random quantities. The crisp baseline of Section 5 replaces $L_{s}$ by one minus the ratio of the visited rating sum to an ideal sum and $L_{t}$ by the fraction of the time window spent traveling, and it has no reliability term; the loss values of the two methods are therefore not comparable, and we compare the itineraries instead.

## 3.4 The two-step violation pattern

The total-time and opening-hours constraints compare Z-number aggregates with crisp thresholds. We separate the decision that a constraint is violated from the magnitude of the violation. The decision is taken by a ranking comparison (Aliev et al., 2016a) on the restriction alone, so that two plans whose restrictions agree are treated identically at this step whatever their reliabilities. Only when the decision is “violated” is a magnitude computed, as the Hellinger-based distance between the aggregate and the nearest feasible Z-number, with the reliability reintroduced. The penalty is therefore graded by the extent of the breach rather than imposed as an all-or-nothing indicator. We note that the experiments reported here do not isolate the effect of this pattern, since both methods use it.

## 3.5 The min- $\tilde{B}$ reliability rule

Exact reliability aggregation under Z-number addition (Aliev et al., 2016b) requires a family of optimization problems per aggregation, and in our implementation it costs between fifty and one hundred times as much as the rest of an optimization step. During search the planner therefore aggregates reliabilities by the min- $\tilde{B}$ rule, which assigns to the reliability of a sum the componentwise minimum of the operands’ reliabilities,

 $\tilde{B}_{1+2}=\bigl[\min(b_{1}^{1},b_{1}^{2}),\,\min(b_{2}^{1},b_{2}^{2}),\,\min(b_{3}^{1},b_{3}^{2}),\,\min(b_{4}^{1},b_{4}^{2})\bigr].$ 

(6)

The rule is a heuristic summary of the least reliable component of a plan, and it should not be read as a bound. In particular, it is not in general a lower bound on the reliability that the exact arithmetic assigns to the sum and can overstate it, since the evidence for a sum of uncertain quantities is in general weaker than the evidence for its weakest summand. The rule preserves the ordering of plans that differ in their least reliable leg, which is what the search requires of it, but the trip-level reliability it reports describes the weakest leg rather than certifying the plan. The experiments reported here do not compare the rule with the exact aggregation, and all reported reliabilities are min- $\tilde{B}$ summaries.

## 4 The Trip Planner System

The system is organized as a four-layer pipeline: data ingestion, Z-number construction, optimization, and user interface. The layers communicate through caches, so that ingestion runs on a slow, cost-aware schedule while the optimizer serves requests from cached data.

## Data ingestion.

For the POI pairs of a city, the ingestion layer first queries the free OSRM table service for road distance
limitations: Seven limitations scope the findings. First, review counts are measured only for Baku; for the other sixty POIs they are estimates, so the rating Z-numbers outside Baku rest on approximate evidence. Second, the comparison involves a single crisp-mean baseline and no ablation, so it shows that the Z-number representation as a whole changes the selected plans but not which of its components is responsible. Third, each catalog holds fifteen POIs, and larger catalogs, which the system supports, may behave differently. Fourth, only one scenario is reported, a ten o’clock start with an eight-hour window and at most seven POIs. Fifth, the pooled inference rests on five cities; the city-clustered bootstrap confirms the sign of the pooled effects but is coarse with so few clusters. Sixth, the routing data are a single snapshot, the cache lacks a fifth of the drive and transit options requested in Tashkent and Abu Dhabi, and the walking legs rest on OSRM tables frozen in October 2026, which differ from those of the original runs in Baku and Istanbul. Seventh, the evaluation is computational: we did not study whether tourists understand, trust, or follow the reliability annotations, which is the question on which the practical value of an evidence-aware planner ultimately depends. The min- $\tilde{B}$ reliability summaries, finally, are heuristic rather than guaranteed (Section 3.5).

title: Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoding of Sperm Whale Coda
abstract: Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.

body_start:
Abstract

Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) communicate through short click sequences called codas, whose structure includes the rhythmic pattern of inter-click intervals (ICI) and the spectral composition of the clicks. In this paper, we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which explicitly encodes rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders before fusing them. We evaluate DCCE on three coda-understanding tasks: social unit, coda type, and individual identification. We compare DCCE against strong baselines from literature under a common linear-probe protocol and analyze the role of each channel and training objective through ablations. On 1,383 codas, shared partitions and validation-only layer selection support three random splits and three recording-date-disjoint folds. DCCE with unit pairing and type supervision achieves mean random-split macro-F1 of 0.901/0.865/0.597 for unit/type/identity. Raw ICI remains strongest for type (0.987), and ICI plus temporal mel statistics is a strong identity reference (0.724). An auxiliary identity objective improves spectral-branch identity prediction but does not improve the mean fused-identity score in this configuration. Date-grouped evaluation and four year holdouts expose generalization limits. The results support task-dependent combinations of timing and spectral information, without establishing independent biological channels or general architectural superiority. Code, notebooks, and complete results are available at https://dcce-research-site.vercel.app.

Index Terms: 

Sperm whale codas, contrastive learning, bioacoustics, representation learning, individual identification

João Victor Quintanilha†,  Emma Virnelli†,  Shuo Zhang

Tufts University, Medford, MA, USA

Joao.Quintanilha@tufts.edu, Emma.Virnelli@tufts.edu, Shuo.Zhang@tufts.edu

## 1 Introduction

Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) live in stable, matrilineal family units that belong to vocal clans, each clan sharing a distinct vocal dialect [1, 2]. That dialect is built from codas: short, stereotyped sequences of clicks that whales exchange during social contact. Deciphering what codas encode is a central goal of computational bioacoustics and of the Cetacean Translation Initiative [1, 3]. The rhythm channel, the pattern of inter-click intervals (ICIs), contributes to coda type: a category defined by click count and timing [2, 4]. The spectral channel, the frequency content within each click, includes vowel- and diphthong-like patterns [5, 6]. The analogy to human voice motivates asking which features distinguish callers, without assuming that the two channels are independent.

The individual signal in a coda depends both on the coda type produced and on the set of whales one compares against. Gero et al. [2] make these two dependencies concrete: discriminant analysis of 5R1 timing classified individuals within units J, U, and F at 73%, 78%, and 83% accuracy, respectively, but at 46% when individuals across units were pooled. The 1+1+3 type did not reliably discriminate individuals within units. Recovering who produced a coda therefore depends on which coda was produced and on how large and diverse the candidate pool is.

In this paper we propose the Dual-Channel Contrastive Encoder (DCCE), which learns a representation of sperm whale codas by encoding rhythm and spectral information with separate encoders followed by a fusion layer. Our guiding question is: does encoding rhythm and spectral texture as separate input channels, rather than learning implicitly from one input representation, improve what a model can learn from sperm whale codas? The study contributes a dual-input architecture, matched supervision and channel ablations, and an evaluation of recording-context generalization.

## 2 Related Work

Coda structure and identity. In the notation of Gero et al. [2], 5R1 denotes a five-click, regularly spaced type, while 1+1+3 groups five clicks into one, one, and three. Sharma et al. [4] showed that rhythm, tempo, rubato, and ornamentation yield at least 143 frequently realized combinations. Beguš et al. [5] identified vowel- and diphthong-like spectral patterns; subsequent work reports interactions between vowel quality and conventional coda type [6]. Bermant et al. [7] already investigated neural sperm whale classification, including individual identity.

Learned models for cetacean audio. WhAM [3] provides a sperm-whale-specific reference, learning acoustic-token representations whose downstream classification ability is evaluated by probing. Broader bioacoustic references are AVES [8] and BirdNET [9]. Tolkova et al. [10] applied BirdNET embeddings to individual identification using 234 upcalls of 11 North Atlantic right whales at three sites.

Representation-learning lineages. Self-supervised audio models such as wav2vec 2.0 [11] and HuBERT [12] demonstrate learning speech representations from unlabeled audio. SimCLR uses the NT-Xent objective [13], while CLIP learns aligned representations across image and text inputs [14]. Finally, the speaker-verification lineage motivates mapping variable-length acoustic input to identity-relevant vectors: i-vectors and x-vectors provide statistical and neural approaches [15, 16], and metric-learning studies examine alternatives to classification losses [17]. These precedents motivate the design, but neither establish its superiority on codas nor turn our closed-set ID task into open-set speaker verification.

## 3 Methodology

We frame coda understanding as a representation-learning problem: given a coda, DCCE learns a single fixed-dimensional embedding from timing and spectral inputs, and we measure how much task-relevant structure that embedding captures with lightweight linear probes. Figure 1 summarizes the design. DCCE is trained by combining a contrastive objective on $z$ with optional auxiliary classification losses on the branches.

Fig. 1: DCCE: separate input encoders, fusion, and optional branch objectives. Positive-pair construction varies across conditions. The linear probe is trained after freezing the representation.

## 3.1 Rhythm Encoder

The rhythm of a coda is captured by its sequence of inter-click intervals (ICIs): the elapsed times, in seconds, between consecutive clicks. A coda of $k$ clicks yields $k-1$ ICIs; since the codas in our data contain up to ten clicks, each coda has at most nine ICIs. Annotated ICIs are zero-padded on the right and standardized using training examples only. A two-layer GRU with hidden size 64 and inter-layer dropout 0.2 reads the sequence one ICI at a time; a linear projection and layer normalization map its final hidden state to $r\in\mathbb{R}^{64}$ . We choose a compact recurrent encoder for these short sequences and the small dataset.

## 3.2 Spectral Encoder

The spectral channel is derived from a log-mel-spectrogram of the coda audio. Each recording is converted to mono and resampled to 48 kHz; native rates are 44.1, 48, 96, and 120 kHz. A short-time Fourier transform uses a 2,048-sample Hann window and a 1,152-sample hop, mapped onto 64 mel bands spanning 0–8 kHz. Log power is peak-relative, clipped to 80 dB, padded at the minimum level to a fixed $64\times 256$ representation, and transformed by $x_{\mathrm{dB}}/40+1$ . No mel input is truncated.

Three convolutional blocks (Conv2d–BatchNorm–ReLU–MaxPool, with 16, 32, and 64 channels) use $3\times 3$ kernels and $2\times 2$ pooling to reduce the input to a $64\times 8\times 32$ feature map. The flattened output passes through dropout 0.3 and a two-layer MLP with layer normalization to $s\in\mathbb{R}^{64}$ . The full-coda spectrogram retains temporal structure, so this branch is not restricted to within-click identity cues.

## 3.3 Fusion MLP

We concatenate $r$ and $s$ , then apply LayerNorm, Linear(128,64), ReLU, and Linear(64,64) to obtain $z$ . Embeddings are normalized inside the contrastive loss. Primary probes use the saved fusion output; separate branch probes are post-hoc diagnostics.

## 3.4 Training Objective

The objective combines NT-Xent [13] with optional weighted cross-entropies for type on $r$ and identity on $s$ . The type head encourages the rhythm branch to retain coda-type information rather than only unit-level structure. The ID head encourages individual discrimination, following the use of identity-classification supervision for speaker embeddings [16]:

 $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NTXent}}+0.5a_{T}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{type}}+0.5a_{I}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ID}},$ 

(1)

where $a_{T},a_{I}\in\{0,1\}$ . Inverse-frequency class weights are computed from training counts only; ineligible identity labels are masked. For positive views $i,j$ , the contrastive term uses

 $\ell(i,j)=-\log\frac{\exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp(\operatorname{sim}(z_{i},z_{k})/\tau)},\qquad\tau=0.07,$ 

(2)

with cosine similarity and a symmetric average over positive pairs. Assigning different auxiliary tasks to the branches encourages discriminative features but does not enforce statistical independence.

## 3.5 Positive-Pair Construction

The primary construction pairs distinct training codas $A,B$ from the same social unit: $f(r_{A},s_{A})$ and $f(r_{B},s_{B})$ . This uses unit supervision. Actual channel swapping instead pairs $f(r_{A},s_{B})$ and $f(r_{B},s_{A})$ . Without unit pairing, positives are independently augmented views of the same coda. Other batch views act as negatives, including possible same-unit examples; the objective is not a full supervised-contrastive treatment of all same-unit codas.

Each view masks a random four-bin frequency band and eight-frame time band, and adds Gaussian noise of SD 0.01 to standardized ICI entries corresponding to nonzero raw intervals. Padded intervals retain their standardized values. All main DCCE conditions use uniform shuffled sampling, 50 epochs of AdamW (learning rate $10^{-3}$ , weight decay $10^{-4}$ ), cosine decay, and batch size 64. Temperature, auxiliary weights, sampling, and optimizer settings were fixed for this exploratory batch, not validation-tuned.

## 3.6 DCCE Variants

We denote unit pairing, type loss, and ID loss by U/T/I; three binary digits specify their presence. The main pair, DCCE 110 versus 111, differs only in ID loss. Both are task-informed models: absence of ID loss does not mean absence of supervision. We tested all eight U/T/I settings; selected contrasts are reported here, including 000, which removes task labels from the representation objective and sampler, but retains annotated ICI and supervised downstream probing.

Rhythm-only and spectrum-only controls apply both auxiliary heads to the available branch, with the same coefficients. Joint concatenation produces 128 dimensions without the fusion MLP; it is not independently trained late fusion. These architectures are evaluated with and without ID loss. Additional conditions test actual swapping and a 16-kHz mel ceiling; the latter also changes filter spacing at fixed band count.

## 3.7 Linear Probe Evaluation

All encoder weights are frozen after training. Balanced logistic regression predicts social unit, coda type, or individual ID. Features are standardized on training data, with fixed $C=1$ and at most 2,000 iterations. WhAM/AVES layers are selected per task using validation macro-F1 only, with earliest-layer tie breaking; BirdNET provides one representation. There is no training-plus-validation refit. Neural checkpoints use a fixed final epoch.

## 4.1 Dataset and Evaluation Protocol

The dataset used in our experiment consists of 1,501 audio recordings from the Dominica Sperm Whale Project (DSWP) public HuggingFace release (orrp/DSWP) [3]. After excluding 118 noise-flagged files, 1,383 clean codas remain, spanning three social units (A, D, F) and 22 coda types. Labels (social unit, coda type, individual ID) are reconstructed from DominicaCodas.csv, using its codaNUM2018 index to match DSWP file indices. Reconstructed metadata place these codas in 2005–2010 and clan EC1. ID evaluation uses 754 codas from 11 individuals: 620 unknown-ID codas, eight ambiguous two-individual annotations, and one identified singleton are excluded from ID training/probing, while remaining eligible for other tasks. Severe class imbalance (unit F contributes 821/1,383 codas, or 59.4%) motivates macro-F1 and balanced class weights. All tasks share the same coda partition, keeping every locally trained representation separate from its test examples.

We use three random splits (seeds 0–2), approximately 64/16/20% train/validation/test, stratifying eligible identities and otherwise unit. Recording-date splits use the first three outer folds (indices 0–2) of a five-fold stratified-group partition (shuffle seed 0), with grouped validation partitions. Dates are session proxies. Four additional year holdouts exclude the test year completely; validation uses a date-grouped fold from the remaining years, and neural seed is fixed at 0.

Primary macro-F1 averages over true test classes observed in training, on supported examples. Grouped ID support is 186/213, 111/121, and 145/145 eligible examples, spanning three, six, and six scored identities. Thus random/grouped ID scores describe different supported populations. Full-eligible secondary scores include unseen classes. We report means and sample SD over three runs, not confidence intervals.

The design is exploratory: earlier unit-balanced experiments informed these comparisons, and year/input-matched controls followed partial main results. Earlier training-regime scores are not pooled with the matched uniform-sampling ablations.

## 4.2 DCCE vs. Baselines

We evaluate three literature-grounded baselines under the same splits and linear-probe protocol as DCCE: WhAM, AVES, and BirdNET. Fixed references are raw ICI, temporal mel means/std within four valid-frame bins (512 dimensions), and their concatenation (521 dimensions). Temporal binning retains coarse timing that a single time-averaged mel vector would discard. Frozen WhAM, AVES, and BirdNET are evaluated both alone and concatenated with ICI. These last controls match timing-input availability, with only probes trained locally.

Pretrained frontends retain native procedures: AVES at 16 kHz over the full segment; the released WhAM codec at 44.1 kHz with mono/loudness processing; BirdNET at 48 kHz with a three-second window. Three waveforms exceed that window.

Supervised AVES adaptation updates the projection and all 12 transformer blocks, keeping the waveform CNN frozen. Unit/type/ID loss weights are 1/0.5/0.5, with uniform sampling. Ten fixed AdamW epochs use backbone/head rates $2\times 10^{-5}/10^{-3}$ , weight decay $10^{-4}$ , microbatches of four accumulated to 64, and clip gradients at 1. Labels are comparable in availability, but objectives, capacity, pretraining, and budgets remain different.

limitations:
Following our analysis, a key limitation is the dataset itself: a single Dominica population with three social units, all from the EC1 clan. Another restriction is that there are no vowel annotations for the 1,383 codas evaluated here: the available hand-annotated vowel metadata covers different coda identifiers. The spectral branch is trained through the fused contrastive objective and optional ID classification, not explicit phonological categories.

Annotated ICI is additional information unavailable to a waveform-only system. Closed-set ID tests do not establish recognition of unseen animals or communicative meaning. Sparse identity coverage and three runs limit precision; recording dates are not verified sessions.

WhAM’s published training uses DSWP+CETI [3], and this evaluation also uses DSWP. Exact checkpoint training membership is unavailable, so local holdouts do not establish external pretraining independence. The exploratory design and heterogeneous model histories further limit causal or universal comparisons.

title: UNIVERS: Learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization
abstract: One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

body_start:
Abstract

One-shot landmark localization in volume scans with varying fields of view (FOVs) is challenging. While existing self-supervised learning methods have shown promising performance, they rely on contrastive learning built upon augmented views of the same image, which inherently limits their generalization in cross-modality scenarios. This motivates research on cross-modality embedding learning using paired multi-modality images. However, existing methods suffer from not only limited training data, but also the requirement of multi-stage iterative training. To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. Our framework leverages diverse pseudo-data synthesized from organ shape templates, with randomization applied to semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. Coupled with cross-domain discriminative voxel-wise contrastive learning, this domain randomization strategy forces the network to disregard domain-specific biases and learn features that are robust against variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Consequently, the trained model enables one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs. In this study, the efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated by applying it to the task of localizing the adrenal glands, which are paired, small, and irregular endocrine organs. In particular, comprehensive experiments are conducted on three challenging adrenal gland datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that UNIVERS consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art (SOTA) one-shot landmark localization approaches, with particularly prominent advantages in cross-modality scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/UNIVERS.

Index Terms: 
Domain randomization, contrastive learning, generalizable landmark matching, adrenal localization

## I Introduction

The adrenal glands are paired, small, irregular endocrine organs located superior to both kidneys [1]. By secreting essential hormones, they play vital roles in regulating stress response, metabolism, electrolyte homeostasis, and sympathetic nervous system [2, 3]. Adrenal disorders, such as adrenal hyperplasia and adrenal tumor, are frequently encountered in routine radiological imaging [4]. Such abnormalities can disrupt hormonal balance, resulting in hypertension and other hormone-related symptoms [5]. Computer-aided interpretation of adrenal imaging offers a noninvasive and effective approach, playing an increasingly critical role in the clinical management of adrenal-related diseases. Due to the extremely small size of the adrenal glands, precise localization of their centers in volumetric medical images becomes an essential preprocessing step for many downstream computer-aided tasks, such as adrenal segmentation [3] and lesion classification [6]. Existing landmark localization methods mostly rely on supervised learning [7, 8], which requires large amounts of manually annotated training data. Unfortunately, annotating medical images is laborious, costly, and requires clinical expertise.

To reduce the annotation burden, recent research has shifted towards one-shot landmark localization, which requires only a single annotated support image to identify corresponding landmarks in query images [9, 10, 11, 12]. An emerging paradigm to find such landmark correspondences is achieved by learning discriminative voxel-wise anatomical embeddings. Typically, two augmented, overlapping views are extracted from the same image and fed into a Siamese network to generate voxel-wise embeddings. Then, self-supervised contrastive learning is applied, which encourages corresponding voxels across the two views to have similar embeddings while pushing non-corresponding voxels apart in the embedding space. Given the anatomical structural consistency, the learned embeddings map corresponding landmarks to similar feature representations. Consequently, annotations from a single support image can be transferred to query images via feature similarity matching. Building on this concept, several strategies have been proposed to enhance landmark localization performance, including negative sampling [10], coarse-to-fine architectures [9, 10, 11], and semantic embedding learning [12]. More recently, Universal Anatomical Embedding (UAE-M) [12] has extended this line of work to cross-modality landmark matching between Computed Tomography (CT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). This method learns voxel correspondences across unaligned multi-modality images via an iterative training process.

Despite significant progress, several limitations persist. First, most existing methods [9, 10, 11] build upon the heuristic that corresponding voxels across augmented views of the same image should yield similar embeddings, while their training is restricted to single-modality data. As a result, these methods struggle to match corresponding anatomical structures across multi-modality images. Second, while UAE-M [12] addresses cross-modality landmark matching, it relies on paired multi-modality images of the same subject. Such image pairs are usually unaligned across modalities, necessitating multi-stage iterative training to establish reliable voxel correspondences. More importantly, existing methods [9, 10, 11, 12] rely heavily on real clinical images, yet it is challenging, if not impossible, to collect large-scale multi-modality datasets. Accordingly, networks are exposed to a limited spectrum of domain variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, spatial resolution, field of view (FOV), and patient pose. Such insufficient data diversity results in suboptimal feature representations that lack robustness to large domain shifts in real clinical scenarios.

To address these limitations, we propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis for generalizable one-shot landmark localization. Instead of relying on real training images, our learning process utilizes synthetic data generated from organ shape templates, where randomization is introduced in semantic layout, visual appearance, FOV, and spatial pose. This strategy exposes the network to a wide range of variability during contrastive learning, forcing it to learn features that are robust to variations in imaging contrast, resolution, and spatial context. Discriminative voxel-wise embedding learning is then achieved via a Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, which encourages the voxel-wise discriminability of domain-invariant features amidst contextual variations. During inference, UNIVERS relies exclusively on anatomical structural consistency to distinguish voxels, generating domain-invariant voxel-wise embeddings for real clinical images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. UNIVERS achieves superior performance compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods under three one-shot evaluation settings: intra-dataset, cross-dataset intra-modality, cross-dataset cross-modality. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We propose UNIVERS, an end-to-end trainable framework for learning UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to learn generalizable, discriminative voxel-wise embeddings exclusively from pseudo-data synthesized via domain randomization.

• 

We design a novel Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, which operates on multi-domain pseudo-patch quadruplets with multiple positives to drive the network toward learning domain-invariant and discriminative embeddings.

• 

We develop a coarse-to-fine one-shot adrenal gland localization framework built upon a single frozen UNIVERS network, which enables landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans with arbitrary FOVs.

• 

We conduct comprehensive experiments under three one-shot settings across three distinct datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed UNIVERS consistently outperforms the SOTA approaches.

## II Related work

## II-A One-shot landmark localization

To mitigate the annotation burden, one-shot landmark localization has garnered increasing research interest. Traditional solutions rely on image registration to establish voxel correspondences, typically employing a two-stage alignment pipeline: a global affine or rigid transformation [13] followed by a deformable registration [14, 15, 16]. By deriving a deformation field that warps the query image into the support image space, registration methods can propagate support landmarks to the query image. However, such methods often incur high computational costs and struggles with large inter-subject variations, including anatomical deformations and FOV shifts.

Alternatively, a growing body of work has explored embedding-learning-based paradigms on 3D CT images [9, 10, 11, 12]. These methods seek to learn discriminative voxel-wise embeddings, so that corresponding landmarks between the support and query images can be matched based on feature similarity. A representative framework is Self-supervised Anatomical eMbedding (SAM) [10], which employs a coarse-to-fine architecture and designs a hard and diverse sampling strategy for effective negative selection. However, SAM primarily captures contextual appearance information and lacks explicit semantic understanding, which hinders its ability to differentiate organs with similar appearances. This limitation motivated UAE-S [12], which extends SAM with an additional semantic head trained via a prototypical supervised contrastive loss. Another line of work is Localize Anything Model for 3D Medical images (MedLAM) [11], which introduces unified anatomical mapping and multi-scale similarity learning. To estimate landmark localization, it applies Relative Position Regression (RPR) [9] followed by multi-scale feature similarity matching. Despite these advances, these methods are trained on datasets within the same modality and contrast voxels across augmented views of the same image, inherently limiting their generalization across heterogeneous imaging domains.

To enable landmark matching in cross-modality scenarios, UAE-M [12] extends the embedding-learning-based paradigm to CT-MRI settings via a two-stage learning process. At the first stage, a modality-agnostic network is trained on single-modality images with strong contrast augmentation. Subsequently, at the second stage, this modality-agnostic network initializes an iterative training process, which alternates between learning cross-modality embeddings from aligned multi-modality images and performing cross-modality registration to align those images. Despite its success, UAE-M relies on computationally expensive multi-stage iterative training to establish robust voxel correspondences between CT and MR images. By contrast, our method offers a simple, end-to-end trainable framework that learns domain-invariant voxel-wise embeddings from a distinct perspective by training on synthetic data generated via domain randomization.

## II-B Domain randomization for medical image analysis

Domain-randomization-based generative models aim to bridge all domain gaps via extreme augmentation beyond realism, eliminating the need for real training images [17, 18]. These methods fully randomize generation parameters to produce highly diverse training data, forcing networks to learn domain-independent features. For brain segmentation, methods like SynthSeg [19] use visually diverse pseudo-images synthesized from brain label maps to train networks, which can be applied to real brain MR scans across multiple domains without retraining. This paradigm has subsequently been extended to other segmentation tasks, including vascular structures [20], cell nuclei [21], and abdominal organs [22]. For image registration, SynthMorph [23] proposed a generative strategy to produce diverse synthetic label maps and images, enabling networks to learn contrast-invariant registration. In the realm of representation learning, Anatomix [24] proposed a data engine that randomizes the spatial configuration of organ shape templates to create paired image samples with distinct appearances. These samples then train a network robust to nuisance imaging variations that do not alter image semantics. However, none of these works were designed for generalizable one-shot landmark localization. This task imposes a unique requirement: each voxel must be encoded with a discriminative embedding that sets it apart from other anatomical regions. Learning such universal discriminative voxel-wise embeddings is the core focus of our work, which is not directly addressed by existing domain-randomization-based methods.

## III Method

## III-A Learning universal voxel-wise embedding

Fig. 1: A schematic overview of UNIVERS. (a) We construct an image pair database and a patch quadruplet database from shape templates. (b) UNIVERS consists of a shared CNN encoder with a Domain-invariant Discriminative (DD) decoder and a Domain-invariant Semantic (DS) decoder. During training, patch quadruplets are randomly sampled to train the DD decoder via a Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss, while image pairs are randomly sampled to optimize the DS decoder via a Cross-domain Prototypical Semantic Contrastive (CPSC) loss. (c) During inference, UNIVERS can generate Domain-invariant Voxel-wise (DV) embeddings for multi-modality volumes with arbitrary FOVs. Embeddings are reduced to 3 dimensions via PCA and visualized as RGB images. RGA: Random Geometric Augmentation. Embed.: Embedding.

UNIVERS learns domain-invariant voxel-wise embeddings without requiring any real training images. For training, we rely solely on freely available organ shape templates from the TotalSegmentator CT dataset [25], which comprises 1,204 volumes with 104 annotated anatomical structures, to synthesize pseudo-training data. To encode precise location information for each voxel, UNIVERS is designed to acquire both high-level semantic understanding to distinguish different organs and low-level discriminative capacity to differentiate adjacent structures. To this end, we generate two specific types of pseudo-data, forming an image pair database and a patch quadruplet database (see Fig. 1-(a)). Each image pair consists of two pseudo-images that share a randomized semantic layout but differ in appearance, thereby facilitating domain-invariant semantic feature learning. In contrast, each patch quadruplet is derived from an image pair and comprises four overlapping pseudo-patches with distinct FOVs and spatial poses, encouraging local discriminability amidst varying contexts. UNIVERS then employs a dual-decoder network design: it comprises a shared Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) encoder with a Domain-invariant Semantic (DS) decoder and a Domain-invariant Discriminative (DD) decoder (see Fig. 1-(b)). The DS decoder is optimized on the image pairs by leveraging a Cross-domain Prototypical Semantic Contrastive (CPSC) loss, while the DD decoder is trained with the patch quadruplets and supervised via a Cross-domain Discriminative Voxel-wise Contrastive (CDVC) loss.

## III-A1 Data generation

For training data, we first build the image pair database, based on which we further construct the patch quadruplet database.

Image pair generation. Randomized image pairs with rich semantic layouts and appearances are synthesized from shape templates via a data engine (see Fig. 1-(a1)). Following the pipeline introduced in [24], the data engine first creates diverse randomized label maps with a fixed size of $S_{I}\times S_{I}\times S_{I}$ voxels using randomly sampled templates. For each randomized label map $\mathcal{M}$ , it then synthesizes two pseudo-images, $I^{1}$ and $I^{2}$ , which share an identical semantic layout but exhibit distinct appearances, effectively simulating aligned scans from two different domains. Such image synthesis involves sampling intensities from Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) with randomized parameters, followed by intensity and geometric augmentations. To preserve semantic alignment while maximizing appearance variance within an image pair, intensity augmentations are applied independently to $I^{1}$ and $I^{2}$ , whereas geometric augmentations are shared. These pseudo-data constitutes the image pair database $\{(I^{1},I^{2}|\mathcal{M})\}$ .

Patch quadruplet generation. Randomized patch quadruplets with diverse FOVs and spatial poses are generated from the randomized image pairs. Specifically, to construct a patch quadruplet, we first randomly sample an image pair $(I^{1},I^{2})$ , where $I^{1}$ and $I^{2}$ are spatially aligned. We then extract two patches from each image— $P_{1}^{1}$ and $P_{2}^{1}$ from $I^{1}$ , and $P_{1}^{2}$ and $P_{2}^{2}$ from $I^{2}$ . As shown in Fig. 1-(a2), we propose two distinct patch quadruplet generation pipelines that separately simulate different sources of spatial variation, and randomly select one per quadruplet:

• 

Random cropping pipeline: This pipeline predominantly simulates patches with large FOV variations. Each patch is randomly cropped from an image at a random location with a random size of $S_{R}\times S_{R}\times S_{R}$ voxels, where $S_{R}$ is sampled from a uniform distribution $U(S_{L},S_{U})$ . Here $S_{L}$ and $S_{U}$ respectively denote the lower bound and the upper bound of $S_{R}$ , which are constrained to ensure that the four cropped patches spatially overlap (see Section III-C for detailed parameter values). All patches are subsequently resized to $S_{P}\times S_{P}\times S_{P}$ voxels.

• 

Random geometric augmentation pipeline: This pipeline primarily simulates patches with large spatial pose variations.
conclusion: In this paper, we proposed an end-to-end trainable framework that learns UNIversal Voxel-wise Embedding via Randomized Synthesis, referred to as UNIVERS, for generalizable one-shot landmark localization in multi-modality volume scans of arbitrary FOVs. For model training, a domain-randomization-based data generation strategy was delicately designed to synthesize pseudo-image pairs and pseudo-patch quadruplets covering a wide range of appearances and spatial contexts. Built upon these pseudo-training data, a cross-domain voxel-wise discriminative contrastive learning strategy was then introduced to establish a domain-invariant embedding space that enables effective differentiation of anatomical structures. For accurate adrenal center localization at inference time, a coarse-to-fine one-shot localization framework was further developed by integrating a single frozen UNIVERS network. Extensive experiments across three challenging datasets, conducted under three one-shot settings with increasing difficulty, consistently demonstrated the superior performance of UNIVERS over the SOTA methods. These findings validate the strong generalization capacity of the proposed framework and position UNIVERS as a promising approach for one-shot landmark localization in real clinical applications.
