title: Agentic Music Post-Production
abstract: We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song. A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix. In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge. We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.

body_start:
Abstract

We introduce MixAgent, an agentic pipeline for music post-production that follows the workflow of audio engineers to build interpretable and editable mixing plans guided by a reference song.
A grouping agent first routes related input tracks, such as drum recordings, into subgroups. A planning agent then uses retrieved examples to choose and order audio effects, such as volume control and reverb, for tracks, subgroups, and the full mix. To refine the mix, a detector identifies what needs correction, and a critic proposes numerical parameter adjustments from tracks to the full mix.
In our experiments, prompting recent multimodal models to listen and revise often worsens the mix, making reliable correction a central challenge.
We therefore build MixCritic, a dataset of 45,657 repair critiques derived from parameters fitted to professional mixes, and train the critic with supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization on rendered audio outcomes. On MedleyDB, learned refinement reduces error by 19% relative to the initial mix, with preference optimization reducing it by 8.4% over supervised training alone. Retrieved examples further improve effects selection, and a human listening test shows that MixAgent gets higher quality ratings than mixes produced by Qwen3-Omni, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-4o-audio.

## 1 Introduction

Language-model agents use tools to write code (Yang et al., 2024) and edit images (Ye et al., 2026). In creative software, a key challenge is turning a high-level goal into precise settings.
Noticing that “the vocal is too quiet” does not specify which control to move or by how much. Music mixing combines separately recorded instruments and vocals (input tracks) into a song by applying audio effects that control volume, frequency balance, and acoustic space.
Related tracks can also be processed together as subgroups, such as all drum recordings, before processing the full mix.
Settings interact, as louder drums can hide the vocal.
Because the desired sound can be difficult to describe in words, we study reference-guided mixing, where a reference song provides an example.

Figure 1: Comparison of music post-production workflows.
(a) Neural mixing systems predict final mixes or audio effects settings without explicit critique–revision loops.
(b) Prior LLM-based approaches focus on audio effects chain prediction and iterative mix refinement.
(c) MixAgent introduces an agentic framework that integrates hierarchical planning, execution, and iterative refinement into a unified music post-production pipeline.

Existing systems address parts of this problem (Figure 1).
Neural and generative models produce competitive audio without exposing
audio effects settings (Koo et al., 2023; Moliner et al., 2026),
while Diff-MST predicts editable parameters for fixed sequences of audio effects (Vanka et al., 2024). Prior LLM-based systems address narrower tasks.
LLM2Fx-Tools predicts audio effects chains for individual tracks (Doh et al., 2026), and RIME edits an existing mix to follow instructions (Schaffer and Singh, 2026).
Building a mix from tracks requires choosing and ordering effects at the track, subgroup, and full-mix levels, setting their parameters, and identifying corrections without editing instructions.
Simply prompting an audio-language model to listen and revise does not consistently improve the mix.

MixAgent builds an editable mixing plan and refines its parameters. A grouping agent organizes related tracks into subgroups. Guided by retrieved examples, a frozen planner chooses and orders audio effects at all three levels, then initializes their parameters. A learned detector selects what needs correction, and a critic proposes how to fix it. Refinement makes one pass at each level, from tracks to subgroups to the full mix, so later stages hear earlier corrections.
Because no known corpus pairs mixing critiques with parameter repairs, we build MixCritic, containing 45,657 critiques.
We train the critic with supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then direct preference optimization (DPO), favoring corrections toward the audio produced by the fitted parameters. Every effect, parameter, and correction remains explicit and editable.

The design also raises a broader question. What makes feedback useful for agents acting through numerical tools?
Our analyses show that retrieved examples improve audio effects selection, while learned refinement improves their parameters.
This refinement benefits from more specific feedback, with numerical corrections giving lower reconstruction error than perceptual or tool-specific advice.
With numerical feedback, DPO reduces this error by a further 8.4% over SFT.
Beyond feedback, selecting correction targets and refining tracks before subgroups and the full mix further reduces error.

Training and objective evaluation use non-overlapping excerpts of the same song as inputs and references, allowing comparison against its professional mix. On held-out MedleyDB songs, MixAgent achieves lowest reconstruction error and higher predicted quality than all tested multimodal LLM baselines. An 11-participant listening test with references from other songs within the same genre also gives MixAgent higher quality ratings. Our contributions are:

• 

To our knowledge, MixAgent is the first LLM mixing agent to combine editable audio effects planning across tracks, subgroups, and the full mix with learned detection and correction of parameter errors.11

 Demo: https://github.com/SonyResearch/Agentic_Music_Post-Production

• 

We construct MixCritic, providing repair critiques in three feedback forms and preference pairs ranked by the resulting audio.

• 

We show complementary reconstruction gains from retrieval and learned numerical refinement, with further improvements from selecting correction targets and refining tracks before subgroups and the full mix.

## 2 Preliminaries

Figure 2: Overview of MixAgent.
(a) The grouping agent assigns tracks to subgroups. (b) Using retrieved examples, the planner selects audio effects chains sequentially at the track, subgroup, and full-mix levels.
(c) After parameter initialization, the detector flags elements for improvement, and the critic provides perceptual, tool-specific, or numerical feedback. Refinement proceeds from tracks to subgroups to the full mix.

## Music Post-production.

The input consists of individual audio recordings, called input tracks, such as a lead vocal, a bass guitar, or a single drum microphone. Mixing proceeds at three levels: individual tracks, subgroups of related tracks summed and processed together (e.g., all drum tracks), and the full mix formed by summing all subgroup outputs. Subgroup and full-mix processing correspond to subgroup buses and the master bus, respectively. The output after all processing is the final mix. Mixing engineers shape the audio at each level with audio effects, signal-processing tools controlled by numerical parameters. Typical audio effects include gain (volume), panning (left–right position), equalization (EQ, the balance of low and high frequencies), compression (reducing loudness fluctuations), and reverb (a sense of acoustic space). An ordered list of audio effects, such as EQ followed by compression, is an audio effects chain.

## Task.

We study reference-guided mixing. The input is a set of unprocessed input tracks $X$ with instrument labels, a library of available audio effects $\mathcal{T}$ (Appendix A.2), and a style reference $r$ , which is a finished mix with the desired mixing style from a different song. LLM2Fx-Tools (Doh et al., 2026) predicts audio effects chains for individual tracks. We extend this task to multitrack mixing, producing a mixing plan $G$ and parameters $\theta$ . The plan assigns the tracks $x_{i}\in X$ to subgroups, where $S_{b}$ is the set of tracks in subgroup $b$ (possibly a single track), and assigns an audio effect chain to each track, each subgroup, and the full mix, written $f_{i}$ , $f_{b}$ , and $f_{m}$ with parameters $\theta_{i}$ , $\theta_{b}$ , and $\theta_{m}$ . Executing the plan, which we call rendering, produces the output mix $\widehat{y}$ in three stages:

 $\displaystyle=f_{i}(x_{i};\theta_{i})$ 

 $\displaystyle\text{(track)}$ 

(1)

 $\displaystyle y_{b}$ 
 $\displaystyle=f_{b}\big(\textstyle\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i};\,\theta_{b}\big)$ 

 $\displaystyle\text{(subgroup)}$ 

 $\displaystyle\widehat{y}$ 
 $\displaystyle=f_{m}\big(\textstyle\sum_{b}y_{b};\,\theta_{m}\big)$ 

 $\displaystyle\text{(full mix)}$ 

We denote the audio after each stage by $R_{1}(\theta)=\sum_{i\in S_{b}}y_{i}$ , $R_{2}(\theta)=\sum_{b}y_{b}$ , and $R_{3}(\theta)=\hat{y}$ .

The agent must infer audio effects chains and settings to match the reference’s mixing style rather than copy audio, since instrumentation, arrangement, or genre may differ. It must also account for interactions across tracks, subgroups, and the full mix.
Our datasets lack ground-truth mixes with references from other songs. We therefore use two non-overlapping excerpts of the same song for training and main evaluation (§4.1).
The listening test uses references from other songs within the same genre (§4.3). MixAgent keeps every audio effect and setting explicit, so users can inspect the plan, change values, and render the mix again. Audio is produced only by applying these audio effects to the input tracks, avoiding hallucinated musical content and artifacts from direct neural audio generation.

## 3 MixAgent

MixAgent runs automatically and splits mixing into three decisions (Figure 2). It decides which audio effects to use (§3.1), what to fix in the current mix, and how to fix it (§3.2). We describe how the components that make the last two decisions are trained (§3.3).

## 3.1 Planning Audio effects Chains with Retrieved Examples

A grouping agent first listens to the input tracks, reads their instrument labels, and assigns each track to a subgroup (e.g., kick, snare, and cymbals form a drum subgroup). A frozen audio-language tool-planning agent then selects audio effects chains.
Without examples, the planner tends to select short chains (§ 5.2). To guide its choices, we use GRAFX (Lee et al., 2024), a differentiable audio-processing library, to estimate example plans.
GRAFX fits audio effect parameters to approximate each database song’s professional mix, then removes effects that barely change the rendered audio (Lee et al., 2025b).
Each database entry stores these pseudo-ground-truth (pseudo-GT) plans and a caption of the rendered mix. For a new song, text retrieval matches automatically generated input-track captions to database captions to find similar instrumentation. Audio retrieval matches the reference to rendered database mixes for similar mixing styles. We provide three text-retrieved and one audio-retrieved plan, excluding all excerpts of the input song.
These examples show effect choices and order, but not parameter values. The planner selects track, subgroup, and full-mix chains in order, with each level guided by earlier choices.
The chains remain fixed.
Appendix B.1 and F provide details and prompts.

Figure 3: 
Data generation for MixCritic. (a) From a fixed tool plan, we obtain parameters through gradient-based optimization against the professional mix with GRAFX (green) and LLM generation (pink). Replacing the optimized parameters of randomly selected tracks with LLM outputs creates corrupted mixing states. (b) The teacher LLM compares the selected track’s corrupted and optimized parameters to generate A1–A3 critiques. The critic agent is trained to repair one corrupted track’s parameters at a time.

## 3.2 Hierarchical Estimation

The planner first sets the initial parameters of selected effect chains based on the reference audio.
MixAgent then revises them bottom-up, following common engineering practice (Fox, 2024), first the tracks, then the subgroups, and finally the full mix (Figure 2). We call each track, subgroup, or the full mix an element $e$ , and two trained components carry out each revision.

## Detector (what to fix).

At the track and subgroup stages, the trained detector hears the processed tracks within a subgroup or the subgroup outputs, together with the reference $r$ , and reads the current plan and parameters. For each $e$ , it predicts the probability $p_{e}$ that an element needs correction and identifies audio effects that may need changes. The critic inspects elements with $p_{e}>\tau$ , starting with the highest probability. The full mix is always inspected. Appendix B.3 describes its architecture and training.

## Critic (how to fix it).

For each selected $e$ , the audio-language critic $\pi_{\phi}$ hears the audio of $e$ with its current audio effects, the current mix, and the reference. Its input $o_{e}$ also includes the detector’s output and the audio effects chain and parameters of $e$ . The critic proposes a correction $a_{e}$ , and $\mathrm{Exec}$ applies it to the parameters of $e$ :

 $a_{e}\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid o_{e}),\qquad\theta\leftarrow\mathrm{Exec}(a_{e},\theta),$ 

(2)

where $\mathrm{Exec}$ changes only the parameters of $e$ . We compare three forms of feedback that describe the same repair (Table 1). For perceptual advice (A1) and tool-specific advice (A2), it asks the planner to turn the advice into numbers. For numerical corrections (A3), it applies the proposed values directly. MixAgent uses A3.

Each refinement pass calls the critic once per selected $e$ , using audio from the pass’s start. Then, applies corrections, re-renders the stage again, so the next stage hears the updated audio. We use one pass per stage, record every parameter change, and study additional passes (Appendix B.2 and D.6).

## Supervised critiques.

For each corrupted state, we select one corrupted track and define a target correction $a^{\ast}$ that restores its pseudo-GT parameters. The other tracks keep their current settings.
A larger teacher LLM (Qwen3.6-35B) receives the corrupted state and the target track’s LLM-generated and fitted parameters, and writes critiques in forms A1–A3, each with a step-by-step rationale.
We keep a critique if its target repair satisfies $s(a^{\ast})>\delta_{0}$ , leaving 45,657 examples. The detector is trained on the same states, plus states with random parameters, to predict which tracks, subgroups, and audio effects were corrupted (class-weighted binary cross-entropy). Pseudo-GT parameters are used only to build MixCritic and never at inference.

## Supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

The critic uses a Qwen3.5-4B language model (Qwen Team, 2026) and a frozen RLAT encoder trained to
limitations:
First, multiple mixes can be valid for the same input tracks, so reconstruction error against one professional mix does not fully capture mixing quality (Moliner et al., 2026).
In our experiments, TuneJury is useful mainly for detecting severe degradation and is not yet sufficient as a standalone objective metric for assessing mixing quality. TuneJury (Kim et al., 2026) operates on mono audio (48 kHz for CLAP (Wu et al., 2023) and 24 kHz for MERT (Li et al., 2024)), while Audiobox Aesthetics uses 16 kHz mono audio. These representations limit direct assessment of stereo imaging and, for Audiobox, high-frequency detail. Developing reliable perceptual metrics for multitrack mixing remains a separate research challenge beyond the scope of this work.
Second, the evaluation sets are small (20 MedleyDB clips from 17 songs, 14 AlbumDB clips, and 10 clips for the listening study), limiting generalizability and the precision of perceptual comparisons. Results on AlbumDB are mixed.
MST accepts only four sources, so we ran it on the separated professional mix rather than on identical input tracks, limiting direct comparability.
Third, supervision and oracles come from GRAFX-fitted parameters, which approximate, but do not recover, the engineer’s settings. The large gap to GT-fitted parameters (1.75 vs. 0.90 MRS) shows that parameter setting remains far from solved.
Fourth, our audio effects library covers only a small subset of the processing tools available to professional audio engineers, creating a tool gap that limits the range of achievable mixes. The plan is also fixed after planning, so the critic cannot add or remove audio effects.
Finally, although explicit plans expose editable audio effects and parameters, we have not evaluated how users interpret or modify them in practice. Producing a mix also requires many calls to large audio-language models, limiting computational efficiency.
conclusion: We presented MixAgent, an audio-language agent that mixes music by building an explicit plan of audio effects over tracks, subgroups, and the full mix, then refines it bottom-up with a learned detector and critic. Our results suggest a broader lesson for agents that act through numerical tools. Targeted, executable feedback trained on outcomes improves mixing. Because each decision logs a named audio effect and value, users can inspect the result, trace corrections, and edit the plan.

title: ReSeg: Retraining-free segmentation of abdominal organs via generalizable semantic representation learning
abstract: Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale image data raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. body_start:
Abstract

Abdominal organ segmentation is essential in modern medical applications including computer-aided diagnosis, therapy planning, and surgical navigation. While existing deep learning approaches demonstrate promising performance, their heavy reliance on large-scale patient image data covering multiple domains raises concerns over generalization capability and privacy risks. This motivates the development of generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis, where networks are trained using synthesized images with diverse contrasts and resolutions, facilitating generalization across unseen real image domains. However, existing paradigms either suffer from limited segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs, or require dataset-specific finetuning. To address these limitations, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for domain-agnostic zero-shot abdominal organ segmentation. At the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by a dedicated data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by another dedicated data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. To enhance organ-relevant region perception, OESNet further incorporates a Semantics-guided Segmentation (SS) decoder, which hierarchically integrates rich semantic priors derived from the well-trained GSRNet. Comprehensive evaluation on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET demonstrates that ReSeg consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods while eliminating the need for real training images. The source code will be publicly available at https://github.com/Kendra9999/ReSeg.

Keywords: 

Domain randomization , Image synthesis , Representation learning , Abdominal organ segmentation

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Illustration of the proposed two-stage retraining-free framework and the zero-shot segmentation performance. (a) We utilize organ shape templates to randomly sample images from a wide range of distributions and train the model on the synthetic images through two learning stages. Stage I learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features that are robust to imaging variations, while stage II leverages these semantic priors to learn abdominal-organ-specific semantic features for image segmentation. In the inference stage, our model can segment real images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. (b) ReSeg achieves superior performance compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on seven abdominal segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI, and PET. In particular, SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023) is trained only on synthetic data while ZeroShotSAM (Shaharabany and Wolf, 2024) leverages Segment Anything Model (SAM) (Kirillov et al., 2023) to perform minimally-guided zero-shot segmentation using foreground prompt points as the input. The solid line in the radar plot depicts the average Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) on each dataset.

Abdominal organ segmentation plays a pivotal role in medical imaging by enabling precise organ localization and volumetric analysis, serving as a foundation for computer-aided diagnosis (Chan et al., 2020), therapy planning (Chen et al., 2021), and surgical navigation (Okamoto et al., 2015). For instance, liver segmentation aids focal lesion detection and liver fibrosis staging (Tong et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2023), and kidney segmentation from preoperative scans is a prerequisite for building 3D models that support augmented reality navigation in laparoscopic partial nephrectomy (Zhang et al., 2019). Manual segmentation of abdominal organs is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and error-prone, thus spurring the need for accurate automatic segmentation algorithms.

Automated segmentation of abdominal organs from volumetric medical images is a challenging task. First, soft tissues usually have low contrast characteristic in abdominal imaging, leading to weak boundaries between adjacent anatomical structures (Wang et al., 2019). Second, the abdominal cavity presents a complex background with highly variable morphological structures, whose shapes and sizes exhibit significant heterogeneity among patients (Ma et al., 2021). Third, abdominal images acquired from different clinical settings often vary substantially in terms of field of view (FOV), introducing inconsistencies in the contextual information associated with organs.

The field has witnessed remarkable progress through deep learning approaches to meet the challenges mentioned above (Isensee et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). This progress has shifted the research focus from dataset-specific models towards universal foundation models, which offer improved performance while enhancing generalization capability. Some studies leverage approaches inspired by Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) (Liu et al., 2023) or Segment Anything Model (SAM) (Du et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; He et al., 2025) to handle diverse segmentation tasks, while others advance representation learning methods to pretrain networks with powerful feature extraction capability. These include reconstruction-based methods like MAE (He et al., 2022), SimMIM (Xie et al., 2022), and MiM (Zhuang et al., 2025a), as well as contrastive learning approaches such as VoCo (Wu et al., 2024), UAE (Bai et al., 2025), and SuperCL (Zeng et al., 2026). Finetuning these pretrained networks on downstream segmentation datasets has yielded promising results.

Despite these advantages, most existing biomedical foundation segmentation methods face a fundamental limitation: they require large amounts of medical image datasets covering multiple domains to achieve excellent generalization performance and inherently have high reliance on real medical images for training (Liu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; He et al., 2025). Such reliance introduces not only privacy risks but also modality-specific biases, as significant domain gaps persist with large-scale data (Huang et al., 2025), leading models to learn suboptimal feature representations. This results in limited generalization in real clinical scenarios, particularly when processing images from entirely unseen biomedical scenarios with variant imaging modalities, such as Computed Tomography (CT), Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), and Positron Emission Tomography (PET). Hence, there is an urgent need for a domain-agnostic zero-shot segmentation approach, where the model can segment images from unseen domains with cross-modality discrepancies and intra-modality variations.

Recently, there have been research efforts dedicated to developing generalizable segmentation training paradigms based on domain-randomized image synthesis strategies in brain MR image analysis (Billot et al., 2023; Ayaz et al., 2024; Gopinath et al., 2025). These approaches train Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) exclusively on synthetic images sampled from a generative model conditioned on label maps, eliminating the requirement for real training images. By leveraging a domain randomization strategy, they generate pseudo training images with varying contrasts and resolutions, exposing models to extensive variability during training. This forces the models to learn domain-independent features, enabling effective generalization to real clinical scans across diverse domains during inference. Beyond brain imaging, such a paradigm has also been extended in existing literature to segmentation tasks targeting other anatomical structures, including vascular structures (Chollet et al., 2024) and cellular nuclei (Dey et al., 2024). Building on the domain randomization concept, Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) further introduced a general-purpose representation learning framework powered by a dedicated data engine, which synthesizes highly variable training samples from compositions of organ shape templates. This enables the pretraining of a network that serves as a strong, dataset-agnostic initialization for finetuning on new segmentation datasets.

Despite significant progress achieved so far, to achieve generalizable segmentation of abdominal organs without access to real training images, several challenges persist. First, most existing approaches are designed for structures with relatively fixed anatomical topology and stable tissue intensity distribution such as the brain (Billot et al., 2023), the vascular structures (Chollet et al., 2024), and the cellular nuclei (Dey et al., 2024), and thus fall short in segmentation performance when applied to abdominal organs (as demonstrated by the experimental results presented in Fig. 1), which exhibit large morphological variations among patients. Second, it is challenging to generate realistic synthetic abdominal data due to the lack of standardized anatomical atlases and refined annotated templates, resulting in severe domain gaps between synthetic and real clinical scans. Third, the existing domain-randomization-based representation learning method Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) focuses on acquiring appearance-agnostic representations, yet overlooks the contextual consistency in the learned features. This may lead to diminished performance when segmenting images across varying FOVs where contextual information changes. Finally, although the existing representation learning method Anatomix (Dey et al., 2025) enhances domain-agnostic features, additional finetuning on downstream datasets is required for adapting the pretrained network to task-specific segmentation, limiting their applicability in retraining-free settings.

To address these limitations, we first propose a Generalizable Appearance (GA) model to generate diversified pseudo-images based on organ shape templates, thereby eliminating the reliance on real annotated images for network training. This model realizes full randomization of image contrast and resolution via domain randomization. On this basis, we further develop two dedicated data engines, namely GenRep and GenSeg, which are respectively devised for organ-agnostic semantic representation learning and abdominal-organ-specific segmentation learning. Specifically, GenRep generates image samples with rich semantic layouts and visual variations to capture organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic representations. In contrast, GenSeg yields appearance-variant pseudo-images while retaining inherent anatomical spatial configurations. Combined with background simulation empowered by a newly designed Label Processing (LP) model, it enables optimization for abdominal organ segmentation without any real training images.

Built upon these two data engines, we propose a two-stage retraining-free framework, referred to as ReSeg, for real-training-image-free abdominal organ segmentation, as visualized in Fig. 1-(a). Specifically, at the first stage, our organ-agnostic synthetic data-driven pretraining approach exploits semantically and visually diverse synthetic images generated by the GenRep data engine to optimize a Generalizable Semantic Representation Network (GSRNet). The network is thereby capable of learning semantic features robust against variations in anatomical structure, imaging contrast, resolution and spatial context, which provide universal representation capabilities that serve as a foundation for segmentation learning. This is done by designing a novel Multi-patch Context-aware Contrastive (MCC) loss that encourages domain-invariant feature alignment amidst contextual variations. Subsequently, in the second stage, we continue to train an Organ-specific Encoder-decoder Segmentation Network (OESNet), whose encoder is initialized with the pretrained weights. This training process is facilitated by the GenSeg data engine, which generates diversified visual images while strictly retaining the inherent spatial layout of abdominal organs. To enhance organ-relevant region perception, OESNet further incorporates a Semantics-guided Segmentation (SS) decoder, which hierarchically integrates rich semantic priors derived from the well-trained GSRNet. During inference, ReSeg can segment real clinical images from multiple domains without retraining or finetuning. ReSeg achieves superior performance compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on seven abdominal segmentation datasets across three different modalities (see Fig. 1-(b)). Our primary contributions are summarized as follows:

1. 

We introduce a Generalizable Appearance (GA) model that can synthesize images with diverse contrasts and resolutions from given organ shape templates. Based on this model, we further introduce two dedicated data engines, referred to as GenRep and GenSeg, respectively designed to support organ-agnostic semantic representation learning and abdominal-organ-specific segmentation learning.

2. 

Built upon these two data engines, we propose ReSeg, a novel two-stage retraining-free framework for real-training-image-free abdominal organ segmentation.

3. 

In the proposed framework, the generalizable semantic representation learning at the first stage is achieved by designing a novel Multi-patch Context-aware Contrastive (MCC) loss that encourages domain-invariant feature alignment amidst contextual variations, while the abdominal-organ-specific segmentation learning at the second stage is facilitated by the pretrained weights and by incorporating semantic priors into a Semantics-guided Segmentation (SS) decoder.

4. 

Comprehensive experiments on seven abdominal organ segmentation datasets across three different modalities including CT, MRI and PET demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed ReSeg over the SOTA approaches.

## 2 Related work

## 2.1 Dataset-specific models for medical image segmentation

The unprecedented developments of deep learning have revolutionized the field of medical image segmentation, driving a paradigm shift from traditional methods (Wolz et al., 2013; Tong et al., 2015) toward deep learning-based approaches (Isensee et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2022). The U-shaped encoder-decoder framework, exemplified by U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) with skip connections and multi-scale feature extraction, has become the dominant architecture. Numerous variants have been developed to further improve segmentation accuracy for various anatomical structures, like abdominal organs (Ma et al., 2021; Ji et al., 2022). One strategy integrates attention mechanisms to recalibrate feature responses and emphasize target regions, thereby mitigating interference from complex abdominal background and enhancing boundary delineation of ambiguous organs (Wang et al., 2019; Zheng et al., 2025). Transformer-based architectures have also been adopted to capture long-range spatial dependencies across volumetric abdominal images, complementing local CNN features with a global perspective (Cao et al., 2022; Ding et al., 2026). More recently, Mamba-based models have emerged as promising alternatives, offering long-range modeling with linear complexity and thus balancing performance and computational efficiency for volumetric abdominal image segmentation (Ruan et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2026). Despite these advances, these methods are typically trained on a single dataset and thus remain dataset-specific, lacking the ability to generalize across heterogeneous imaging domains.

## 2.2 Self-supervised learning for medical image segmentation

To improve model generalization capability, remarkable progress has been witnessed in developing foundation models pretrained on large-scale medical image datasets (Butoi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024; He et al., 2025). A key direction within this effort involves designing self-supervised proxy tasks to enhance representation learning. These approaches typically fall into two categories. The first employs reconstructive losses to model anatomical structures and their spatial relationships, with representative works including MAE (He et al., 2022), SimMIM (Xie et al., 2022), and MiM (Zhuang et al., 2025a). The second category, by contrast, utilizes contrastive losses to learn consistent semantic representations. This is achieved by enforcing feature similarity within a predefined semantic space, as exemplified by VoCo (Wu et al., 2024), UAE (Bai et al., 2025), and SuperCL (Zeng et al., 2026). Despite significant progress, existing representation learning methods remain limited by their high reliance on heuristics tailored to their target datasets and typically learn feature similarity within a single imaging modality. This leads to compromised generalization when applied to new biomedical domains. Although UAE (Bai et al., 2025) extends feature learning to cross-modality CT-MRI scenarios, its iterative training process is computationally intensive, and the learned features remain insufficient under significant domain shifts (e.g. CT or MRI to PET). To gain domain-agnostic performance, our work introduces domain-randomization-based data engines that synthesize images with diverse resolutions and contrasts, thereby facilitating generalizable semantic representatio
conclusion:
Domain-randomized image synthesis offers a promising way to eliminate the need for real training images and support generalizable segmentation learning. However, it remains underexplored whether such synthetic data-driven training paradigms can be effectively applied to generalizable abdominal organ segmentation without requiring domain-specific adaptation. To mitigate the gap, we propose ReSeg, a two-stage retraining-free framework for zero-shot segmentation of abdominal scans. Built upon two delicately designed data engines, our proposed two-stage network first learns organ-agnostic, generalizable semantic features, and then transitions to acquiring abdominal-organ-specific semantic features. We conducted comprehensive experiments on seven abdominal segmentation datasets encompassing different imaging modalities (CT, MRI, and PET), varying spatial resolutions, and diverse patient demographics to evaluate the generalization capability of ReSeg to various unseen domains. Across all evaluation datasets, our method consistently outperformed the competing SOTA approaches, as evidenced by the results presented in Tables 1, 2, and 3, and Figures 8, 9, 10, and 11. To further investigate the effectiveness of the proposed GA model, the MCC loss, and the architectural components of the proposed OESNet, we conducted comprehensive ablation studies. The experimental results presented in Tables 4, 5, and 6 provide a detailed assessment of how different components of the proposed method contribute to the segmentation generalization performance.

Direct application of existing domain-randomization-based segmentation training paradigms like SynthSeg (Billot et al., 2023) to abdominal organ segmentation proved ineffective (Tables 1, 2, and 3). Thus, we develop two dedicated data engines with the newly designed GA model to enhance feature learning in the complex scenarios of volumetric abdominal images. In particular, the GA model uses a dynamic lower bound for the mean parameters in the GMMs to better capture the large contrast variations encountered in abdominal imaging. This strategy significantly enhances the generalization capability of the segmentation network, as evidenced by the improved performance shown in Table 4. Our delicately designed data engines enable generalizable segmentation learning for abdominal anatomy, which exhibit high variations in appearance and background among patients and thus pose significant zero-shot segmentation challenges.

title: Value-Rectified Distillation for Flow-based Offline Reinforcement Learning
abstract: We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging, a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q, which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R, which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets.

Abstract

We aim to address the problem of Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Mode Averaging, a critical problem that emerges when distilling Flow Matching (FM) based behavior policies in offline Reinforcement Learning (RL): When learning over multi-modal datasets, standard distillation inadvertently forces the policy to interpolate across different behavioral modes, causing the generated actions to collapse into invalid, OOD regions. To resolve this, we propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. By employing a dynamic coupling mechanism, VRD actively rectifies flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes, cleanly isolating high-value actions. Specifically, we instantiate VRD through two complementary algorithms: VRD-Q, which utilizes value-quantile behavior distillation to statistically filter out low-value behaviors, and VRD-R, which reorganizes the latent space to geometrically isolate high-value generative trajectories from the FM-based behavior policy. Extensive empirical evaluations demonstrate that VRD improves existing generative baselines across diverse continuous control and planning tasks on the D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks, especially over those multi-modal, non-expert datasets.

## 1 Introduction

Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to derive a high-capacity policy from a fixed, pre-collected dataset without further environment interaction [17, 15], which is particularly vital for the applications where online exploration is costly or hazardous. Recently, generative models, particularly Flow Matching (FM) [18], have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional Diffusion-based methods [9, 2, 5], where FM-based policies, such as Flow Q-Learning (FQL) [21], offer significant advantages in modeling complex, multi-modal behavior distributions while circumventing the training instabilities typically associated with backpropagating through ODE solvers.

Figure 1: Problem of Latent Fusion (left) and the OOD Mode Averaging problem caused by FQL-style behavior distillation (right).

Despite their empirical promise, we identify a fundamental pathology in how current flow-based RL frameworks distill high-value actions from multi-modal behavior policies. Specifically, when learning from multi-modal data, our analysis reveals that Flow Matching networks inherently suffer from Latent Fusion: the topological entanglement between the generative trajectories of optimal and sub-optimal behavioral modes, caused by the vector field’s training dynamics, as is shown in Figure 1 (left). In previous works, like FQL [21], it first pre-trains a behavior flow policy to capture the full multi-modal behavior distribution [4] from the dataset, and subsequently applies Q-value guidance to distill the optimal policy. However, because such distillation operates on a continuous vector field where trajectories are already topologically entangled by the MLE pre-training, the Q-guided objective, as is shown in Figure 1 (right), inadvertently forces the sampled actions to linearly interpolate across distinct modes during inference, which triggers the OOD Mode Averaging disaster, where it is risky for the generated actions to collapse into low-density regions of the state-action manifold, ultimately causing performance degradation. Although recent approaches like Guided Flow Policy (GFP) [24] incorporate reward information to amplify optimal behavior modes in FM-based behavior policy, their FQL-style distillation mechanism still suffers from OOD Mode Averaging.

To address this issue, our core insight is that during the distillation phase, policy refinement must go beyond simply cloning from FM-based behavior policy; rather, it inherently requires rectifying the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple distinct behavioral modes along the data manifold. Therefore, we introduce Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a novel framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem, of which the core lies in a dynamic coupling mechanism that precisely modulates the flow dynamics to explicitly decouple and exclude sub-optimal behavioral modes, ensuring that the generated actions are confined to the optimal action manifold during inference.

To instantiate this unified framework, we derive two distinct algorithms from complementary mathematical perspectives: VRD-Q (Statistical Rectification): this variant performs in-place vector field alignment by employing asymmetric weight modulation based on value quantiles, which statistically filters sub-optimal regions without altering the underlying flow topology. VRD-R (Geometric Rectification): this variant actively reshapes the flow’s topology, which constructs a value-gravity field that transports the generative trajectories toward a highly compact optimal support set, geometrically isolating them from sub-optimal modes.

In summary, our primary contributions include: 1) Tracing OOD Mode Averaging: We theoretically trace the root cause of the OOD Mode Averaging problem in FQL-style distillation mechanism, revealing how its distillation objective interacts with latent fusion to generate invalid OOD actions on multi-modal data. 2) The VRD Framework: We propose Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) with two implementations VRD-Q and VRD-R, reformulating offline policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment problem to safely extract high-value policies without mode averaging. 3) Empirical Validation: Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VRD-Q and VRD-R effectively mitigate this OOD issue, outperforming or performing competitively with existing generative baselines across various continuous control and planning tasks.

## 2 Preliminaries and motivation

## 2.1 Offline RL and Flow Q-Learning

Suppose a Markov Decision Process $\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},r,\rho,p)$ , then the goal of offline RL is to learn a policy $\pi$ that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted return using a static dataset $\mathcal{D}$ collected by a behavioral policy. Previous work adopted the FQL framework [21] to avoid the instability of backpropagating through ODE solvers. FQL consists of three components:

Critic: A value function $Q_{\phi}(s,a)$ trained to minimize the Bellman error.

BC Flow Policy: A flow-matching policy $\mu_{\theta}(s,z)$ defined by a vector field $v_{\theta}$ , trained purely on Behavioral Cloning (BC) to capture the dataset distribution:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{s,a\sim\mathcal{D},t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1),x^{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}[\|v_{\theta}(t,s,x^{t})-(a-x^{0})\|_{2}^{2}]$ 

(1)

where $x^{t}=(1-t)x^{0}+ta$ .

One-Step Actor Policy: An expressive feed-forward network $\pi(s,z):\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathcal{A}$ that maps latent noise $z$ directly to actions.

In standard FQL, the actor $\pi$ is trained to maximize $Q$ -values while being regularized via distillation from the frozen flow policy $\mu_{\theta}$ . The standard objective uses an unstructured Gaussian prior $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})$ for this coupling:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\pi}=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D},z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d})}[-\lambda\cdot Q_{\phi}(s,\pi(s,z))+\|\pi(s,z)-\mu_{\theta}(s,z)\|_{2}^{2}]$ 

(2)

, while the Q-networks $Q_{\phi}$ are learned by minimizing a standard double Temporal Difference (TD) objective:

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\phi_{i})=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\left(Q_{\phi_{i}}(s,a)-r-\gamma\min_{j=1,2}Q_{\bar{\phi},j}(s^{\prime},\pi(s^{\prime},z))\right)^{2}\right],\ z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ 

(3)

This implies that the latent space of the actor is isotropic; the position of $z$ carries no semantic information regarding the quality of the action.

## 2.2 Latent fusion and OOD mode-averaging problems of FQL in multi-modal data

According to Flow Q-Learning, we can fit the action distribution of the behavior policy $\pi_{\beta}(a|s)$ , by the flow model $\mu_{\theta}(s,z)$ , where $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ . Then we define the support action set given $s$ , as $\mathcal{A}(s)=\{a|\pi_{\beta}(a|s)>0\}$ , and OOD action set $\bar{\mathcal{A}}=\{a|\pi_{\beta}(a|s)=0\}$ . Furthermore, given a Q-function $Q(s,a)$ as the evaluator, we can define the optimal and suboptimal action sets as,

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\{a|a\in\mathcal{A}(s),Q(s,a)\geq\max_{a^{\prime}}Q(s,a^{\prime})-\epsilon_{opt}\}$ 

(4)

 $\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{-}_{Q}(s)$ 
 $\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(s)/\mathcal{A}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ 

(5)

In our work, we focus on the setting of multi-modal data, which has raised attention in the field [3, 10] recently. Specifically, in our work, we focus on the isolated multi-modal data as,

 $\displaystyle\inf_{a^{*}\in\mathcal{A}^{*}_{Q}(s),a^{-}\in\mathcal{A}^{-}_{Q}(s)}\|a^{*}-a^{-}\|_{2}=D>0$ 

(6)

which means that there exists a gap between the optimal and sub-optimal data modes. Under such kind of data, the first problem we encounter in flow-based offline RL is the Latent Fusion for the flow policy $\mu_{\theta}$ learned by $\mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow}}(\theta)$ in Eq.(1):

Proposition 1 (Latent Entanglement of OOD Generation).

Suppose the latent space $\mathcal{Z}$ (support of $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ ) is connected, and the flow mapping $\mu_{\theta}(s,z)$ is $L$ -Lipschitz continuous w.r.t. $z$ . Let $\mathcal{Z}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ , $\mathcal{Z}^{-}_{Q}(s)$ , and $\mathcal{Z}_{OOD}(s)$ denote the latent preimages of $\mathcal{A}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ , $\mathcal{A}^{-}_{Q}(s)$ , and $\bar{\mathcal{A}}(s)$ , respectively. If the model expresses both optimal and sub-optimal modes ( $\mathcal{Z}^{*}_{Q}(s)\neq\emptyset,\mathcal{Z}^{-}_{Q}(s)\neq\emptyset$ ), the following holds:
(1) The optimal latent boundary is non-empty ( $\partial\mathcal{Z}^{*}_{Q}(s)\neq\emptyset$ );
(2) The OOD latent set is strictly non-empty ( $\mathcal{Z}_{OOD}(s)\neq\emptyset$ );
(3) Any $\epsilon$ -neighborhood of a boundary point $z_{bd}\in\partial\mathcal{Z}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ intersects non-optimal regions: $\forall\epsilon\!>\!0,\mathbb{B}_{\epsilon}(z_{bd})\cap\big(\mathcal{Z}^{-}_{Q}(s)\cup\mathcal{Z}_{OOD}(s)\big)\neq\emptyset$ .

Proof is shown in Appendix A.1. Proposition 1 formalizes the Latent Fusion dilemma. Because $\mu_{\theta}$ is continuous and $\mathcal{Z}$ is connected, the model cannot safely isolate optimal latents. Property (2) proves that to bridge the physical gap $D>0$ , any continuous curve connecting the modes must structurally intersect the OOD space (a topological necessity, though without quantifying probability mass). Furthermore, Property (3) shows $\mathcal{Z}^{*}_{Q}(s)$ is inextricably entangled with sub-optimal/OOD regions at its boundary.

While Proposition 1 leverages the potent multi-modal modeling capabilities of Flow matching for targeted policy extraction, the extreme topological entanglement within the latent space, as characterized by the Latent Fusion in Proposition 1, renders such distillation and mapping via continuous, smooth networks susceptible to mode-averaging, as shown in Theorem 1. This phenomenon forces the policy to generate interpolated, OOD actions ( $\overline{a}\notin\mathcal{A}(s)$ ) that collapse into off-manifold regions.

Theorem 1 (OOD Mode Averaging in FQL).

Suppose the Q-function satisfies $\mu$ -strong concavity in the region bridging the modes and is $L$ -Lipschitz smooth.
Consider the FQL-style distillation that minimizes the regularized objective in Eq.(2).
Under multi-modal data with gap $D>0$ as Eq.(6) and any non-zero value regularization penalty $\lambda>0$ ,
FQL generates OOD actions with a minimum expected error bounded by $D^{2}/4$ .

Proof is shown in Appendix A.2. Theorem 1 reveals a fundamental limitation of FQL: under the latent mode entanglement established in Proposition 1, the explicit Euclidean regularization (e.g., $-\lambda Q+\|a-\mu_{\theta}\|_{2}^{2}$ ) blindly forces policy updates to perform linear interpolation across the action space. Because multi-modal data manifolds are topologically separated by a physical gap $D>0$ , this shortest Euclidean path traverses low-density OOD valleys, which triggers the Mode Averaging disaster with a strict expected error bounded by $D^{2}/4$ . Consequently, we conclude that action-space Euclidean constraints are structurally incompatible with multi-modal offline RL. Besides, assuming local $\mu$ -strong concavity in the valley between modes serves as an analytical abstraction to capture the optimization tension in FQL.

In other words, in probability density estimation, a smoothly connected set of feasible actions (like slightly different stable walking postures) topologically constitutes a single, broad, and continuous mode. Flow Matching naturally and gracefully captures this continuous variance. However, we suggest that arises specifically when the behavioral distribution contains structurally distinct peaks separated by low-density valleys (OOD regions).

Motivation. The observation that standard Euclidean distillation is vulnerable to mode averaging on multi-modal datasets motivates our Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework. As analyzed in this section, directly penalizing the action difference can inadvertently pull the actor into OOD regions. To effectively mitigate this issue, policy extraction must move beyond simple action-space regularization. Instead of linearly interpolating actions across empty spaces, VRD rectifies the continuous latent mapping by dynamically aligning the flow dynamics with value guidance, hence encouraging the policy to safely extract high-value actions along the data manifold.

## 3 Methodology

## 3.1 Unified framework: kernel-coupled value rectification

In Flow Q-Learning, while the initial behavior cloning phase effectively captures the multi-modal data distribution via the flow model $\mu_{\theta}$ , it absorbs suboptimal behavioral modes (as discussed in Section 2). To distill $\mu_{\theta}$ into an optimal policy $\pi$ that exclusively outputs actions within the optimal set $\mathcal{A}^{*}_{Q}$ , a principled rectification mechanism is essential. Rather than treating this process as isolated heuristic regularizations, we cast the value rectification as a latent distribution alignment problem.

To this end, we propose a generalized Value-Rectified Functional Space. We define the rectification objective $\Psi(\pi;\mu_{\theta})$ as an expected kernel-coupled divergence over the joint latent space $\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Z}$ :

(7)

conclusion:
This paper proposes the Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD) framework, reformulating policy distillation as a value-guided trajectory alignment process to solve the latent fusion problem in offline RL over multi-modal dataset. VRD-Q and VRD-R mitigate OOD Mode Averaging problem via statistical filtering and geometric reshaping respectively. Experiments show VRD successfully decouples the high-value behavior mode from the multi-modal data, which enables VRD outperform baselines on various benchmarks and datasets, demonstrating exceptional robustness for sub-optimal data noise.

Limitations (see Appendix D).

The proposed VRD relies on the underlying value network’s accuracy, where severe Q-value overestimation may mislead the alignment process. Future work could explore more robust value estimation or extend this framework to discrete action spaces.

title: A Large-Scale Evaluation of Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Prompting
abstract: This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework's scalability is validated across model sizes (2b-14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.

Abstract

This paper proposes Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that systematically integrates domain-specific expert roles to enhance reasoning in large language models (LLMs) without task-specific examples. We assess two versions of our approach. In the first version, static role selection, we evaluate eight predefined expert roles across arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension benchmarks to determine their impact on reasoning performance. In the second version, dynamic role selection, each model autonomously selects the single most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling adaptive task-role alignment without manual specification. Across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, RE-ZS-CoT frequently surpasses zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, achieving performance improvements of up to 44 percentage points. The results reveal a strong correspondence between static and dynamic versions; the benchmarks where static roles yielded improvements were almost always those where dynamic roles also outperformed baselines, though static selection achieved peak performance. Ablation studies further show that unconventional roles degrade performance, underscoring the necessity of task-role alignment. The framework’s scalability is validated across model sizes (2b–14b parameters), with smaller models like Granite3.3-8b achieving remarkable proficiency in arithmetic reasoning. RE-ZS-CoT advances zero-shot prompting by unifying role specialization with chain-of-thought reasoning, offering a practical, resource-efficient solution for improving LLM capabilities across diverse domains.

Fig. 1: Examples of prompts and corresponding responses generated by Gemma3:12b model on the AQuA-RAT benchmark comparing zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines to our RE-ZS-CoT and RE-ZS. The reasoning of the model is omitted for readability.

## I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) exhibit enhanced reasoning capabilities when directed by structured prompting techniques, such as chain-of-thought (CoT) [1] and zero-shot-CoT [2]. However, these methodologies frequently demonstrate inconsistent performance across various tasks, particularly in zero-shot scenarios where task-specific examples are unavailable. Recent studies explore various strategies to enhance reasoning in large language models, including decoding techniques to elicit CoT reasoning without explicit prompts [3], structured prompting methods like Plan-and-Solve to improve zero-shot reasoning [4], and frameworks such as Graph of Thoughts that model LLM outputs as graphs for complex problem-solving [5]. Additionally, LLMs demonstrate improved reasoning by taking on a persona, which often leads to greater accuracy, though not consistently [6], [7]. However, evaluations of role-enhanced prompting, particularly regarding its scalability, adaptability, and effects across reasoning domains, remain unexplored.

We present Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought (RE-ZS-CoT), a prompting framework that integrates expert role specification into single-turn, zero-shot reasoning without requiring task examples (Fig. 1). Unlike previous work relying on fixed templates ([6], [7], [8]), RE-ZS-CoT fills the above-stated gap by evaluating two versions. Version 1 assesses eight roles across three prompt variants (pre-question, post-question, split-phrase; Fig.2) and uses self-alignment, leveraging recent advances in aligning LLM behavior [9]; [10]; [11]. Version 2 shifts to an adaptive framework where each LLM independently selects the most suitable role for each benchmark, enabling self-optimization of task-role alignment without manual adjustment, using the same three prompt variants.

In version 1 (static self-alignment), we identify optimal roles for open-weight models under computational constraints. For OpenAI models, we test all eight roles on GPT-4o-mini, while larger models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1) use only the best-performing role due to cost. Open-weight models (2–3b, 7–9b, 12–14b) use quantized instruct-tuned versions (q4-K-M). We evaluate 20 LLMs across seven benchmarks spanning arithmetic, commonsense, and reading comprehension. RE-ZS-CoT yields 12–44% higher accuracy than zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines, with the largest gains in arithmetic tasks (AQuA-RAT, MATH). Role effects vary: domain-specific roles (e.g., mathematician) outperform general ones in arithmetic structured tasks, consistent with findings from a previous study [7].

The contributions of this paper are: (1) We introduce RE-ZS-CoT, the first framework that unifies role-enhancement with zero-shot-CoT reasoning, demonstrating broad applicability across seven benchmarks and 20 LLMs. (2) We show that the efficacy of role specialization is task-dependent, with math reasoning benefiting the most from domain-aligned roles. (3) We provide actionable insights for prompt engineering, highlighting the superiority of pre-question prompts and adaptive role selection for open-weight models. (4) Our ablation studies reveal novel findings regarding the impact of non-traditional roles and lexical variations, advancing the design of context-aware prompting strategies.

## II Related Work

## II-A Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Reasoning.

CoT prompting enhances complex reasoning by eliciting intermediate steps [1]. [2] showed zero-shot-CoT via simple prompts like "Let’s think step by step," but such prompts remain sensitive to phrasing, producing unstable outputs. Techniques like self-consistency decoding [12] and instruction tuning [13] improve the reliability of CoT and zero-shot prompting, respectively, but rely heavily on generic or example-based prompts. Smaller models (<100B parameters) particularly struggle without fine-tuning [14]. Syntactic variations were explored by [15], but without domain-specific reasoning. Recent work emphasizes instance-adaptive prompts [8], variability among equivalent prompts [16], and reasoning via decoding alone [3], highlighting the need for methods like RE-ZS-CoT to improve zero-shot reliability without extensive prompt engineering.

Recent advancements in reasoning architectures have shifted the paradigm toward models that natively generate reasoning traces via large-scale reinforcement learning (RL), often referred to as test-time compute or System 2 thinking models [17, 18]. Unlike standard CoT prompting, which relies on explicit user instructions to elicit step-by-step logic, these native reasoning models automatically allocate additional computational resources at inference time to plan, search, and self-correct. While these approaches achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex benchmarks, they introduce substantial latency and inference-time overhead. In contrast, RE-ZS-CoT explores the orthogonal direction of maximizing the reasoning efficiency of standard, non-RL-tuned language models by leveraging domain-specific personas.

## II-B Role-Based Prompting

Role-enhanced prompting improves LLM reasoning by biasing models toward domain expertise. [6] show that instructing models to "act as a domain expert" boosts accuracy, and [7] demonstrate that role-playing enhances zero-shot reasoning. However, prior methods rely on curated examples [19], narrow domains [7], or manual prompt templates [20]. These results create inconsistencies and reliance on a rigid template, which is not always effective. Moreover, the research on role prompting has not been conducted on a large scale, particularly in the zero-shot-CoT domain. Recent work has systematically evaluated social roles in system prompts, finding that interpersonal roles such as "friend" or "teacher" outperform generic "helpful assistant" across diverse tasks, although optimal role prediction remains challenging [21]. Others explore role-playing for domain adaptation, using unique role prompts per domain alongside self-distillation to prevent catastrophic forgetting during multi-domain fine-tuning [22]. Interpretable steering via sparse autoencoders extracts role-specific features for fine-grained control over reasoning behavior [23].

In mathematical reasoning, role-play prompts such as "helpful mathematician," combined with zero-shot-CoT, were tested but showed no improvements and sometimes degradation due to role-task mismatch and over-prompting [24]. These works, often limited to a few datasets and models without testing role placement variants or dynamic selection, underscore RE-ZS-CoT’s advantages: it scales across 20 LLMs and seven benchmarks, incorporates static/dynamic role selection with prompt variants (pre-question, post-question, split), and unifies role specialization with zero-shot CoT in single-turn prompts, achieving 12–44% higher accuracy.

Fig. 2: Our approach’s pre and post questions, and split-phrase variants with example prompts. Figure 1 demonstrates the 2nd variant in action.

Fig. 3: RE-ZS-CoT Framework.

## III Role-Enhanced Zero-Shot Chain of Thought

We introduce RE-ZS-CoT as shown in Figure 3 , a prompting technique that integrates role-based prompting within a zero-shot-CoT reasoning framework. Building on previous research [2, 7, 6, 24], our approach adheres to a zero-shot methodology for CoT reasoning while incorporating role-enhanced prompts to bolster the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Distinct from traditional zero-shot-CoT, which relies on a generic template applicable across diverse tasks and often leads to suboptimal performance in specific evaluations, such as those requiring commonsense reasoning, we utilize two versions of our approach.

In the first version, there are eight specialized roles: Mathematician, Physicist, Physician, Scientist, Literacy Specialist, Engineer, Software Developer, and Polymath. This targeted role assignment allows us to create prompts that are more finely attuned to the requirements of each task. The second version examines whether a more adaptive, on-the-fly selection can enhance the roles identified in version 1. For this, we implemented a dynamic role selection mechanism. In this experimental setup, we prompted each model to choose the single most suitable role for each specific benchmark. In addition, unlike the two-step prompting approach employed in zero-shot-CoT, where, according to its original form, reasoning is first extracted before generating the final answer, RE-ZS-CoT leverages a single prompt to extract answers from the model’s response. Figure 1 shows an example of our approach compared to zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT.

It is important to note that we do not benchmark RE-ZS-CoT against existing role-prompting frameworks. The fundamental integration of role-playing with zero-shot chain-of-thought reasoning is not in itself a novel concept; prior studies have already established that domain-specific personas can improve reasoning [7, 24]. However, existing literature has largely overlooked the critical mechanics of how these roles are selected and where the role phrases are placed within the prompt. Therefore, our approach serves as a rigorous, large-scale evaluation of these underexplored dimensions. We introduce unique role selection techniques, specifically contrasting static, predefined assignments with dynamic, autonomous inference, and systematically investigate the structural impact of role-phrase placement (R→Q, Q→R, and R→Q→R). Because our primary contribution lies in isolating the effects of these specific selection and placement strategies across 20 distinct LLMs, we strictly compare our framework against standard zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT baselines rather than other specialized role-prompting methods.

## III-A Prompt Variants

Our prompt consists of: (i) a role prompt R and (ii) the task question Q. We evaluate three placement strategies, as shown in Fig. 2: R→Q, Q→R, and the split form R→Q→R. This setup allows us to examine whether the placement of the role phrase affects the performance of LLMs, and whether defining a role beforehand, as done in a previous study [7], can enhance the LLM’s role-playing capabilities. Prior studies have shown that role-play phrases can improve factuality and reasoning ([7]. Our strategy tests whether these improvements persist under strict zero-shot settings at scale, across LLMs of varying sizes and benchmarks.

## IV Implementation Details

## Benchmarks

We evaluate our approach on seven datasets in three categories: arithmetic reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and reading comprehension. These datasets are commonly used in the benchmarking of LLMs. For a detailed description of each dataset, see [Appendix A].

For arithmetic reasoning, we consider the following three datasets: AQuA-RAT [25], and GSM8K [26]. AQuA-RAT contains algebraic word problems. It is designed to assess a model’s ability not only to solve the problem but also to generate a detailed, step-by-step rationale for its answer in natural language. GSM8K contains grade school math word problems that are linguistically diverse. It primarily checks a model’s ability to perform multi-step reasoning, as the questions require between two and eight steps using basic arithmetic to arrive at the final answer.

For commonsense reasoning, we use OpenBookQA [27], and StrategyQA [28]. OpenBookQA contains questions that require multi-step reasoning and the use of commonsense knowledge. StrategyQA requires models to infer an implicit multi-hop reasoning to answer questions.

For reading comprehension, we use RACE (h&m) [29] and TriviaQA [30]. RACE is a reading comprehension dataset containing questions from the examination of middle (RACE-m) and high school (RACE-h) students. TriviaQA is a reading comprehension dataset containing question-answer pairs authored by trivia enthusiasts and independently gathered evidence documents.

## Large Language Models

We conduct experiments utilizing a total of 20 LLMs, ranging from 2b to 14b open-weights models along with large closed-source models from OpenAI. This exploration aims to investigate the impact of our approach on varying parameter sizes, extending from large to small. For the main experiments, we use all 20 models, which are listed as follows: GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1-nano, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Phi4:14b [31], Qwen2.5:14b [32], Gemma3:12b [33], Mistral-nemo:12b-instruct [34], Gemma2:9b-instruct [35], Granite3.2:8b-instruct [36], Granite3.3:8b [37], Llama3.1:8b-instruct [38], Mistral:7b-instruct [39], Qwen2.5:7b-instruct [32], Llama3.2:3b-instruct [40], Qwen2.5:3b-instruct [32], Granite3.2:2b-instruct [36], Granite3.3:2b [37], and Gemma2:2b-instruct [35].

All the open-weights models are used with the latest available versions at the time of writing. We explicitly list the full names of all models [see Appendix A-C], including the closed-source OpenAI models, to ensure traceability in case of future updates.

## Baselines and Answer Detection

We compare our approach with standard zero-shot prompting and zero-shot-CoT. This is done to verify the effectiveness of our approach as we measure both zero-shot-CoT and zero-shot versions of our method. For our experiments, we use the same prompt for zero-shot and zero-shot-CoT, with the difference being the added “Let’s think step by step.” at the end of the question for zero-shot-CoT; see Fig. 1 for an example. In contrast to the two-stage prompting employed in prior research conducted by [2], we utilize a one-stage approach for all prompts, including zero-shot-CoT, to ensure an equitable comparison.

For answer detection in evaluation, drawing inspiration from previous research [2], we examine the model’s output and select the first token that aligns with the dataset’s answer specifications (for instance, a capital letter A–E for multiple-choice questions, the first valid numeral for arithmetic problems. The captured string is subjected to a cleaning process: punctuation, LaTeX wrappers, currency symbols, and thousands separators are removed, and logical terms (True/False) are converted to their corresponding letter equivalents prior to being returned as the prediction. In instances where we fail to identify an explicit cue, such as “The answer is …,”, we resort to this reverse scanning method; if no matches are found, we document a failure and classify the item as incorrect. In summary, all tasks adhere to the same procedure: identify the earliest compliant answer token, normalize it, and compare it to the answer label.

## Static Role Self-Alignment

For the static roles, we asked the open-weights LLMs themselves to select the most suitable roles from a predefined list based on the provided task description. Each LLM was queried 100 times, and we selected the two most frequently chosen roles to use in the experiments. This approach is inspired by previous work [9]; [10]; [11], which leverages LLMs to self-align themselves on specific tasks. We adopted this method for several reasons, besides our financial and computational constraints. Namely, unlike complete pilot runs, which require testing all role-prompt combinations, this strategy uses just a few lightweight meta-prompts per benchmark, making it ideal for resource-constrained settings. As new tasks or roles emerge, the same self-assessment procedure can be reused without manual ontology construction or extensive sampling. This property can offer a notable engineering advantage. Full details are provided in [Appendix V-C].

For closed-source models, we executed all roles for each task on GPT-4o-mini and subsequently selected the most effective role for the larger and more costly models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1), considering financial limitations. Furthermore, we implemented all roles for each task on GPT-4.1-mini and nano. We tested all roles on GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, and nano to not only cross-validate the self-alignment approach but also to assess the performance of all roles on all tasks for a broader impact and analysis.

## Dynamic Role Self-Alignment
