limitations:
While RE-ZS-CoT demonstrates broad empirical success, our study has several important limitations. First, the lack of transparency in LLM training constrains our work. Many models, especially closed-source ones like GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, lack public documentation on their training datasets. This opacity makes reproducibility difficult and obscures whether the observed improvements stem from genuine role-based reasoning pathways or latent memorization. Consequently, this limits our ability to conduct comprehensive fairness and bias evaluations, as the composition of the training data heavily influences how a model defines and operationalizes a given "expert" role.

Second, while our massive-scale evaluation highlights the variance in RE-ZS-CoT’s efficacy, most notably its degraded performance on generalized commonsense tasks like OpenBookQA, we do not conduct a deep qualitative or mechanistic error analysis. Our current study successfully identifies when and where the method struggles, but leaves the precise how and why unanswered. We hypothesize that rigid role constraints may induce overthinking in intuitive contexts, but further interpretability research is required to map exactly how persona adoption shifts internal representations of reasoning.

Third, our study relies on the broad empirical consensus generated by testing 20 distinct LLMs across seven datasets, reporting absolute accuracy gains rather than conducting paired statistical significance testing (e.g., McNemar’s test) for every individual model-task pair. While macro-trends and double-digit percentage surges (e.g., on AQuA-RAT) provide robust evidence of structural shifts in reasoning, smaller single-digit improvements on datasets with limited sample sizes should be interpreted as competitive performance rather than definitive algorithmic superiority.

Fourth, our evaluations exclusively focus on standard autoregressive language models. With the recent paradigm shift toward test-time compute and natively reasoning models (System 2 thinkers) that utilize reinforcement learning to automatically generate search and reasoning traces (e.g., OpenAI o-series, DeepSeek-R1), the interaction between explicit zero-shot role prompting and implicit RL-driven reasoning remains unexplored. Finally, our experimental scope is constrained to English text-only corpora. Evaluating the efficacy and cultural nuances of RE-ZS-CoT in non-English corpora, conversational multi-turn tasks, and multimodal environments remains an important area for future exploration

Future studies need to focus on RE-ZS-CoT through several perspectives. Firstly, testing our approach with the two-stage prompting method along with RS-few-shot will reveal the extent of its usefulness. Secondly, examining multi-role collaboration will evaluate whether using specialized personas can create a division of cognitive labor that offers benefits beyond single-role configurations. Finally, we will test RE-ZS-CoT in areas like code gener
conclusion:
Our experiments show that role-enhanced prompting boosts zero-shot reasoning across tasks and model sizes. RE-ZS-CoT biases LLMs towards domain-specific reasoning. This aligns with previous research on plan-and-solve strategies [4]. The placement of the role phrase (pre-question, post-question, split-phrase) affects performance, and variability across models and benchmarks necessitates adaptive prompt engineering rather than rigid templates. Unconventional roles led to lower performance, revealing that LLMs struggle with conflicting or irrelevant expertise. Lexical variation experiments confirm that terms like "expert" in role prompts are significant; substituting them with "amateur" or omitting them lowered accuracy, reinforcing that explicit expertise cues guide LLMs toward structured, factual reasoning.

Our experiments reveal an interesting interaction between the role self-alignment strategy and the nature of the reasoning task. Static role self-alignment demonstrates superior efficacy in highly structured domains that benefit from specialized knowledge. This is most pronounced on the AQUA-RAT benchmark, where leveraging a specific role like "Mathematician" consistently yields peak performance. Conversely, the dynamic role selection mechanism, which permits the model to infer the most suitable persona autonomously, often proves more advantageous for tasks requiring broader or more adaptive reasoning. On commonsense reasoning benchmarks, such as StrategyQA, and reading comprehension tasks, like RACE (h&m), the dynamic approach frequently leads to improved outcomes, suggesting that flexibility in role adoption is beneficial when the reasoning path is less prescribed. These findings suggest a fundamental trade-off: static roles maximize performance when a task’s requirements align perfectly with a known expert archetype, but this specialization can be suboptimal for more multifaceted problems. Dynamic selection, while not always reaching the same performance ceiling on specialized tasks, offers a more robust and generalizable strategy, mitigating the risk of a misaligned persona.

The rapid emergence of test-time compute and natively reasoning models raises a critical question: Does role-based zero-shot prompting still hold value when models are trained to reason automatically via reinforcement learning? title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.

headings: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
body_start:
Abstract

Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types.
Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector.
We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target.
AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers.
It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus.
Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings.
A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.

## 1 Introduction

Time series anomaly detection (TSAD) is a critical problem in industrial monitoring [1], cyber-physical systems [2], and sensor analytics [3, 4, 5].
Because anomalies are open-set events and anomaly labels are scarce, TSAD is often addressed in an unsupervised setting.
In this setting, the anomaly criterion is ambiguous, and a detector must infer which temporal deviations should be treated as abnormal from the training series alone.
Recent benchmark studies [6, 7, 8] highlight that this ambiguity leads different detectors to define and detect anomalies under their own criteria, with no single detector dominating across datasets.
Together, these observations suggest that improving TSAD performance requires using multiple anomaly-scoring principles.

Existing TSAD detectors already provide a rich source of such complementary scoring principles.
Reconstruction-based models emphasize reconstruction failure [9, 3], forecasting models emphasize predictive residuals [10, 11], latent-space models emphasize deviation from compact normal representations [12, 13], and association-based models emphasize structural and temporal dependency mismatch [14, 15].
Because their scores reflect different abnormality criteria, these detectors can complement one another [16].
A direct way to exploit this complementarity is to deploy them together and combine their scores.
However, such ensembles preserve the inference cost and maintenance overhead of all individual models [17, 18, 19].
A more practical goal is to transfer the complementary scoring principles into one lightweight student.

Knowledge distillation appears to be a natural route toward this goal because teachers can be used during training while only the student is deployed at inference [20, 21].
However, applying distillation to unsupervised TSAD raises a more fundamental question than how to compress a model: what exactly should be distilled?
In supervised classification, teacher and student models predict probabilities over the same set of classes, and ground-truth labels anchor the meaning of the teacher signal [21].
In unsupervised TSAD, neither condition holds.
Although each teacher outputs anomaly scores, the scores are continuous and detector-specific, and the label-free setting provides no direct way to verify whether they are correct.
When multiple teachers are used, this mismatch becomes more pronounced because their numerical magnitudes reflect different abnormality criteria and different calibrations.
Therefore, direct score regression is structurally mismatched with this setting, as it asks one student to fit multiple teacher-specific score scales as if they formed a single consistent target.

Our key insight is that imperfect teacher scores can still provide useful weak supervision through pairwise anomaly comparisons rather than through pointwise regression targets.
Although two teachers may use different score scales and abnormality criteria, they can still agree that one time point appears more anomalous than another.
We call this relation a pairwise anomaly preference.
Such preferences provide a more stable supervision form than pointwise regression targets because they compare samples within each teacher score sequence instead of requiring a shared calibrated score scale across teachers.
Moreover, when multiple heterogeneous teachers support the same pairwise direction, their agreement suggests that the comparison is informative.
Thus, unsupervised TSAD distillation becomes feasible by training a single student to learn reliable pairwise anomaly preferences from multi-teacher score sequences computed on the training data.

Building on this insight, we introduce AnoMix, a label-free multi-teacher distillation framework for learning
a neural anomaly-scoring function. Unlike conventional TSAD models that derive
anomaly scores from reconstruction, forecasting, association, or representation discrepancies,
AnoMix trains a student to directly output the anomaly score used at inference.
Since no labeled anomaly-score target exists, AnoMix supervises this scalar score through
pairwise anomaly preferences derived from frozen teacher score sequences.
First, AnoMix normalizes each frozen teacher score sequence independently and then trains a compact student using CoRank, a consensus-ranking objective over mini-batch time-point pairs.
CoRank constructs consensus support from teacher-level score gaps, assigns a consensus direction induced by normalized teacher differences, and weights each comparison by consensus confidence.
The student is therefore not asked to reproduce teacher-specific pointwise score magnitudes.
Instead, it learns a neural anomaly-scoring function aligned with the teacher-consensus ordering induced by CoRank.

Our contributions are as follows:

• 

We formulate label-free multi-teacher TSAD distillation as direct anomaly-score prediction for deployment, where a lightweight student learns a neural anomaly-scoring function from heterogeneous unsupervised teacher score sequences.

• 

We propose AnoMix, which turns normalized teacher score sequences computed on the training data into pairwise anomaly-preference supervision, allowing a single student to learn anomaly-scoring principles without regressing to teacher-specific pointwise scores.

• 

Across TSAD benchmark datasets and the zero-shot cross-dataset setting, AnoMix and AnoMix-ZS achieve strong performance against individual detectors, static score-ensemble baselines, and pretrained foundation-model baselines, demonstrating that pairwise anomaly preferences from multiple teachers can be distilled into a single lightweight student.

## 2 Related Work

## Knowledge Distillation.

Knowledge distillation (KD) was originally introduced as a way to compress a large teacher into a compact student by matching softened output distributions [21].
Later KD methods broadened the transferred signal from logits to intermediate features [22], contrastive representations [23], and sample relations such as activation similarities, similarity rankings, and relational structures [24, 25, 26].
Multi-teacher KD further aggregates supervision from several teachers into a single student [20].
Together, these lines show that KD need not be limited to output matching, but they still typically assume a well-defined transfer target.
For anomaly detection, distillation has been explored primarily in the image domain, often with a single teacher and with teacher–student discrepancy itself serving as the anomaly signal [27, 28].
In time-series anomaly detection, distillation remains relatively underexplored.
Recent work such as AnomalyLLM studies single-teacher transfer through feature mimicry and discrepancy-based detection [29].
However, prior work does not address the AnoMix setting of label-free transfer from heterogeneous TSAD teachers to a single student.

## Learning-to-Rank Methods.

Learning-to-rank methods learn scoring functions from relative ordering constraints rather than calibrated target values.
Existing ranking objectives, however, typically assume that the target ordering is already available.
Pairwise methods such as RankNet [30] optimize pairwise preferences or teacher-induced orderings, max-margin ranking losses [31] impose ordered margin constraints, and listwise methods such as ListNet [32] optimize an ordering distribution over a set of samples.
More recent differentiable sorting and ranking surrogates [33] further make rank-based objectives compatible with gradient optimization.
Relation-based distillation similarly transfers sample-level structure rather than only pointwise outputs [24, 25, 26].
These methods primarily specify how to optimize a given target ordering or relation.
AnoMix addresses a different setting.
In our setting, the target relation is not given by labels or by a single calibrated teacher.
AnoMix must construct pairwise supervision from heterogeneous teacher score sequences.

Figure 1: Training overview of AnoMix.
(a) Frozen teachers () score the unlabeled training series, followed by score normalization.
(b) CoRank selects informative pairs and derives their consensus direction and confidence.
(c) A trainable student () learns the pairwise ordering through a confidence-weighted loss.

## 3 Methodology

Figure 1 follows a concrete pair of endpoints through AnoMix.
In panel (a), each teacher $f_{m}$ produces raw anomaly scores $z_{i}^{(m)},z_{j}^{(m)}$ aligned with endpoints $i,j$ of the unlabeled training series, with its parameters fixed throughout student training.
Per-teacher min–max normalization using training statistics yields the scores $\tilde{z}_{i}^{(m)},\tilde{z}_{j}^{(m)}$ in row $m$ of the figure.
In panel (b), CoRank retains the pair if any teacher provides a sufficiently large score gap, combines the signed gaps into a consensus direction, and measures their agreement as a confidence weight.
The illustrated pair remains informative despite one opposing teacher: its consensus favors $i$ over $j$ with confidence $2/3$ .
In panel (c), the same lightweight student processes both windows and learns this preference through a confidence-weighted pairwise loss.
At inference, all teachers are discarded, leaving only the student to produce pointwise anomaly scores.
A detailed rationale for CoRank-based multi-teacher ranking distillation is provided in Appendix A.

## 3.1 Problem Setup

Let $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{train}}=(\mathbf{x}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}$ denote an unlabeled multivariate training time series.
For each endpoint $t\geq L$ , we form a sliding-window sample $\mathbf{W}_{t}=(\mathbf{x}_{t-L+1},\dots,\mathbf{x}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D}$ .
We assume access to $M$ frozen pre-trained teacher detectors $\{f_{1},\dots,f_{M}\}$ .
Each teacher provides an anomaly score $z_{t}^{(m)}$ aligned with endpoint $t$ , and these teacher scores are normalized independently.
The student takes the sliding-window sample $\mathbf{W}_{t}$ as input and outputs a scalar prediction $\hat{z}_{t}$ for the same endpoint.
No anomaly labels are used, and the normalized teacher scores provide the only supervision signal for training.
After training, the teacher detectors are discarded, and the student alone processes each test window to produce a scalar anomaly score.
The goal is to learn a single deployable student from unlabeled data and frozen teacher score sequences by capturing pairwise anomaly preferences supported by multiple teachers.

## 3.2 Teacher Score Normalization

Each teacher produces anomaly scores on a detector-specific scale.
We therefore min-max normalize each teacher score sequence independently using only training-set statistics.
This yields normalized teacher scores $\tilde{z}_{t}^{(m)}\in[0,1]$ on the training series.
This preserves within-teacher ordering while reducing cross-teacher scale mismatch for distillation.
Although teacher score normalization does not make teacher scores a reliable shared regression target, it makes teacher-specific score gaps comparable enough for pairwise supervision because their possible ranges are aligned.
AnoMix then computes pairwise teacher score gaps from these normalized scores.
These gap magnitudes are used later to select informative pairs and weight pairwise comparisons derived from teacher scores.

## 3.3 Student Architecture

We use a lightweight causal temporal convolutional network (TCN) student with one scalar output.
This architecture matches the endpoint-based scoring protocol, where each input window is assigned the anomaly score of its final timestep.
Given a window $\mathbf{W}_{t}$ , a linear projection maps it to $\mathbf{H}^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times H}$ , $N$ causal temporal blocks [34] produce $\mathbf{H}^{(N)}$ , and the endpoint representation $\mathbf{h}_{t}=\mathbf{H}^{(N)}_{L}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}$ is mapped to a scalar score $\hat{z}_{t}=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_{t}+b$ .
This lightweight design helps separate the effect of AnoMix’s multi-teacher ranking distillation from gains due to a complex student architecture.
Architectural details for both the main student and the zero-shot variant are provided in Appendix B.

## 3.4 CoRank Loss

The main challenge is not choosing a ranking loss, but constructing reliable ranking supervision from heterogeneous teachers.
CoRank therefore uses a standard pairwise logistic form, but differs from conventional ranking losses in the situation it addresses.
RankNet [30], max-margin ranking [31], listwise ranking [32], and differentiable sorting and ranking objectives [33] can be considered when a target ordering is already available.
In AnoMix, no anomaly labels are available, and no single teacher provides a reliable target ordering on its own.
A straightforward baseline is to regress student outputs directly to teacher scores.
In TSAD, however, direct regression can spend student capacity fitting the score scale of many normal or low-score regions, and detector-specific calibration differences remain even after normalization.
AnoMix instead learns from pairwise score gaps whose directions are supported by multiple teachers.

Consider a mini-batch of $B$ windows.
Let $\tilde{z}_{i}^{(m)}$ denote the normalized score assigned by teacher $m$ to sample $i$ , and let $\hat{z}_{i}$ denote the corresponding student prediction.
We denote teacher $m$ ’s signed score gap by $\Delta_{ij}^{(m)}=\tilde{z}_{i}^{(m)}-\tilde{z}_{j}^{(m)}$ .
From the batch, we enumerate all unordered non-identical pairs $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ and retain only those pairs for which at least one teacher exhibits a meaningful score gap:

 $\mathcal{P}=\left\{(i,j)\;:\;1\leq i<j\leq B,\;\max_{m}\left|\Delta_{ij}^{(m)}\right|>\delta\right\}.$ 

(1)

The pair selection step in panel (b) of Figure 1 removes pairs whose teacher score gaps are too small to provide meaningful anomaly-preference supervision.
The resulting set $\mathcal{P}$ defines the consensus support and contains the meaningful teacher-induced comparisons used for consensus supervision before teacher scores are averaged.

Once a pair $(i,j)$ is retained in $\mathcal{P}$ , every teacher contributes its signed score gap $\Delta_{ij}^{(m)}$ .
Using all teacher score gaps for each retained pair allows the final supervision to reflect the full degree of cross-teacher agreement or disagreement on that pair, rather than only the strongest response.
We aggregate these signed gaps to form the teacher consensus

 $v_{ij}=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\Delta_{ij}^{(m)},\qquad c_{ij}=\frac{|v_{ij}|}{\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left|\Delta_{ij}^{(m)}\right|}.$ 

(2)

Here, $y_{ij}=\mathrm{sgn}(v_{ij})\in\{-1,0,1\}$ defines the consensus direction, where $\mathrm{sgn}(\cdot)$ is the sign function: $y_{ij}=1$ if $v_{ij}>0$ , $y_{ij}=-1$ if $v_{ij}<0$ , and $y_{ij}=0$ if $v_{ij}=0$ .
The quantity $c_{ij}\in[0,1]$ quantifies how consistently teachers support that direction, as visualized by the confidence bar in Figure 1.
When all nonzero signed gaps point in the same direction, $c_{ij}=1$ .
When their signed score gaps strongly conflict, $c_{ij}$ approaches $0$ .
A high confidence weight indicates agreement among teacher score gaps, not correctness of the resulting preference.
If $v_{ij}=0$ , then $y_{ij}=0$ , $c_{ij}=0$ , and the pair contributes no effective supervision.

The student’s pairwise anomaly preference is represented by the score margin $d_{ij}=\hat{z}_{i}-\hat{z}_{j}$ , the signed difference between student predictions for samples $i$ and $j$ .
The CoRank loss in panel (c) of Figure 1 penalizes student margins $d_{ij}$ that disagree with the teacher consensus direction $y_{ij}$ , with each pair weighted by its consensus confidence $c_{ij}$ :

 $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CoRank}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}c_{ij}\log\!\Big(1+\exp\!\big(-y_{ij}d_{ij}\big)\Big).$ 

(3)

If no valid pair is retained in a mini-batch, we define the batch loss as zero and skip its contribution.

CoRank can be viewed as confidence-weighted distillation of pairwise anomaly preferences induced by normalized teacher scores.
It avoids fitting teacher-specific pointwise scores and does not construct pairwise supervision from an averaged teacher score alone.
Instead, it first constructs the pair support from teacher-level score gaps, assigns the consensus direction, and then uses consensus confidence to down-weight conflicting comparisons.
CoRank contributes a multi-teacher procedure for constructing and weighting pairwise supervision before applying the pairwise logistic objective.
This trains the student network to act as a neural anomaly-scoring fun
conclusion:
We studied whether unsupervised time series anomaly detection can be effectively addressed through knowledge distillation despite the absence of labels and the heterogeneity of teacher anomaly scores.
Our experimental results suggest that it can.
We introduced AnoMix, a multi-teacher distillation framework that learns a single lightweight student by transferring pairwise anomaly preferences from multiple heterogeneous TSAD teachers, rather than directly imitating raw teacher scores.

Across benchmarks, the empirical evidence consistently shows that the benefit of multi-teacher TSAD comes from distilling complementary teacher scoring principles into a new student predictor, not merely from combining teacher scores.
AnoMix outperforms individual detectors and score-ensemble baselines, while teacher-set and correlation analyses further indicate that it learns beyond static ensemble behavior and remains effective under broader teacher pools.
The zero-shot cross-dataset results further show that AnoMix-ZS remains effective on unseen datasets and can compete with much larger pretrained time-series foundation models.

Although teachers use complex, detector-specific models, their scoring principles are ultimately expressed through scalar anomaly scores.
Our results suggest that learning pairwise preferences from these scores allows a compact student to integrate complementary scoring principles without reproducing the teachers’ internal models.
A more detailed discussion of limitations and future directions is provided in Appendix Q.

title: Our Own Jev: Typed Decisions in One Forward Pass, from an In-House Judge to Open LoRA Models
abstract: A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option, computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model's logits or a small head over its hidden states, instead of generating and parsing text. The commercial system Jev popularised this System~1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We report two uses of the pattern. \emph{Part I} describes an in-house System~1 judge that triages about 148K agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of \$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9\% of the sessions where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about \$0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1\% of the frontier judge's cost, and keeps every session inside the organisation. \emph{Part II} asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones (1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3\%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0\%, unadjusted $p=0.12$) and ahead of five open systems after Holm--Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain on a later corpus release moves the 2B's hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations resolve.

body_start:
Abstract

A typed decision maps evidence, a question and a fixed set of options to a probability for every option,
computed in one forward pass, by reading a language model’s logits or a small head over its hidden states,
instead of generating and parsing text.
The commercial system Jev popularised this System 1 interface, and open reproductions have followed. We
report two uses of the pattern. Part I describes an in-house System 1 judge that triages about 148K
agentic coding session records for a training corpus. It replaces a frontier LLM judge that cost on the order of
$1,000 per pass and whose stored labels matched a fresh two-judge consensus on only 26.9% of the sessions
where the two judges agreed; a self-hosted frozen backbone with a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head
answers three typed questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU,
about $0.06 at a reference rate and roughly 1% of the frontier judge’s cost, and keeps every session inside
the organisation. Part II asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive and whether training one
helps. Applying the public Eikos recipe and corpus of about 25K decisions to three further backbones
(1B, 2B and 35B), we read the frozen output layer of a LoRA-adapted decoder. On the 111 public hard items of
JevBench our single-seed 35B, developed with those items in view, scores 79.3%, not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0%, unadjusted
 $p=0.12$ ) and ahead of five open systems after Holm–Bonferroni correction; our 2B is ahead of all four kev
checkpoints on the leaderboard. A single-seed ablation finds no detectable benefit from training the 26 letter rows of the output layer, and a retrain
on a later corpus release moves the 2B’s hard-tier accuracy by 11.7 points, which shows how little small evaluations
resolve.

## 1 Introduction

“System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary
control. System 2 allocates attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it.”
 — Kahneman (2011)

Many operational decisions have a fixed set of allowed answers: which queue a ticket goes to, whether a
clause in a document is satisfied, whether a coding session is worth keeping as training data. Today they are
usually automated with System 2 machinery: prompt a chat model, ask it for JSON and parse the reply. That spends
hundreds of generated tokens on a choice among a handful of options, fails whenever the model writes prose instead
of an object, and returns a confidence value the model composes as text rather than computes.

A typed decision interface is the System 1 alternative. Given evidence, a question and the
options, the model returns a probability for every option from a single forward pass, read from the model’s outputs
(its logits, or a small head over its hidden states) rather than generated. The commercial system Jev
(TypeSafe AI, 2026) popularised this interface, and JevBench (Standhartinger, 2026) benchmarks systems that implement
it on accuracy, calibration, speed and cost. Because the product is closed, an open-source race followed, with
reproductions built on encoders, frozen base models, pointer heads and new readouts (Section 2);
a fifth project, Eikos (Vicentino, 2026), releases a corpus, a training recipe, an evaluation harness and models that
read letter logits without adding parameters.

This paper reports two efforts with the same pattern in two settings.

Part I: an in-house System 1 judge (§2–2). We
collect agentic coding sessions, about 148,000 session records and growing, as training data for an in-house
coding model, and each must be triaged by three typed questions before it enters the corpus. A frontier
LLM judge cost on the order of $1,000 per pass, needed about 73 hours of judging time, and its stored labels
had drifted to the point that, where two fresh judges agreed, their label matched the stored one on only
26.9% of sessions; the data also could not leave the organisation. A self-hosted judge built on the kev
architecture (a frozen 4B or 27B backbone, a rank-16 LoRA adapter and a pointer head) answers all three
questions in one forward pass, judges 1,000 sessions in about three minutes of one GPU, about $0.06 at a
reference rate and roughly a hundredth of the frontier judge’s cost, and reaches 83–85% (coding),
91–92.5% (in-domain) and 68–69.5% (eight-way domain) agreement with frontier-judge labels on a fixed,
class-balanced held-out set of 200 sessions (1.5 to 3.8 points lower on the 144 of them that share no state
with the training records).

Part II: open typed-decision models (§5–9). Part II asks whether a readout that adds no parameters can be competitive, and whether training one helps. We read the existing output layer of a decoder language
model at the single position where the answer letter would be generated, restrict it to the letters in play, and
train only a LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022) with soft cross-entropy. The prompt format (SemIf’s), the training
recipe, the evaluation battery and the corpus of about 25K public decisions are those of the open Eikos project, which
pairs a letter-logit readout with task training; ours are the adapters for three further backbones (a 1B, a 2B and a
35B mixture of experts), the paired comparisons on JevBench’s 111 public hard items and a single-seed test of
whether training the readout helps. The 35B reaches 79.3%: after Holm–Bonferroni correction it is significantly
ahead of five open systems, but not significantly different from the commercial reference (73.0%, unadjusted
 $p=0.12$ ). Training the readout buys nothing we can measure, and a
retrain of the 2B on a later corpus release moved its hard-tier accuracy from 61.3% to 73.0% although the two runs
differ in more than the seed (Sections 8 and 9).

All JevBench numbers in Sections 6–8 are on the public half (version 1.4.2.2); the
sealed half is scored only by its operator. Section 9 discloses provenance and which builds were
developed with the public items in view.

## 2 Background and related work

Typed decisions and JevBench.

An item consists of a state $s$ (free text or structured evidence), a question $q$ of one of three types
(boolean, categorical choice, or ordinal score), and options $O=(o_{1},\dots,o_{K})$ ; a system returns
 $p\in\Delta^{K-1}$ . JevBench (Standhartinger, 2026), in version 1.4.2.2, publishes 231 items in three tiers (easy 48,
standard 72, hard 111); the rest, including a judge tier, are held by the operator and scored only on submission.

Open reproductions.

Table 1 summarises the open reproductions whose code we read; they differ mainly in where the
decision is computed. Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) is a ModernBERT encoder (Warner et al., 2024). SemIf (Lee, 2026) reads option-letter logits from an unmodified Qwen3.5-4B, with a
structured prompt that Eikos later adopted. kev (Palmer, 2026) adds a pointer head and a block-causal option-isolation
mask that lets one pass answer several questions (Part I builds on kev). imajev (Garg, 2026) adds a 256-code
readout, copied from the output layer and then trained on about a million decisions. Eikos (Vicentino, 2026), the
source of Part II’s recipe, data and evaluation battery, reads the same letter logits with no added parameters from
LoRA-adapted Qwen backbones trained on its own corpus of about 25K decisions. The other systems we compare, from
the JevBench leaderboard (“the board”), are reflex (kshetrajna12, 2026) (a Qwen model read by direct logits),
Winnow (Ring, 2026) (a LoRA-tuned Gemma), djev (Maisa, 2026) (an inference method on a diffusion language
model), jqv (Octalab, 2026) (a zero-shot Qwen3-32B) and OpenJev Verdict (heman10x, 2026) (a 151M encoder). None of
Laya, SemIf, kev and imajev combines task training with a readout that adds no parameters; Eikos does (as do other
board entries such as reflex-4B), and we build on that idea rather than claim it. Part II supplies evidence on other
backbones, paired comparisons with a selection of the field, and a test of whether the readout needs training at all.

Related techniques.

Scoring multiple-choice answers by the probability of an option symbol is standard in LLM evaluation
(Hendrycks et al., 2021; Robinson & Wingate, 2023) and can be well calibrated (Kadavath et al., 2022); models are
sensitive to option order and label bias (Zheng et al., 2024a; Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2024; Zhao et al., 2021), which
motivates our per-example reshuffling.
We measure calibration with expected calibration error (Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017), consider
temperature scaling and report error under selective prediction (El-Yaniv & Wiener, 2010; Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017).
Soft targets follow knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015), the rationale loss follows
Hsieh et al. (2023), and we adapt with LoRA through PEFT (Mangrulkar et al., 2022). Our analysis draws on work on
significance testing and power in NLP (Card et al., 2020; Dror et al., 2018; Berg-Kirkpatrick et al., 2012), error
bars and small test sets (Miller, 2024; Bowyer et al., 2025) and seed and numerical variance
(Dodge et al., 2020; Bouthillier et al., 2021; Madaan et al., 2024; Summers & Dinneen, 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022),
and uses McNemar’s exact test (McNemar, 1947; Dietterich, 1998), the paired bootstrap
(Efron & Tibshirani, 1993) and the Holm–Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979). Our contamination check is an
 $n$ -gram overlap test in the tradition of Brown et al. (2020), with the caveats of Sainz et al. (2023). The judge
of Part I replaces an LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023).

## 5 Part II. Open typed-decision models: readout, recipe and data

The judge of Part I reads its answer through kev’s trained pointer head. Part II asks whether a readout that
adds no parameters at all can be competitive, and whether training one helps. The recipe, the corpus and the
evaluation battery are those of the open Eikos project (Vicentino, 2026), whose released models already read letter
logits this way; Part II adds adapters for three further backbones, paired comparisons with the commercial system
and a selection of the open field on JevBench, and a single-seed test of whether training the readout helps
(§8). It does not compare a pointer head with the letter readout under matched conditions.
The two parts share an interface and a lesson, not an experiment: Part I shows what the pattern buys in a deployment,
Part II tests the readout on a public benchmark, and in both the evaluation sets (200 sessions, 111 items) are too
small to resolve the differences that matter.

## 5.1 A readout with no new parameters

We render the state, the question and the options into a prompt in which option $k$ is introduced
by a letter token $\ell_{k}\in\{\texttt{A},\texttt{B},\dots\}$ , and end the prompt exactly where the
answer letter would be generated. The prompt is SemIf’s structured format (Lee, 2026) as adopted by Eikos:
a JSON object with the evidence, the criterion and a list of options, each with a letter and a description, under a
system instruction to answer with the uppercase letter of one option. Let $h_{t}(\theta)$ be the final hidden state at
that position for a backbone with frozen weights and LoRA parameters $\theta$ , and let $W_{\!U}$ be the backbone’s
own, frozen, unembedding matrix. The decision is

 $p_{\theta}(o_{k}\mid s,q,O)\;=\;\frac{\exp\big(z_{\ell_{k}}\big)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp\big(z_{\ell_{j}}\big)},\qquad z=W_{\!U}\,h_{t}(\theta).$ 

(1)

We call this the letter readout (Figure 5). Only $\theta$ is trained. Boolean, choice and ordinal score questions share
it. With single-letter labels, the configuration we use, one pass handles up to 26 options; larger sets are
answered by a tournament over blocks of at most 26 whose winners are asked again.

Equation 1 is the standard way of reading a class probability from a pretrained output layer, as in the
verbalizers of prompt-based fine-tuning (Schick & Schütze, 2021; Gao et al., 2021) and monoT5’s “true”/“false”
logits (Nogueira et al., 2020), and it keeps the backbone’s calibration over those letters. kev learns a pointer
head from scratch and imajev trains a new $256\times d$ layer initialised from the rows of $W_{\!U}$ ; SemIf and Eikos add no
parameters. Section 8 tests training the 26 letter rows.

## 5.2 Recipe and data

The recipe is Eikos’s and we tuned none of it: LoRA adapters of rank 64 on every linear projection, one epoch,
learning rate $10^{-4}$ , effective batch 32, soft cross-entropy against a full target distribution over the options, an
auxiliary loss on a short written rationale (weight 0.3, never used at inference (Hsieh et al., 2023)) and
option order re-permuted per example. The 1B and 2B follow Eikos’s 4B settings (its first run, without weight
averaging or auxiliary terms) and add a symmetric KL divergence (weight 0.5) between the option distributions of an item
and of its English or Brazilian-Portuguese view; the 35B follows its 27B settings (no views, a 14,000-token context).
Apart from the readout we ablated none of these choices. The data is the public eikos-decisions corpus (Vicentino, 2026) (CC BY 4.0), as cloned on 2026-09-24:
programmatically generated items with computed answers, teacher distributions, derivatives of FinEntity
(Tang et al., 2023), TAT-QA and GSM8K training data, long-context dossiers and the views. Our 1B and 2B used
a snapshot of 25,130 rows (a task family, a topic and a language held out whole, 1,191 rows) plus 1,619 view rows;
our 35B used 24,447 rows. A subset was retracted by the corpus author after our snapshot was taken
(Section 9). Inference is one forward pass and a softmax over at most 26 logits at temperature 1;
several questions about one state share a prefix, as in Eikos’s serving code
(Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024b).

## 6 Experimental setup

Models and benchmark.

We adapt MiniCPM5-1B, MiniCPM5-2B (Hu et al., 2024) and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
(Qwen Team, 2025) with Eikos’s settings by size (Section 5.2); each is
trained once, with a single seed, and the 2B is released as a merged standalone model (Kailune-AI, 2026). We score the
231 public JevBench items (commit fd54ea7, v1.4.2.2; later versions are not rerun) and recompute competitors from its published per-item records, so comparisons are paired (52
systems have such records; we use 15, selected by us; imajev-4b publishes aggregates only). To measure what 111
items cannot, we also use the seven-suite battery of the Eikos repository (7,371 items: the JevBench public items,
DecisionBench, Eikos’s template-generated trade and rulebook suites, which make up 31%, a general battery and two
finance suites) and its policy of deciding at confidence $\geq 0.9$ .

Statistics.

Paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test, and 95% intervals are exact Clopper–Pearson
intervals (mapped to the difference for paired comparisons), except the ECE interval, a 20,000-sample bootstrap.
Because we report many paired tests, we apply the Holm–Bonferroni correction (Holm, 1979) within the
comparisons we report for each model (11 for the 35B, 15 for the 2B and 3 for the 1B, whose comparison with the
commercial reference is descriptive; our selection, not preregistered), call a difference significant only if its
adjusted $p$ is below 0.05, and call the rest not significant, which on 111 items is not evidence of equivalence. A
111-item tier has 80% power only for differences of about ten points between two runs of one recipe (twelve to
twenty between unrelated systems, which disagree on more items).

## 7 Results on JevBench

## 7.1 Accuracy and paired comparisons

Table 3 gives hard-tier accuracy for 15 of the 52 systems whose outcomes the benchmark publishes (our
selection; imajev-4b is added from its published aggregates) and the paired differences of our 35B and 2B from each.
Of the 37 systems we did not compare, 11 score higher than our 2B (up to 76.6%) and none higher than our 35B.
The 35B is significantly ahead of five open systems (Laya, kev 8B, reflex-4B, SemIf and jqv, the last two untrained)
and behind the two frontier LLMs by 17.1 points. Against the commercial reference it is $+6.3$ points (unadjusted
 $p=0.119$ ), so on 111 items we can say neither that it is better nor that the two are equivalent; so does djev, Winnow-
limitations:
• 

Part I evidence. The in-house judge uses kev’s pointer head rather than the readout of
Part II. It is evaluated against the labels of a single frontier judge, which also confirmed the bank
strata, on 200 class-balanced held-out sessions, 56 of which overlap the training records (the conclusions
hold without them). The domain question covers eight of fourteen legacy categories, with no “other”
option. Numbers come from the deployment’s own harness; self-hosted costs are GPU time priced at a reference
rate, and full-pool figures are projections from measured latency.

• 

Borrowed recipe, data and evaluation. The training recipe, the corpus, the prompt format and
the seven-suite evaluation battery with its confidence-0.9 decision policy are Eikos’s. Besides the readout we
ablated only an exploratory ordinal-loss arm and two data-addition runs (Section 8), and our adapters inherit the corpus’s coverage, its teacher and its licence mix.

• 

No matched comparison and no untrained baselines of our own. We did not train a pointer head or
an encoder on the same backbone and data, so the comparison with kev is across checkpoints that differ in base
model, data and training, and we did not score our own backbones untrained, so what the adapters add is not
measured (two board systems run the 35B’s backbone, Section 7). Nor did we train a cheap non-LLM
classifier on Part I’s rendered state, the natural cost competitor to the typed judge, so Part I does not show that
the typed interface is needed for its savings. The ablation tests a 26-row version of imajev’s readout, not its shipped configuration.

• 

No sealed measurement. Every JevBench number above is on the public half of v1.4.2.2, and systems score
far lower on the sealed half than on the public items; we report no sealed result.

• 

One seed and selection. The observed difference between near-identical runs is about one point on a 7,371-item battery
(1.1 and 0.6 in two pairs; we treat differences below 1.5 as unresolved)
and, from one retrain that differs in more than the seed, about ten points on the hard tier; effects below those
sizes are unresolved, including the readout ablation. The 1B
and the 35B were developed with the public items visible, the upstream recipe was itself exposed to them indirectly
(§9), and we chose the comparison systems and multiplicity families from 52 systems with
per-item records.

• 

Retracted training rows. All Part II models were trained on since-retracted rows; only the 2B was
retrained without them, in a run that differs in more than the data.

• 

Evaluation suites. The trade and rulebook suites are template siblings of training data (up to 31% of the
battery), so battery-wide confident-error rates are lower than on external suites. The commercial reference appears
only through JevBench’s per-item records and, for confident-decision error, Eikos’s published figure. The raw $p$ -values of the 35B and 1B comparisons come from the original

title: HumanCentric-Scenes-AI: A Human-Curated Multimodal Dataset of AI-Generated Human-Centric Scenes Across Surveillance, Occupational Portraits, AI-Edited Images, and Short-Form Video
abstract: We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56 AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and per-stimulus metadata. We report depicted-gender distributions from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset and subject-category coverage for the Video subset. HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research, and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of generative models.

body_start:
Abstract

We introduce HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a human-curated dataset of 296
AI-generated stimuli that depict people across four contexts in which
people encounter AI-generated media. The Surveillance subset contains 85
AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset contains 128
AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired design covering
64 occupations with one female and one male version of each. The
AI-edited subset contains 27 real photographs in which a region was
altered or replaced by a generative model. The Video subset contains 56
AI-generated short videos. We curated the images and videos manually over
multiple rounds to make them as photorealistic as possible. For each
stimulus we release the file, the generation prompt where recorded, and
per-stimulus metadata (Table 2). We report depicted-gender distributions
from an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender and compare them with U.S. Bureau of
Labor Statistics occupational gender shares. We report edit-region size
and its association with zero-shot detection difficulty for the AI-edited
subset. We report image-quality distributions for the Surveillance subset
and subject-category coverage for the Video subset.
HumanCentric-Scenes-AI is intended first for human-perception research,
and also for calibration of AI-detection classifiers and bias analysis of
generative models.

The dataset is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license covering
the AI-generated stimuli and the metadata.

https://huggingface.co/datasets/Nima0Kamali/humancentric-scenes-ai

## 1 Introduction

Generative image and video models now produce scenes of people that
viewers often cannot distinguish from photographs
[15, 12, 8].
Detection research has responded with large benchmarks of AI-generated
media. Widely used examples consist of face swaps and reenactments in
otherwise authentic video [17, 11, 5] or of whole-image generations from many generators
[20, 16].

We focus on four contexts in which people encounter AI-generated depictions of people. Surveillance footage is low-resolution and heavily
compressed, and the forensic traces that diffusion-image detectors rely
on weaken under compression and resizing [4].
Occupational portraits carry gender associations that generative models
are known to amplify [1, 7].
Partially manipulated photographs alter only a region of an authentic
image and leave most pixels untouched [14]. Short-form video is a common format on social media, and several commercial generators now produce it.

We release HumanCentric-Scenes-AI, a dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli
that covers these four domains (Table 1). The Surveillance
subset contains 85 AI-generated CCTV-style images. The Occupations subset
contains 128 AI-generated occupational portraits in a balanced paired
design covering 64 occupations with one female and one male version of
each. The AI-edited subset
contains 27 AI-edited derivatives of public-source photographs. The Video
subset contains 56 videos from Veo, Sora and Kling. Every stimulus
carries its generation prompt where recorded and structured metadata
(Table 2). We curated every stimulus manually, selecting for photorealism.
Earlier work found that human curation raises the photorealism of
AI-generated images [8]. The dataset is
built for research on human perception of AI-generated media.

We find that Midjourney images prompted toward CCTV degradation remain sharper than
real CCTV frames (Section 4). We find that Midjourney depicts a man
in 73.9% of generations under gender-neutral occupational prompts and
that descriptive phrasing softens the skew (Section 5). In the 25 characterized AI-edited images, larger edits are
associated with higher zero-shot classification accuracy
(Section 6). The Video subset spans six subject categories, and
the characterized videos have median durations similar to those of their
real references (Section 7).

## Contributions.

We release a four-domain multimodal
dataset of 296 AI-generated stimuli in full, with per-stimulus metadata
for every file (Table 2). We characterize each domain
(Sections 4, 5, 6 and 7) against third-party
statistical references where applicable, such as U.S. BLS occupational
gender shares for the Occupations subset. We additionally analyze an initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender across 67 occupations, which shows the generator default that the balanced release set cannot show.

## 2 Related Work

Several widely used deepfake detection datasets consist of faces
manipulated in otherwise unaltered video. FaceForensics++ [17],
Celeb-DF [11] and the DeepFake Detection Challenge
dataset [5] are widely used benchmarks for face-swap and reenactment forensics. Deepfake-Eval-2024 extends this line to manipulated media flagged in the wild across platforms and languages [2]. Earlier work by Korshunov and Marcel
[9] framed face swaps as a threat to biometric
verification. In FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF and DFDC, a face is replaced or
reanimated while the rest of the scene is held fixed.

Other datasets contain fully AI-generated images. GenImage
[20] pairs over a million generated images with real
counterparts across eight generators, targeting classifier generalization
across architectures. Community Forensics scales generator coverage to several
thousand models to improve detector generalization
[16]. Corvi et al. show that the forensic traces
such detectors learn weaken under the compression and resizing that
shared media undergo [4]. Our Surveillance subset
contains AI-generated images prompted toward such degraded capture
conditions, and we find that they remain sharper than real CCTV frames
(Section 4). For partial manipulation, TGIF releases roughly
80,000 text-guided inpainting forgeries for detector training
[14]. Our AI-edited subset is a small curated set built
for human-perception research, and in it larger edits are associated with
higher zero-shot classification accuracy (Section 6).

Several studies measure demographic bias in text-to-image models. Bianchi
et al. [1] show that simple occupational prompts
amplify demographic stereotypes at scale, and DALL-Eval
[3] probes social biases across generation models.
Stable Bias quantifies demographic representation in diffusion output
[13]. Paired stereotype testing reports
gender-occupational bias in over 74% of DALL-E 3 generations
[19]. Our Occupations subset contributes a complementary design. The same 67
occupations are prompted twice, once by name and once by paraphrased
description. This design separates the generator’s male default (82.1% under
occupation-name prompts) from a prompt-phrasing effect of 16.4 percentage
points (Section 5).

Our dataset differs from these datasets in purpose. It was curated as stimulus material for human-perception research,
extending the curation practice of our earlier work
[8] to four domains. The release is small, and each stimulus carries structured metadata. It follows the datasheet
reporting framework of Gebru et al. [6]
(Appendix A).

## 3.1 Curation procedure

Curators reviewed every candidate generation manually over multiple
rounds and kept those without visible artifacts that would make them
immediately distinguishable from photographs.
All images in the Surveillance and Occupations subsets were generated
with Midjourney. We generated the CCTV-style set with degradation-oriented
prompts (Section 4). We generated the gender–occupation set as a balanced paired design in
which each occupation is prompted once per gender (Section 5). The AI-edited subset applies AI edits to regions of
public-source photographs, released as derivative works. Video-subset stimuli were generated with Veo, Sora and Kling from
category-matched prompts. Each AI video was developed against a real
reference clip from the same subject category.

53 prompts do not specify a version. The characterization below compares a

## 5 Images with Gender–Occupation Pairings

The Occupations subset comprises 128 Midjourney occupational portraits in
a balanced paired design. Each of 64 occupations is prompted once with a
female subject and once with a male subject (e.g., “portrait of a female
model on catwalk, shot on Kodak, grainy”). The balance is by construction, so the released subset
supports studies of occupation–gender congruence. The generator’s
unconstrained gender prior is observable in the initial set of generations without a specified gender
instead.

## 5.1 Gender distribution under gender-neutral prompts

Before building the balanced release set, the same 67 occupations were
generated once per prompt style with no gender specified, yielding a
initial set of 134 generations without a specified gender. This initial set is analyzed here and is not part of the release. Under
these gender-neutral prompts, Midjourney depicted a man in 73.9% of
generations (Table 4). The share is 82.1% when the prompt names the occupation and 65.7% when it
describes the role. The direction is consistent with bias audits of other
text-to-image models [1, 13, 19]. Eleven of the 67 occupations are rendered female under occupation-name
prompts. Seven of the eight with a published BLS share are female-majority
occupations in U.S. labor statistics (Table 5).

## 5.2 Gender-stereotype congruence

Occupations carry measurable gender associations. Guilbeault et
al. [7] quantify them as a gender association
score derived from the proportion of male and female faces in online
images for an occupation, where $-1$ indicates fully female
representation and $+1$ fully male. The released metadata supports the
same congruence analyses, since every Occupations stimulus carries its
occupation and depicted gender. We treat a generation as
stereotype-congruent when its depicted gender matches the
female-majority or male-majority direction of the occupation in U.S. labor statistics. Of the eleven occupations that Midjourney renders female under
occupation-name prompts, seven are female-majority in BLS data,
newscaster is male-majority, and model, florist and cheerleader have no

## 6 Partially AI-Generated Images

The AI-edited subset comprises 27 partially manipulated images. Each was
made from a real photograph in the dataset of Kamali et al. [8] with Midjourney inpainting, which
removes, modifies or adds content and leaves the rest of the scene
intact. The results are released as derivative works. The pairwise analyses below cover the 25 pairs with aligned source photographs, and edit-region statistics appear in Table 7.

We coded each of the 25 pairs manually into one of five mutually exclusive edit types by comparing the source photograph with the edited image and its pixel-difference map (Table 8). Replacing one person with another person is the most common edit (9 of 25), followed by background replacement (6) and object insertion or replacement (5), and four edits replace a person with an object or an animal. One edit re-renders a hat and a pair of sunglasses without removing the sunglasses that its prompt asked to remove. Edits that replace a person with an object or an animal and edits that replace the backgrou
limitations:
Several statistics are computed on 25-stimulus characterization subsets,
and the same scripts can be applied to the full subsets. Every difficulty
estimate also ages as generators improve, and the release records the
generator of each stimulus so future work can measure that decay.
conclusion:
HumanCentric-Scenes-AI releases 296 AI-generated stimuli across four
domains of human-centric media. In our analyses, Midjourney CCTV-style images are sharper than the real
frames they mimic. Depicted gender under gender-neutral prompts is
associated with the gender composition of occupations. Zero-shot
classification accuracy is lower for smaller edits. The released metadata lets other researchers test these regularities on the full subsets.

headings: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits
body_start:
Abstract

Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work.
As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention.
Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication.
Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

Index Terms: 
design, mechanisms, humanoid hands, dexterity, grasping, manipulation

## I Introduction

This paper discusses the design of linkage-driven dexterous humanoid robot hands.
With the recent breakthroughs in perception and reasoning powered by artificial intelligence (AI), replicating the dexterity of human hands is increasingly considered the last physical bottleneck that holds back the robotics industry.
Having humanoid dexterous hands not only allows robots to seamlessly handle objects in our daily lives, but also enables robot learning of hand skills directly from native human demonstration.
Other than resembling the appearance of human palm and digits11
 1

 In human anatomy, the thumb is not a finger - i.e., a regular human hand has five digits, including one thumb and four fingers.,
a humanoid robot hand ideally should have at least three degrees of actuation (DOA)22
 2

 Because of the complex kinematics of dexterous robot hands, the term “degrees of freedom (DOF)” has been used to indicate quite different meanings in the literature.
Instead, we have found “degrees of actuation (DOA)” to be a more precise term.

per digit.
The “root joint” of a digit should have two DOAs for tilting, while the “upper two joints’’33
 3

 For a finger, the root joint is an MCP joint, and the upper two joints include a PIP joint and a DIP joint.
For the thumb, the root joint is a CMC joint, and the upper two joints include an MCP joint and an IP joint.
To keep the narrative concise and friendly to a broader audience, instead of the anatomical terminology, we use the terms “root joint” and “upper two joints” in this paper.

almost always flex/extend together and share a single DOA44
 4

 The thumb actually moves differently from the fingers, though the difference is not that significant.
.

A straightforward way to build such a digit is to place the actuators inside or on the digits to drive the joints “locally” with a structure similar to serial robot manipulators (e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4]).
This results in a dilemma of the digit either having weak actuation or being oversize and overweight.
It is therefore desirable to have the actuators placed off the digits, which requires additional drivetrain(s) to deliver actuation to the upper two joints.
The most common solution is to use tendon drives.
The design is largely inspired by human anatomy and has been the mainstream choice of dexterous robot hands [5].
However, without self-healing, the complex tendon systems required for dexterity wear out and loosen up quickly, which leads to demanding maintenance and short life span [6].
Performance of tendon-driven hands is often jeopardized by cable fraying, knot slippage, and tension drift [7][8].
In particular, cable rupture is the top failure mode [8].
In addition, tendon-driven bidirectional actuation requires either two actuators per DOA (leads to sizing problems) or closed-loop tendon routing (prone to loosening and slacking) [9].
The absence of bidirectional actuation excludes the hand from performing certain skills.

Compared to tendon-drives, rigid drivetrains do not have weaknesses mentioned above.
They also provide better precision and can bear higher load [10].
Some designs use geared drivetrains to transmit actuation from actuators placed off the digit to the upper two joints.
[11] shows a representative design in this category.
Each of its digits has a 2-DOA root joint and 1-DOA coupled upper two joints.
Actuation is transmitted to the upper two joints using a bevel gear drive coaxially located with the drive shafts of the root joint. Other than the fabrication hassle and inevitable backlash, complexity of the design results in a hand size significantly larger than human hands.

Alternatively, linkage-driven designs have the potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon and gear-based designs [12].
However, integrating three DOAs with linkage drivetrains in one digit (while keeping the actuators off the digit) poses a great challenge for design and fabrication.
There are only a few presentations [13, 14, 15, 16, 17], which share similar designs and have only emerged over recent years.
Among them, the design presented in [13] is both pioneering and most ready for practical use.
It adopts a novel 5-joint linkage drivetrain to deliver actuation to the upper two joints through the root joint (Fig. 1-a, the portion circled in red).
As impressive as the prototype and demonstration are, the nontrivial number of miniature parts (Fig. 1-b) require serious fabrication capability and make it challenging to balance between durability, size, and cost.
The prototype in [13] has a hand length around 218 mm which is 13% larger than average male human hands.
The design is replicated in [14] and improved in [15] with hand lengths of 255 mm and 219 mm respectively.
In addition, the kinematics of the root joint and upper two joints is partially coupled, which complicates the control.
More details of these designs will be examined later in Section II with a summarizing comparison to our work.
Some other designs work around the challenge by strategically reducing the number of DOAs based on human hand synergies - e.g., [18, 19, 20, 21].
Despite being able to realize a decent variety of hand functions, the strategy does not provide the potential of advanced dexterity that the robotics community is currently wishing for.

Fig. 1: A representative existing design of linkage-driven 3-DOA digit [13], a - schematic, b - parts and components

Our work aims at developing a dexterous humanoid robot hand that

• 

Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints);

• 

Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash;

• 

Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer;

• 

Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance.

As explained earlier, these requirements exclude conventional designs that use tendons, gears (other than in the actuators), or place actuators inside/on the digits, and leaves a full linkage-driven design the most feasible option.
Thanks to a unique design of the root joint, our hand has much fewer parts than existing designs that have a similar dexterity, and can be sized closer to human hands.
In addition, our design also completely decouples the kinematics of the root joint and the upper two joints, which simplifies modeling, estimation, and control.

This paper continues from our earlier publication [22], which introduces the flexure design of the root joint and presents a preliminary prototype of three digits, together with strength test results.
Our prior work suffers from a series of problems, including mechanical interference, non-humanoid topology, and fabrication complications.
The new design in this paper resolves those problems and demonstrates legitimate humanoid dexterity.
In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

## II Design and Fabrication

Figure 2 illustrates our proposed design.
The root joint is the key element.
We present a unique design in the form of a flexure hinge.
The design is inspired by stress-relieving structures commonly used to protect cable connectors.
As a single-piece anisotropic flexible structure, it provides two DOFs of tilting motion while restraining axial rotation.
It gives a wide motion range to satisfy the need of dexterity, yet does not bend sharply.
This is an important feature that allows an elastic drive rod made of spring steel to go through its center and smoothly deliver bidirectional actuation to the upper two joints without the need of complicated mechanisms and many moving parts (as opposed to the designs in [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]).
In addition, bending of the flexure hinge does not force/require the elastic rod to move axially.
This completely decouples the drivetrain kinematics of the root joint and the upper two joints, which greatly simplifies modeling, estimation, and control.
In terms of actuation, the root joint is driven by two RC servos that connect to the root phalanx of the digit through two rigid drive rods and four ball joints.
The design evolves from the classic 2-DOF planar 5-bar mechanisms.
Note that the axial rotation of the drive rods is not constrained because of the ball joints, though it does not affect the function of the drivetrain.
The upper two joints of the digit are coupled by a cross 4-bar mechanism, which is a commonly used design.
Reported coupling ratios of the upper joints of human digits fall between 0.75 and 0.8 [23].
We find a ratio of 0.77 optimal for our design.
The cross 4-bar mechanism is actuated by the elastic drive rod that passes through the root joint.
As of now, we have decided to make the coupling rod go from outside of the middle phalanx.
Other than minimizing mechanical interference and providing a bigger motion range, the option allows easy shaping of the coupling rod to give it certain flexibility, which helps realize the passive compliance desired in hand-object interaction [24][25].

Fig. 2: The proposed design of a digit

Fig. 3: Prototype - (a) whole hand, (b) modular digit, (c) 3D printing of the 2-DOF flexure hinge

Figure 3-a shows a prototype.
The digits are modular (Fig. 3-b), allowing easy reconfiguration of the hand topology and repair.
Thanks to the unique design, the hand can be fabricated using a budget FFF 3D printer, generic hardware (ball joints, rods, pins, and fasteners), and generic mini-scale RC servos commonly available on the market of crafting hobbies.
Because of its nontrivial shape, 3D printing of the root joint can be tricky but can still be done reliably with carefully tuned settings.
We recommend using TPU 95A filament, a 0.4 mm nozzle, a nozzle temperature of 215 °C, a bed temperature of 55 °C with an enclosure, a printing speed of 100 mm/s, a layer height of 0.15 mm, and 15% infill, with the print placed horizontally without any supports (Fig. 3-c).
The upper two joints are made as flexible strips 3D printed with TPU.
The phalanges can be either 3D printed with PETG for higher rigidity or with TPU so that the whole digit body can be made in one single piece to
further simplify assembly.
The elastic drive rod is cut from 304 stainless spring steel wires of 0.6 mm thickness.
It is flexible enough to bend with the root joint without causing significant resistance, while is strong enough to avoid buckling when pushed.

Our literature survey has found four existing designs that are fully linkage-driven, have at least three DOAs per digit, and with all actuators placed off the digits.
Three of them are presented in research papers while the other one is a commercial product.
As detailed in Table I, the parts of our design are not only significantly fewer but also can be affordably made without industrial-level fabrication.
The advantage greatly lowers the barrier to entry for the use and development of dexterous robot hand functions.
The concise design also allows the hand to be made at a more compact size closer to regular humans.
Instead of the custom linear actuators with leadscrews used in other designs, our design uses generic RC servos.
Despite giving a raised back-palm, the choice not only simplifies fabrication but also provides a good backdrivability.

## III Kinematics Analysis

Thanks to our unique design, kinematics of the root joint and the upper two joints is completely decoupled.
That is, when the root joint tilts, the servo that actuates the upper two joints does not need to move coordinately to preserve their flexion, and vice versa.
Kinematics of the cross 4-bar mechanism that drives the upper two joints is simple and well documented in textbooks.
This section focuses on discussing the kinematics of the root joint.
With its parallel drivetrain, the 2-DOA root joint system is a closed-chain mechanism, which means its kinematics cannot be derived easily using a DH-parameter model.
Below, we first present a particular solution to derive its inverse kinematics.

Fig. 4: Notations for inverse kinematics of the root joint

Figure 4 illustrates the notations.
Given the tilting angles of the root joint ${\bf{q}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , the goal is to find the rotating angle $\theta$ of each servo.
Consider a digit frame $\left[D\right]$ attached to the root phalanx and a servo frame $\left[S\right]$ attached to the servo body.
Consider one of the drive rods and its two ends A and B.
The position of point A in $\left[D\right]$ is a constant ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,D}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ .
Its representation in $\left[S\right]$ is

 ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,S}}={\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,D}}\cdot{\bf{R}}_{{}_{D2S}}\left({\bf{q}}\right)+{\bm{\delta}}_{{}_{D2S}}$ 

(1)

where the rotation matrix ${\bf{R}}_{{}_{D2S}}$ is parameterized by $\bf{q}$ , and the displacement vector $\bm{\delta}_{{}_{D2S}}$ is a constant (because $\left[D\right]$ is originated at the rotation center of the root joint).
Given ${\bf{q}}$ , ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,S}}=\left[x_{{}_{A}},y_{{}_{A}},z_{{}_{A}}\right]^{T}$ can be easily calculated using the coordinate transformation.
Meanwhile, the position of point B in $\left[S\right]$ is ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{B,S}}=\left[h\cos{\theta},h\sin{\theta},0\right]^{T}$ , where $h$ is the length of the servo horn.
 ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,S}}$ and ${\bf{p}}_{{}_{B,S}}$ are related by the length of the drive rod

 $L=\left|\left|{\bf{p}}_{{}_{A,S}}-{\bf{p}}_{{}_{B,S}}\right|\right|_{{}_{2}}$ 

(2)

which gives

 $\left(x_{{}_{A}}-h\cos{\theta}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{{}_{A}}-h\sin{\theta}\right)^{2}=L^{2}-z_{{}_{A}}^{2}$ 

(3)

from where $\theta$ can be found using trigonometric addition identities.

The forward kinematics is much more complicated because the two drive rods cannot be considered individually like in the analysis of inverse kinematics.
Nevertheless, we have discovered that kinematics of the root joint can actually be well approximated by an affine mapping

 $\bf{q}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\
c&d\end{pmatrix}\text{\large$\bm{\uptheta}$}+\begin{pmatrix}e\\
f\end{pmatrix}$ 

(4)

where $\text{\large$\bm{\uptheta}$}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ includes rotation angles of the two servos, and $a,b,c,d,e,f$ are scalar coefficients.
We first use the inverse kinematics derived earlier to calculate the servo angles $\bm{\uptheta}$ of 10,000 samples of $\bf{q}$ across the motion range of the root joint.
The $\{{\bf{q}},\text{\large$\bm{\uptheta}$}\}$ pairs are then run through a least squares regression which identifies the coefficients as

with a very good regression R value at 0.981.
