conclusion:
This paper presents a new design of linkage-driven dexterous humanoid robot hands.
Thanks to the use of a unique flexure hinge and elastic drive rods, the design requires much fewer parts than its peers and can be fabricated at a size closer to regular human hands with merely a budget 3D printer.
The advantage helps improve reliability, durability, cost-effectiveness, as well as lower the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions.
In addition, the design greatly simplifies the kinematics of the drivetrains, which is beneficial to modeling, estimation, and control.
Dexterity of the hand is validated using the thumb opposition test, grasping according to Feix’s GRASP taxonomy, and a variety of object manipulation tasks.
In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics analysis and AI-aided control.

As a preliminary reference for reliability and durability, at this point, we have conducted a total of around 200 hours of tests on the same prototype.
Majority of the tests ran over one hour, with the longest one lasted for two hours.
Throughout all the tests we have conducted, two mechanical glitches happened during the early stage of validation.
Both were caused by the breaking of an elastic drive rod.
One was because of a stock defect.
The other was because of improper tooling for shaping the connectors.
Other than those, no sign of mechanical degradation has been observed.

Our study will next address the following aspects:

• 

Rigorous and quantitative study on reliability and durability, especially regarding fatigue of the elastic drive rods.

• 

Refining the topology of the hand to better resemble human hands.
Other than adjusting the dimensions and motion ranges of the digits and their placement on the palm, this also includes reforming the palm surface and adding a thenar web space between the thumb and index finger.

• 

Optimizing the coupled kinematics of the upper two joints. In particular, the coupling rod shall be redesigned to go through the middle phalanx instead of from outside.
Its shaping shall be studied in detail to obtain a proper nonlinear flexibility for passive compliance.

• 

Redesigning the root joint of the thumb. Specially, the 2-DOF flexure hinge shall be redesigned to couple an axial rotation to the lateral swing of the thumb.

• 

Exploring 3D printing settings for reliably printing a whole digit body in one piece while achieving proper flexibility at the joints and s

title: Enhancing Cross-Grade Generalization in Banana Variety Classification via Hybrid CNN-Transformers and Knowledge Self-Distillation
abstract: In recent years, automated fruit classification systems have become a more critical component in precision agriculture for efficient yield estimation, quality control, and supply chain optimization. However, they still face significant challenges under varying quality, fruit maturity, illumination, texture degradation, morphological attributes, domain shift, and post-harvest handling conditions. In this study, we address the challenging issue of cross-grade banana variety classification. This is a real-world setting where models that have been trained on specific quality grades must generalize to unseen grades to handle significant domain shift. Under a rigorous Leave-One-Grade-Out evaluation protocol, we present a thorough comparative analysis of CNNs, ViTs, and dual-stream hybrid architectures using a large-scale dataset of 31,678 banana images with three varieties and three quality grades. Specifically, to address the drawbacks of single-paradigm frameworks, we present a dual-stream Swin ResNet hybrid framework enhanced with KL-divergence-based self-distillation to align probabilistic feature representations across the CNN and Transformer streams. Comprehensive experimental analyzes show that the presented hybrid framework with KL-divergence based self-distillation achieves better overall performance, i.e., it attains a mean accuracy of 81.25% and significantly surpasses CNN and Transformer baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirms that the hybrid framework in this study improves discriminative feature transferability, improves attention localization, and stabilizes optimization.

Abstract

In recent years, automated fruit classification systems have become a more critical component in precision agriculture for efficient yield estimation, quality control, and supply chain optimization. However, they still face significant challenges under varying quality, fruit maturity, illumination, texture degradation, morphological attributes, domain shift, and post-harvest handling conditions. In this study, we address the challenging issue of cross-grade banana variety classification. This is a real-world setting where models that have been trained on specific quality grades must generalize to unseen grades to handle significant domain shift. Under a rigorous Leave-One-Grade-Out (LOGO) evaluation protocol, we present a thorough comparative analysis of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Vision Transformers (ViTs), and dual-stream hybrid architectures using a large scale dataset of 31,678 banana images with three varieties and three quality grades. Specifically, to address the drawbacks of single-paradigm frameworks, we present a dual-stream Swin ResNet hybrid framework enhanced with KL-divergence-based self-distillation to align probabilistic feature representations across the CNN and Transformer streams. Comprehensive experimental analyzes show that the presented hybrid framework with KL-divergence based self-distillation achieves better overall performance, i.e., it attains a mean accuracy of $81.25\%$ and significantly surpasses CNN and Transformer baseline models. Qualitative analysis further confirm that the hybrid framework in this study improves discriminative feature transferability, improves attention localization, and stabilizes optimization. Overall, the experimental results demonstrate how well hybrid distillation techniques can lead to domain robust agricultural systems and can be considered a promising direction for robust agricultural vision frameworks in the real world.

## 1 Introduction

Automated fruit variety classification is becoming increasingly vital in modern farming, as it supports large-scale yield estimation, quality control, and a smooth supply chain. But variations in growing regions, inconsistent cultivation practices, improper handling during harvest and distribution, inadequate disease and pest management make bananas susceptible to quality issues like bruising, peel discoloration, premature ripening, fungal lesions, splitting, shape deformities, and uneven coloration Al-Dairi et al. (2023). These imperfections significantly diminish retail value and marketability, resulting in substantial economic losses for producers and supply chain stakeholders Fernando et al. (2019). At present, the prevailing grading approach still depends heavily on manual inspection that suffers from low throughput, high labor costs and variable assessment criteria influenced by human subjectivity. Although mechanical sorting systems can enhance grading accuracy, they remain incapable of effectively assessing surface imperfections like bruising, spotting, or peel discoloration. Also, physical contact during sorting often results in secondary damage.
These challenges and bananas being one of the world’s most vital staple crops (e.g., global production exceeding 114 million tonnes annually and serving as a primary food source for over 400 million people worldwide Yasin et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026)) have motivated extensive research into automated classification systems using machine learning and computer vision techniques Zhang et al. (2024).

Machine learning and computer vision-based automated classification systems offer substantial benefits, such as increased processing speed, consistent quality evaluation, reduced labour costs, and enhanced traceability throughout the supply chain Zhang et al. (2024). Early techniques mainly employed hand-crafted features (e.g., color histograms, texture descriptors) combined with classical machine learning algorithms such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and Random Forests. For example, the method in Zhuang et al. (2019); Santos Pereira et al. (2018) extracted peel color, local texture, and local shape features from different banana regions using local binary pattern (LBP) and classifying them using (Naive Bayes) NB, Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and SVM algorithms Ghazal et al. (2021). While Fu et al. (2019) presented a multi-scale method that used VM and AdaBoost algorithms with fused LBP (local binary pattern) and HOG (histogram of oriented gradients) features. Nonetheless, these methods demonstrated limited generalization capability (i.e., failing to capture the complex hierarchical representations), especifically when confronting variations in lighting conditions, camera angles, and fruit quality grades.

With recent advances in computer vision and deep learning, intelligent inspection and sorting systems have emerged as a critical solution to overcoming these limitations. The deep learning algorithms have catalyzed a paradigm shift in agricultural automation, including fruit quality assessment and variety classification. In particular, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized computer vision tasks by enabling automatic feature extraction directly from raw image data Li et al. (2021). CNNs have demonstrated exceptional success across various agricultural applications, including crop disease detection, fruit ripeness assessment, and variety classification Wallelign et al. (2018); Olisah et al. (2024); Gurjar et al. (2026); Ponce et al. (2019). For instance, the study in Sheikh et al. (2025); XU2 (2026) employed deep convolutional features learned from banana images using a transfer learning framework. Specifically, a fine-tuned deep learning classifier was used to distinguish banana varieties based on shape, color, and texture cues captured in the learned feature maps. While, the work in Shuprajhaa et al. (2023) proposed a CNN-XGBoost hybrid model for classifying banana ripening stages, where a convolutional neural network extracts deep visual features such as color, texture, and shape, and XGBoost performs the classification. Moreover, the proposed system used Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) for dimensionality reduction, thereby enabling effective training with smaller datasets.

Despite remarkable advances in deep learning for automated classification of fruit and banana varieties, several crucial challenges remain inadequately addressed Too et al. (2019); Mehdipour et al. (2026); Sarode and Patil (2026). Most current models (e.g., CNNs, Vision Transformers (ViTs), or hybrid architectures) perform well on in-distribution data but struggle to generalize across domain shifts commonly encountered in real-world banana production and distribution as well as other agriculture settings. These shifts arise from variations in quality grades, maturity levels, lighting conditions, and camera setups, leading to substantial degradation in model performance when confronted with unseen distributions of visual or quality-grade features. CNNs, while effective at capturing local texture and shape information, often fail to model global structural relationships critical for distinguishing visually similar varieties. Conversely, ViTs capture long-range dependencies and global context but typically require large datasets and may underutilize local texture cues that remain discriminative under quality degradation. Hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of both paradigms show promise, yet their efficacy for cross-grade and cross-domain agricultural classification remains largely unexplored. Consequently, ensuring robust, reliable performance across diverse fruit quality conditions remains an open and pressing research problem in precision banana agriculture. All in all, not only do existing methods struggle to generalize when confronted with unseen quality grades (particularly in settings where inter-class differences are subtle and intra-class variability is high), but the effectiveness of hybrid architectures that combine complementary strengths for cross-grade classification remains underexplored.

As deep learning and vision-based systems are increasingly being deployed in banana orchards, packing houses, and markets, robustness to variations in grades, lighting, maturity, and surface quality is as crucial as classification accuracy. Thus, in this work, we focus on cross-grade banana variety classification, a challenging yet practically relevant task. To address the limitations of single-paradigm models, we propose a dual-stream CNN-Transformer hybrid architecture augmented with KL-divergence-based distillation. By encouraging alignment between the predictive distributions of a Swin Transformer (teacher) and a ResNet-based CNN (student), the model learns grade-invariant representations that are more robust to domain shift.
The primary novelty of this work lies not only in the proposed CNN-Transformer architecture, but also in establishing cross-grade generalisability as a distinct and practically meaningful evaluation problem for banana variety classification. This paper makes the following key contributions:

• 

We establish a Leave-One-Grade-Out (LOGO) cross-validation framework, in which each grade is completely held out during testing, providing a more realistic assessment of model robustness to unseen grades than conventional random splits.

• 

We systematically evaluate CNNs, Vision Transformers, and hybrid architectures under the LOGO protocol, thereby offering one of the first large-scale studies of banana variety classification under a rigorous cross-grade evaluation protocol.

• 

We introduce a hybrid model integrating a Swin Transformer and ResNet backbone to leverage feature fusion to improve cross-grade generalization and outperform pure CNN or Transformer baselines.

• 

We propose a self-distillation mechanism that aligns probability distributions between architectural streams, significantly improving robustness on challenging domains and accelerating convergence.

• 

Through attention-based visualizations (Grad-CAM and Score-CAM), inter-stream alignment analysis, and training dynamics studies, we offer in-depth insights into how hybrid representations and knowledge distillation jointly mitigate domain shift effects.

To the best of our knowledge, we present the first systematic investigation of banana variety classification under a rigorous cross-grade generalisation setting. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work, and Section 3 describes the dataset. Section 4 presents the problem formulation, our proposed hybrid architecture, and KL-divergence-based feature alignment. Section 5 details the experimental analysis, including quantitative, interpretability, and qualitative results. Section 8 presents conclusions with future research directions.

## 2 Related Work

The utilization of computer vision (CV) and machine learning (ML) to horticultural variety classification has evolved considerably over the past two decades. CV and ML have been widely applied to fruit detection and classification tasks, including apple, mango, citrus, and banana varieties Too et al. (2019). In particular, most initial works in this field typically involved manual feature engineering, i.e., extracting local and texture characteristics, e.g., color histograms, image texture descriptors and shape features Liakos et al. (2018). For example, the study in Dittakan et al. (2017) extracted scale-invariant shape features and used a Bayesian-based classifier for banana cultivar classification. Other works include the use of geometrical, shape, and color features with discriminant analysis for corn variety recognition Chen et al. (2010), principal component analysis for basmati rice classification Kambo and Yerpude (2014), color statistical and texture features for tomato grading Arakeri and Lakshmana (2016), and morpho-colorimetric descriptors and LDA to classify plum varieties Sarigu et al. (2017). Such traditional ML based systems achievied moderate success under controlled settings but demonstrated lower robustness to environmental variations and required significant domain expertise for feature design.

The rise of deep learning reduced dependence on hand-crafted features and traditional machine learning classifiers. Researchers have successfully employed deep learning architectures for various fruit classification applications and achieved higher accuracy than traditional techniques. In particular, most studies have used CNNs as the dominant approach in agricultural image analysis Zangana et al. (2024). Models such as AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, and EfficientNet have achieved strong performance in fruit defect detection, classification, and grading. For instance, authors in Al Haque et al. (2021) devised a CNN-based framework for strain detection and quality identification of bananas. The work in Dinata et al. (2021) utilised a CNN-based classification framework for strawberry plant disease detection. Recently, Vision Transformers (ViTs) have provided an alternative to CNNs by modeling self-attention mechanisms to model global dependencies in images and videos Mehdipour et al. (2025). Research studies have shown that ViTs can rival or exceed CNNs on some agriculture tasks. For instance, the study in Sharma and Vishwakarma (2024) classified banana plant leaves based on nutrient deficiency using a vision transformer. The problem of fine-grained, multi-defect classification for green plums was addressed using an improved vision transformer in Su et al. (2023). Nonetheless, Transformer-based frameworks usually require large-scale data and fail to assess cross-domain robustness.

Hybrid CNN-Transformer methods aim to integrate the complementary strengths of CNNs, which efficiently capture local texture features, and transformers, which model long-range dependencies Khan et al. (2023). Various fusion schemes, including early, late, and attention-based, have been developed to combine these paradigms. A hybrid CNN?Transformer model was proposed in Li et al. (2020) for multitemporal crop classification, where multisensor data are aligned and Transformer encoders are employed to capture temporal correlations. Furthermore, a framework that integrates local and global feature representations using a CNN?Transformer architecture was introduced in Tiwari et al. (2024). Similarly, Knowledge-distillation (KD), which was traditionally utilized for model compression, has been extended to feature alignment and cross-architecture learning Moslemi et al. (2024). KL-divergence has been widely employed to align probability distributions between teacher and student networks. The systems in Wang et al. (2025) used KD to train a lightweight MobileNetV3 with a ViT as the teacher for green plum defect classification. Despite the remarkable success of deep learning, including hybrid CNN?Transformer models and KD in other vision tasks, these approaches remain largely unexplored for agricultural generalization classification under cross-domain conditions. Thus, our work seeks to address this gap.

## 3 Dataset

This study used a comprehensive dataset consisting of 31,678 high-resolution banana images collected across three commercial varieties (i.e., Pachbale, Rasbale, and Elakki-bale). Such varieties are mainly grown in South Asian agricultural regions Guru and N (2025). These varieties exhibit subtle morphological differences that challenge both automated classification systems and human experts. Three quality grades (e.g., Grades 1: heavily blemished, 2: moderate defects, and 3: premium quality) are utilized to represent each variety. These grades do not reflect variety-specific attributes but rather differences in ripeness, physical condition and marketability. Overall, the dataset is evenly balanced across varieties and grades (as detailed in Tables 1 and 2), ensuring that no single class dominates the training and evaluation.

As shown in Table 2, each quality grade comprises approximately 10,000 samples, resulting in a relatively uniform distribution across grades. This even distribution ensures that accuracy differences largely come from domain shift rather than class imbalance. Grade 1 samples (i.e., 32.87%) show the highest visual noise and variability, and Grade 3 samples (i.e., 32.94%) are the most visually consistent and represent the easiest domain.

## 4 Proposed Cross-Grade Banana Variety Classification Methodology

## 4.1 Problem Formulation

Under domain generalization, we formulate the cross-grade banana variety recognition as a multi-class classification problem. The objective is to accurately identify the banana variety samples that come from an unknown grade by acquiring samples that belong to specific quality grades. Let $X$ and $Y=\{\text{Pachbale},\text{Rasbale},\text{Elakki-bale}\}$ denote the input sample space and set of variety labels, respectively. The dataset $D$ is splited into three quality dependent domains, i.e., $D_{1}$ , $D_{2}$ , and $D_{3}$ matching to Grade 1, Grade 2, and Grade 3, respectively. More formally, let $D=\{(x_{i},y_{i},g_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ , where $x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}$ , $y_{i}\in Y$ , and $g_{i}\in\{1,2,3\}$ indicate an RGB sample, variety label, and
conclusion: Robust automated fruit classification frameworks must obtain reliable performance under different quality and post-harvest handling conditions. This study addressed the challenging issue of cross grades banana variety classification such that the frameworks are trained on specific quality grades and tested on unseen grades. Using a large-scale database with three commercial quality grades and three varieties, we comprehensively compared CNN, Vision Transformer, and hybrid architectures using a strict Leave-One-Grade-Out (LOGO) evaluation protocol. We presented a dual-stream Swin?ResNet hybrid system augmented with KL-divergence based self-distillation in order to overcome single-paradigm models? limitations. The presented hybrid approach learns more robust and grade-invariant representations by explicitly aligning predictive distributions and by using global context and local texture cues. According to experimental results, the hybrid framework achieved the best overall performance and the fastest convergence over baseline models. The enhanced stability and discriminative power are further validated by grade-wise analysis and attention visualizations under difficult low-quality conditions. In spite of these encouraging outcomes, a number of areas still remains for future work such as if using domain generalization and data augmentation schemes could improve robustness even more in extreme visual variability, investigating lightweight hybrid variants might allow for real-time deployment in agricultural settings with limited resources, and applying the framework to multiple fruits or regions datasets would aid in evaluating its wider generalization potential. All in all, this study shows that distillation guided CNN-Transformer hybridization is an efficient and intelligent approach for cross-grade agricultural image classification and inspection systems.

title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents
abstract: A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce \textsc{VeriEvolve}, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent. From task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them. During each round of workflow evolution, the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds, VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases. Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. Cross-environment studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, and GitHub further expose complementary limits from observability, state representation, and search/execution capacity. These results show that executable evaluators can be synthesized and used to guide search when task success is observable and an external verifier is available for calibration.

6.3 RQ3: Refining Evaluators from Execution States
body_start:
Abstract

A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce VeriEvolve, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent.
From each task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them.
During each round of workflow evolution,
the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds,
VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases.

Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. Cross-environment studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, and GitHub
further expose complementary limits from observability, state representation, and search/execution capacity. These results show that executable evaluators can be synthesized and used to guide search when task success is observable and an external verifier is available for calibration.

## 1 Introduction

A self-improving agent can optimize only what its evaluator can reliably
measure. In program synthesis, formal reasoning, and scientific optimization,
candidate quality is often supplied through unit tests, proof checkers, or
explicit numerical objectives
(Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b).
Realistic tool-use workflows rarely come with an equivalent fitness function.
Instead, agents must translate natural-language instructions into structured
changes across filesystems, databases, repositories, productivity platforms,
and browsers. Extending self-improvement to these settings therefore requires
not only better search but also the scalable construction of deterministic,
machine-checkable evaluators.

This evaluation bottleneck is especially pronounced in stateful,
create–read–update–delete (CRUD) workflows. Correctness is determined by the
resulting environment state rather than the final natural-language response,
and may depend jointly on artifact existence, content, hierarchy, consistency,
preservation, and the absence of unintended side effects. These constraints are
implied by the instruction but are generally not supplied as a complete
executable specification. Human-authored verification scripts can represent
them reliably, but they are costly to design and validate; MCPMark reports several
hours of expert effort for constructing each task and its verifier
(Wu et al., 2026). LLM-based judges are easier to
scale, but semantic assessment alone cannot reliably establish that all required
properties of the final state hold.

We study whether this missing evaluation layer can itself be constructed by
agents. Our central question is: Can an agent synthesize a
task-grounded executable evaluator that is informative enough to guide
workflow improvement without access to an externally authored verifier during
search? Our goal is not to reproduce an expert verifier perfectly in one step.
Instead, we ask whether an initially constructed evaluator can bootstrap useful
optimization, and whether the resulting execution states can subsequently
reveal missing constraints and support sharper evaluation artifacts.
We treat this as a feasibility question in a deliberately favorable
setting: task success is observable through the environment state, and an
independent benchmark verifier exists, which we use only outside the search
loop: to admit evaluators, identify false positives, and measure outcomes.

We introduce VeriEvolve, an evaluator-first framework with four
model-backed roles: a Test-Suite Generator, Verifier Evolver, Workflow
Evolver, and Workflow Executor. In Stage 1, the framework derives positive,
negative, and adversarial challenge states from the task instruction and
observable initial environment. Deterministic category adapters materialize
these specifications, and the Verifier Evolver constructs a task-specific
executable evaluator that is frozen after passing internal gates. In Stage 2,
this evaluator supplies a stationary fitness signal for evolving a
tool-use workflow whose nodes retain persistent behavioral alternatives.
Stage 3 then compares high-confidence strong-executor states with
internally accepted weak-executor states, mines instruction-grounded
differences into paired counterfactual cases, and promotes a revised evaluator
only after cumulative regression. The revised evaluator is frozen before
workflow search resumes. The external MCPMark verifier is never shown
to a model-backed role and never ranks workflows or edits an evaluator. It is
used outside the loop for three purposes: admitting evaluators to Stage 2,
identifying which accepted states are false positives and therefore enter
Stage 3, and measuring results.

Our primary controlled study covers all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks. Stage 1
constructs 30/30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, including
62 adversarial near-misses, with 141/141 agreement against the external
verifier on the generated suites. On 122 distinct states later produced
by the executor agents, which no evaluator saw during construction, agreement
is 113/122. Under the weaker GLM-5.2 executor, workflow
evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 at round 0 to
18/30; under Claude, it increases success from 27/30 to 30/30.
Three internally accepted GLM-5.2 states nevertheless fail external
verification, showing that an evaluator can guide effective search while
remaining incomplete. In all three cases, strong–weak state differences yield
regression-verified evaluator revisions that eliminate the original false
positives; for structure_mirror, the weak executor reaches an externally
valid state after a single revision. An expanded PostgreSQL study covers all 21 standard tasks: 15
synthesized evaluators meet the Stage 2 admission threshold, and workflow
evolution closes three weak-executor gaps that the strong executor solves at
round 0, while neither executor reaches internal convergence on the
remaining 12 eligible tasks within the configured limits. Playwright, Notion,
and GitHub stress tests further expose complementary limits imposed by
observability and state representation.

Our contributions are:

• 

We identify the scalable construction of deterministic,
machine-checkable evaluators as a missing prerequisite for self-improving
agents in realistic stateful tool-use workflows.

• 

We introduce VeriEvolve, which constructs task-grounded
challenge states and executable evaluators before evolving persistent
multi-alternative workflows under a frozen fitness signal, and
revises an evaluator from differences between strong- and weak-executor
final states.

• 

On MCPMark, we show that the synthesized evaluators agree with
the external verifier on their own challenge states and on held-out
agent-produced states, that they guide externally measured workflow
improvement for a strong and a weak executor, and that state-difference
refinement removes all three false positives the external verifier
exposed.

• 

We will release the framework code and the resulting artifacts
upon publication: challenge states and frozen evaluators for 30 Filesystem
and 18 PostgreSQL tasks, the 258 agent-produced states with internal and external labels used
for held-out evaluation, and the evolved workflows.

## 2 Related Work

## Self-improving agents and their evaluators.

Language models are increasingly used as search operators over programs and
agents. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve evolve programs against automatically
computed objectives (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025);
the Darwin and Huxley Gödel Machines evolve self-modifying coding agents
scored on coding benchmarks
(Zhang et al., 2026a; Wang et al., 2026b); and
HyperAgents jointly represent task-solving and self-modification roles
(Zhang et al., 2026b). These systems start from a supplied benchmark or
utility. Recent work allows the evaluation criterion to change: the Red Queen
Gödel Machine co-evolves agents with learned evaluators, freezing each
evaluator within an epoch and promoting challengers against held-out
ground-truth anchors (Iacob et al., 2026); self-modifying Lean agents
co-evolve their benchmark while keeping Lean as a fixed trusted verifier
(Li et al., 2026); and the Verification Horizon argues that
verification must develop alongside increasingly capable generators
(Wang et al., 2026a). In each case, an improved evaluator is
still validated against an external benchmark, formal verifier, ground-truth
anchor, or human judgment. VeriEvolve shares this dependence: it builds
evaluators for stateful tool-use tasks without the benchmark’s verifier but
uses that verifier afterward to admit evaluators, select false positives for
refinement, and measure their performance.

## Evaluation of stateful tool use.

LLM judges scale feedback for open-ended text and dialogue
(Liu et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023), but a
semantic judgment cannot establish that every required state invariant holds.
Agent benchmarks therefore check the resulting artifacts or the environment state
programmatically
(Jimenez et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2024; El Hattami et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026),
and agent harnesses build on such executable feedback
(Ning et al., 2026). These checks are written by hand: MCPMark
reports several hours of expert effort per task and verifier
(Wu et al., 2026). LLMs can generate tests and
checks from source code, formal specifications, or agent traces
(Wang et al., 2025; Cunha and Macedo, 2026; Kohl et al., 2026);
VeriEvolve instead synthesizes evaluators of final environment states from a
task instruction and its initial state, and revises them using states that
agents produce.

## 3 Problem Setting

A stateful tool-use task is a tuple $\tau=(x,s_{0},\mathcal{O})$ : a
natural-language instruction $x$ , an initial environment state $s_{0}$ , and a
read-only observation interface $\mathcal{O}$ that exposes the state available
for evaluation. Executing a workflow $W$ with the task’s tools yields a final
state $s_{W}$ . The correctness of $s_{W}$ depends on constraints implied by the
instruction (existence, content, structure, consistency, and preservation of
artifacts), which are not given as an executable specification. We consider
only tasks whose success is observable through $\mathcal{O}$ .

## Evaluator.

An evaluator $E$ is a deterministic program that maps $\mathcal{O}(s)$ to a
verdict $\hat{y}(s)\in\{0,1\}$ , a partial score $r(s)\in[0,1]$ , and
check-level evidence. VeriEvolve builds $E$ from $x$ , $\mathcal{O}(s_{0})$ ,
a set of synthesized challenge states with instruction-derived labels,
 $\mathcal{C}=\{(s_{i},y_{i})\}$ , and deterministic execution feedback; it does not
use the benchmark’s verifier. Workflow search maximizes $r(s_{W})$ while $E$ 
is held fixed, and a workflow is internally converged when
 $\hat{y}(s_{W})=1$ .

## Refinement.

Evaluators are versioned $E^{(0)},E^{(1)},\ldots$ together with their
challenge sets $\mathcal{C}^{(k)}$ . Refinement round $k$ compares a reference
state $F^{+}$ produced by a strong executor with a weak-executor state
 $F_{k}^{-}$ that $E^{(k)}$ accepts. Their observable difference
 $\Delta^{(k)}=\mathrm{Diff}\bigl(\mathcal{O}(F^{+}),\mathcal{O}(F_{k}^{-})\bigr)$ 
is turned into new labeled challenge states, giving $\mathcal{C}^{(k+1)}$ , and
into a revised evaluator $E^{(k+1)}$ ; weak-executor search is then rerun.
 $F^{+}$ is treated as one high-confidence valid execution, not as a
ground-truth oracle, so a revision may add only instruction-grounded
distinctions and must preserve all earlier verdicts.

## 4 VeriEvolve Framework

Figure 1: 
Overview of VeriEvolve.
Stage 1 constructs challenge states and an executable evaluator; Stage 2 freezes
that evaluator while evolving workflows; and Stage 3 mines strong–weak
execution-state differences to extend the challenge set and revise the
evaluator.
One Stage 3 update followed by a Stage 2 rerun is a refinement round.
Purple nodes are model-backed roles, green nodes are persisted artifacts or
states, and gray nodes are deterministic operations.

Figure 1 operationalizes the objects defined in
Section 3. Model-backed roles propose challenge states,
evaluator revisions, and workflow alternatives, while deterministic components
materialize states, execute and gate evaluators, compute state differences, and
version the resulting artifacts. The evaluator is frozen within each
workflow-search run and may be revised only between runs. Figure 2
shows a task example following all three stages.

## 4.1 Evaluator Construction

The Test-Suite Generator maps the task instruction and observable initial state
to declarative positive, clean-negative, and adversarial challenge cases. A
category-specific deterministic adapter materializes each specification in an
isolated copy of the task environment, producing executable states with
instruction-derived labels.

The Verifier Evolver constructs a sandboxed executable evaluator over the
read-only observation interface $\mathcal{O}$ . A deterministic harness runs
each evaluator candidate on the materialized challenge states and returns
case-level failures as refinement feedback. Once the candidate satisfies the
construction gate, it is frozen as $E^{(0)}$ . The initial output of Stage 1
is therefore the challenge set and evaluator

 $\left(\mathcal{C}^{(0)},E^{(0)}\right).$ 

## 4.2 Workflow Evolution under Frozen Evaluation

A workflow contains five functional nodes for task understanding, planning,
ReAct execution, artifact inspection, and post-processing. Each node maintains
a pool of prompt or behavior alternatives, following the persistent
multi-alternative representation of EvoLattice (Yuksel, 2025), and a candidate path selects one
alternative from every active node. The Workflow Executor runs the selected
path in an isolated task environment and returns the final state and execution
trace.

The frozen evaluator $E^{(k)}$ scores the observable final state and provides
partial fitness and check-level evidence. Artifact inspection separately
summarizes execution behavior that may explain the failed checks. The Workflow
Evolver uses these signals to append new node alternatives for subsequent
rounds. Because earlier alternatives remain available, promising partial
behaviors can be retained and recombined rather than overwritten by each
mutation. Throughout a Stage 2 run, however, $E^{(k)}$ is immutable; the
search changes how the task is understood, planned, executed, inspected, or
post-processed, but not the criterion used to compare candidates. The
multi-alternative workflow representation is shown in Appendix B.2
(Figure 3).

## 4.3 Execution-State Refinement

## State-difference mining.

At refinement round $k$ , a deterministic adapter first removes known
environment-specific artifacts symmetrically from $F^{+}$ and $F_{k}^{-}$ .
The State-Diff module then organizes the remaining observable differences into
factual clusters, such as missing or extra artifacts, content mismatches, and
structural deviations. Only clusters that can be grounded in the task
instruction are eligible for refinement.

## Counterfactual challenge states.

For each selected cluster, the Test-Suite Generator constructs paired
counterfactual states using $F^{+}$ and the current $F_{k}^{-}$ as immutable
anchors. The negative state reproduces the selected difference, while the
positive control removes it and holds the unrelated state fixed. A deterministic
label-consistency gate verifies the expected verdicts, and a coverage gate
checks that the pair actually introduces and removes the targeted difference.
Cases that fail either gate are rejected before evaluator refinement.

## Evaluator promotion and workflow rerun.

The Verifier Evolver receives the current evaluator, the cumulative challenge
set, and factual observation-level contrasts between the paired states. It
proposes a localized revision targeted at the uncovered constraint. A candidate
is promoted to $E^{(k+1)}$ only if cumulative regression verifies that it
accepts $F^{+}$ , rejects all prior weak false-positive states, preserves all
previous challenge-state verdicts, and correctly classifies the new cases.
The promoted evaluator is then frozen, and weak-executor workflow evolution is
rerun under the sharper criterion.

A further refinement round is useful only when the new weak state exposes a novel,
instruction-grounded difference that the current evaluator does not already
cover. VeriEvolve terminates when the weak state matches the reference or no
actionable difference remains; when the evaluator stabilizes on a repeated,
already-covered difference; or when workflow search, evaluator refinement, or
the refinement-round budget is exhausted. Repeated production of an error already
detected by the evaluator is therefore attributed to workflow-search or
executor insufficiency rather than treated as another evaluator gap.

Each accepted refinement round appends paired challenge states, a strong–weak state
contrast, and a new evaluator version, yielding an ordered and reusable
evaluator lineage. The external benchmark verifier is not part of
this loop: its source, verdicts, and diagnostics are never provided to any
model-backed role or used for workflow ranking, evaluator repair, or
termination. In our experiments, however, external verdicts decide which
evaluators enter Stage 2 and which internally accepted states are false
positives that trigger refinement, and the r
conclusion:
Once a calibrated task-specific evaluator is available, the bottleneck can
shift from evaluation to search and execution: neither executor converges on 12
of the 15 admitted PostgreSQL tasks, and on the three solved tasks only the weak

title: Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective
abstract: Tokenization that partitions time series into subsequences has become a foundational paradigm in modern time series modeling. However, we find that current tokenization strategies inherently introduce spectral distortions, forcing the learned representations to diverge from the true underlying patterns such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, thereby impairing model performance. Through theoretical analysis from a frequency perspective, we derive the boundary conditions under which such distortions occur. To overcome this distortion, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data. TimeFT obtains tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting, and Nyquist sampling. The method is parameter-free, incurs negligible computational complexity, and can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizers. Our extensive experiments on diverse tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that TimeFT consistently and significantly improves performance.

headings: Rethinking Time Series Tokenization from a Frequency Perspective
3.2 Frequency Domain Decomposition Based on Boundary Conditions
body_start:
Abstract

Tokenization that partitions time series into subsequences has become a foundational paradigm in modern time series modeling. However, we find that current tokenization strategies inherently introduce spectral distortions, forcing the learned representations to diverge from the true underlying patterns such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, thereby impairing model performance. Through theoretical analysis from a frequency perspective, we derive the boundary conditions under which such distortions occur. To overcome this distortion, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data. TimeFT obtains tokens through frequency-domain partitioning, frequency shifting, and Nyquist sampling. The method is parameter-free, incurs negligible computational complexity, and can serve as a drop-in replacement for existing tokenizers. Our extensive experiments on diverse tasks such as forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection demonstrate that TimeFT consistently and significantly improves performance. The code has been made available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TimeFT-75E3/.

## 1 Introduction

Figure 1: Left: The processes of patch and phase tokenization in the time domain. Right: Spectral shifting moves the frequency spectrum, thereby preventing high frequency components from aliasing into low frequencies.

Models [22] such as PatchTST [30], PatchMLP [36] and PhaseFormer [31] have established a tokenization paradigm [11, 18] for time series data by partitioning the raw sequence into a set of non-overlapping (or overlapping) segments:

 $\begin{split}\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{patch}\ i}:=&X\!\left[\,\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}S_{j}\,:\,\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}S_{j}+L_{i}\,\right]\\
&i\in\{1,2,\dots,I\}\end{split}$ 

(1)

 $\begin{split}\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{phase}\ i}&:=\left[\,X[\;j\;]\;\text{ for }\;j=i,i+S,\dots\right]\\
&j\leq N-1,\ i\in\{0,1,2,\dots,I\}\end{split}$ 

(2)

where $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{patch}\ i}$ is the patch token [30] and $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{phase}\ i}$ is the phase token [31], which represent two main classes of tokenization methods. $X$ denotes the original input sequence of length $N$ , $L_{i}$ is the length of each patch, $S_{i}$ or $S$ is the stride, and $I$ is the number of tokens. As shown in Figure 1, the patch tokenizer can be seen as segmenting the sequence in the time domain, and the phase tokenizer can be regarded as downsampling in the time domain. Extensive existing work shows that the tokenization paradigm has become a fundamental component of modern time series modeling (§5). However, the frequency domain effects of tokenization remain largely unexplored.

For patch tokens, rectangular window truncation in the time domain leads to issues such as information loss and spectral leakage in the frequency domain (§A.1). For phase tokens, downsampling in the time domain leads to frequency aliasing in the frequency domain (§A.2). These distortions in tokenization cause the patterns of tokens, such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality, to diverge significantly from those of the original time series, thereby leading the model to learn erroneous patterns and degrading model performance. The fundamental reason for this phenomenon lies in distortions caused by tokenization methods and the constraints that the sequence length imposes on the frequency. Towards this, we propose TimeFT, a nearly distortion-free frequency-based tokenizer for time series data in a model-agnostic and parameter-free manner.

 $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{TimeFT}}:=\operatorname{Reshape}\Big(\operatorname{Nyquist\ Sampling}_{S}\Big(\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}^{-1}\big(\operatorname{Shift}\big(\operatorname{Block}_{K}\big(\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}(X)\big)\big)\big)\Big)\Big)$ 

(3)

where $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathrm{TimeFT}}$ is the set of TimeFT tokens, $S$ is the sampling stride, and $K$ is the number of blocks. $\operatorname{Block}_{K}(\cdot)$ , $\operatorname{Shift}(\cdot)$ , $\operatorname{Nyquist\ Sampling}_{S}(\cdot)$ and $\operatorname{Reshape}(\cdot)$ denote the operations 7, 9, 12 and 13 of TimeFT, which split the time series spectrum into multiple sub-bands that satisfy the alias-free condition, shift all of them to baseband, and then apply Nyquist sampling. $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}^{-1}$ denote the real-valued fast Fourier transform (RFFT) and its inverse transform. The comparison of three tokenization methods is illustrated in Figure 2.

Figure 2: The comparison of tokenization methods across the time domain, frequency domain and reconstruction versus origin. (a) Patch tokens lead to a completely different frequency spectrum and cause the loss of all information outside the rectangular window. (b) Phase tokens cause frequency components above the Nyquist frequency to completely alias into the low frequencies, thereby exhibiting erroneous patterns. (c) Our TimeFT effectively solves the above issues and achieves almost distortion-free tokenization. The details of reconstruction methods are provided in the Appendix B.

As mentioned, TimeFT is a parameter-free method that can serve as a fundamental time series tokenization module for a wide range of models, and its time complexity is negligible (§4.3). We prove that our method solves the above data distortion issue (§A.4). As a result, TimeFT can consistently and effectively improve model performance in various tasks (§4.2). The main contributions of this work are as follows.

• 

We find that the existing time series tokenization paradigm causes distortions in the frequency domain, which leads the data to exhibit erroneous temporal patterns. We then derive the transformation relationships in the time domain and the frequency domain during tokenization and further establish the boundary conditions of such distortions.

• 

We propose TimeFT based on the above boundary conditions, which generates tokens while preserving frequency information by employing frequency-domain partitioning, spectrum shifting, and Nyquist sampling. Our method effectively solves the frequency distortion issue during tokenization.

• 

Extensive experiments demonstrate that TimeFT achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing tokenization methods in forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection tasks. As a plug-in module, TimeFT results in an improvement of nearly 10% in many cases, and the time cost is consistently less than 1.4% of the training time per epoch.

## 2 Preliminaries

In this section, we first define the tokenization problem. Then, from a frequency-domain perspective, we theoretically analyze the causes of the distortions shown in Figure 2 for patch and phase tokens.

Problem Definition.

Consider a multivariate time series input denoted as $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times N}$ , where $V$ is the number of variates (channels) and $N$ is the length of the temporal sequence. The fundamental objective of our tokenization strategy is to discretize time series $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times N}$ into a finite collection of tokens $\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times S\times*}$ that can be learned by models, where $S$ and $*$ are the shapes of the tokens.

Patch Tokenization in Frequency Domain.

Let $x[n]$ , $n\in\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}$ , be a discrete sequence of finite length $N$ . The patch tokenization in Equation 1 can be equivalent to the operation of rectangular windowing. The subsequence of length $L$ is obtained by extracting the segment in the rectangular window and re-indexing it from zero, i.e., $y[m]=x[n_{0}+m]$ for $m=0,\dots,L-1$ . This is equivalent to convolving with a shifted Dirichlet kernel in the frequency domain.

Intuitively, it is easy to assume that patch tokens distort high frequency information [45, 15, 50] due to reduced data length, but the actual situation is much more complex. Applying a rectangular window of length $L$ to a sequence of length $N$ induces three main distortions. First, the kernel’s slowly decaying sidelobes produce spectral leakage, spreading energy from each frequency component across the entire spectrum and potentially obscuring weak signals. Second, the width of the mainlobe establishes an absolute resolution limit: components spaced closer than half this interval merge into a single broadened peak, irrespective of the original sequence length $N$ . Moreover, the windowed sequence is further truncated to length $L$ , so it discards information beyond length $L$ while inheriting identical leakage and resolution penalties.

Phase Tokenization in Frequency Domain.

The phase tokenization in Equation 2 is equivalent to the operation of downsampling, i.e., $y[k]=x[kS]$ for $k=0,1,\dots,L-1$ , where $L=\lceil N/S\rceil$ . If the original frequency spectrum contains nonzero energy for frequencies higher than the bound $B$ , the adjacent replicas will overlap when downsampling, causing the higher frequency components to fold into lower frequencies. This phenomenon is known as spectral aliasing and constitutes an irreversible distortion. To avoid aliasing, downsampling must satisfy the Nyquist sampling theorem [32].

 $2\pi\frac{B}{f_{s}}\leq\frac{\pi}{S}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B\leq\frac{f_{s}}{2S}$ 

(4)

where $f_{s}$ represents the sampling frequency of the original discrete time sequence. The downsampled signal will be free from aliasing if and only if the original continuous-time signal is bandlimited to less than or equal to the new Nyquist frequency $f_{s}/2S$ . Sampling that satisfies this condition is referred to as Nyquist sampling. Detailed theoretical analysis and illustrations are provided in the Appendix A.

## 3 Methodology

As shown in Figure 3, our TimeFT consists of three principal stages: (1) frequency-domain decomposition based on boundary conditions that extracts different sub-bands, (2) frequency shifting translates high-frequency components into the low-frequency band, and (3) information-preserving token extraction that transforms these representations into final tokens.

## 3.1 Boundary Conditions for Distortion-Free Tokenization

Section 2 shows that for any finite discrete sequence $\mathbf{X}$ , there exists a simple method (such as Digital-to-Analog Conversion) that can reconstruct it into a continuous process $\mathcal{X}$ (an infinite sequence) over a period of time. $\mathbf{X}$ can be regarded as being obtained from $\mathcal{X}$ . When the boundary conditions are satisfied, both the sampling and reconstruction processes are invertible and lossless, and in this case $\mathbf{X}$ is equivalent to $\mathcal{X}$ . However, due to the finite length constraint on the information contained in $\mathbf{X}$ , an incorrect $\mathcal{X}$ is often reconstructed, leading to tokens of erroneous patterns. We next present the boundary conditions for this conversion.

Boundary Condition for Patch Tokenization.

Patch tokenization multiplies $x[n]$ by a rectangular window of length $L$ and extracts the non-zero segment. The necessary and sufficient condition for the token to retain all the information required for an exact reconstruction of the original signal is that the entire valid sequence of $x[n]$ is contained within the windowed interval. For a finite-duration sequence of length $N$ , this condition is satisfied if and only if the window covers all non-zero values. If $x[n]$ is periodic with period $T$ , the condition becomes $L=mT$ ( $m\in\mathbb{N}^{+}$ ), which means that any contiguous $L$ sample block then suffices for perfect periodic extension, completely eliminating information loss. However, these situations rarely occur for general time series.

Boundary Condition for Phase Tokenization.

Compared to patch tokenization, the boundary condition of phase tokenization is much simpler. Due to the Nyquist sampling theorem, the alias-free condition requires $x[n]$ to satisfy Equation 4. Therefore, for any discrete $x[n]$ , we define:

 $B_{N}=\lfloor\frac{N}{2S}\rfloor$ 

(5)

As long as the maximum frequency component of $x[n]$ is less than or equal to $B_{N}$ , it satisfies the boundary condition for phase tokenization. In this case, the original sequence can be perfectly recovered from the tokens, making the tokenization free from information loss.

## 3.2 Frequency Domain Decomposition Based on Boundary Conditions

Figure 3: The pipeline of TimeFT is implemented by (1) frequency domain decomposition, (2) spectral shifting and (3) information-preserving token extraction. Different colors and markers are used to denote the processes of operations. Based on the frequency threshold $B_{N}$ derived from downsampling without information loss, TimeFT shifts all spectra of bandwidth $B_{N}$ to the baseband, and then obtains almost distortion-free tokens by Nyquist sampling.

In order to achieve lossless tokenization in the frequency domain, we first project the input time series into the frequency domain via the real-valued fast Fourier transform applied along the temporal axis, as shown in Stage 1 in Figure 3. Let $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}$ denote the RFFT operator. The resulting complex-valued tensor is as follows:

 $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{freq}}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{C}^{V\times N_{f}}$ 

(6)

where $N_{f}=\lfloor N/2\rfloor+1$ is the number of frequency bins corresponding to the non-negative frequencies of a real signal of length $N$ . We adopt a channel-independent approach for different variables to avoid frequency domain mixing. For a univariate real sequence $\mathbf{x}=(x_{0},\dots,x_{N-1})$ , its $k$ -th RFFT coefficient is given by $[\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbf{x})]_{k}=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x_{n}\cdot e^{-i2\pi kn/N},\ k=0,1,\dots,N_{f}-1$ . To retain multi-frequency information, we partition the frequency representation along the spectral dimension into $K$ contiguous blocks, each of size $B_{N}$ . This makes the spectral bandwidth satisfy Equation 5 and the boundary condition in §3.1. For the $k$ -th band ( $k=0,\dots,K-1$ ), we define a full extraction that retains only the frequency components within the interval $[kB_{N},kB_{N}+B_{N}-1]$ and zeros out the rest:

 $\bigl[\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{block}}^{(k)}\bigr]_{v,f}=\begin{cases}[\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{freq}}]_{v,f},&\text{if }\ kB_{N}\leq f<(k+1)B_{N},\\[4.0pt]
0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\quad f=0,\dots,N_{f}-1$ 

(7)

 $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{blocks}}=\bigl[\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{block}}^{(0)};\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{block}}^{(1)};\dots;\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{block}}^{(K-1)}\bigr]\in\mathbb{C}^{V\times K\times N_{f}}$ 

(8)

where $K=\lceil N_{f}/B_{N}\rceil$ denotes the total number of spectral blocks, and the last portion of $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{freq}}$ is filled by zero-padding. In this step, we separate the frequency components that correspond to characteristics such as trend, periodicity, and seasonality. Through this partitioning, we obtain a series of sequences in the frequency-domain that satisfy the required frequency band length under the boundary conditions, which is the first step in avoiding aliasing.

## 3.3 Spectral Shifting

However, existing effective frequency bands are located at high frequencies, causing high frequency components to irreversibly alias into low frequencies during downsampling. Therefore, we need to shift the high frequency information down to the low frequency range. As shown in Stage 2 in Figure 3, we align all bands to the baseband and multiply by a factor that compensates for the band starting frequency:

 $\bigl[\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}\bigr]_{v,k,b}=\bigl[\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{blocks}}\bigr]_{v,k,\,kB_{N}+b}\cdot e^{-i2\pi(kB_{N})b/N},\quad b=0,1,\dots,B_{N}-1$ 

(9)

The frequency portion of $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}$ from $B_{N}$ to $N_{f}$ is zero-padded. Equivalently, one may view this as applying the shifting operator $\mathcal{S}$ to each band, which is $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}=\mathcal{S}\bigl(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{blocks}}\bigr)\in\mathbb{C}^{V\times K\times N_{f}}$ . The resulting sequences $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}$ satisfy the Nyquist sampling condition when sampled with a step size of $S$ , ensuring that no aliasing occurs. In Equation 9, the factor is applied to align the phase reference with the time origin after shifting the frequency band. It compensates for the phase shift introduced by the translation without altering the magnitude of the complex signal in the frequency domain. Since TimeFT does not compress the temporal dimension, the phase factor in Equation 9 is ignored for models (§A.4.2). Therefore, Equations 7-9 can be simplified to the following form to avoid computing the above complex steps:

 $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}=\operatorname{ZeroPad}_{B_{N}\to N_{f}}\Bigl(\operatorname{Reshape}\bigl(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{freq}},(V,K,B_{N})\bigr)\Bigr)\in\mathbb{C}^{V\times K\times N_{f}}$ 

(10)

where the $\operatorname{ZeroPad}_{B_{N}\to N_{f}}$ operation denotes appending zeros to the end of each frequency-domain sequence of length $B_{N}$ to extend its dimension to $N_{f}$ . The $\operatorname{Reshape(\cdot)}$ operation zero-pads at the end if the dimension is insufficient. Here, the spectrum will slightly lose the imaginary part at zero frequency. In this way, we obtain a frequency-domain sequence that satisfies the Nyquist sampling theorem.

## 3.4 Information-Preserving Token Extraction

However, the tokenization extraction operation should be performed in the time domain. As shown in Stage 3 in Figure 3, to recover the corresponding time domain sequence, we apply the inverse real fast Fourier transform (IRFFT) $\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}^{-1}$ to every frequency block independently.

 $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{time}}=\mathcal{F}_{\mathbb{R}}^{-1}\bigl(\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{shift}}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times K\times N}$ 

(11)

where $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{time}}$ denotes the time-domain representation of the sequences of $K$ different frequency bands of width $B_{N}$ for each variable $V$ . Then we perform dense sampling: for every possible off

Extensive experiments on various tasks showcase that TimeFT outperforms existing practices and yields nearly 10% improvement as a plug-in module in many cases.

title: SSMCGM-Stream: A Streaming State-Space Model for Personalized Diabetes Management
abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring supports diabetes management but requires forecasting models that are accurate, interpretable, and efficient enough for real-time deployment. We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space model that maintains a personalized hidden state updated with each incoming glucose reading to provide constant-time forecasting, physiologically structured counterfactual reasoning, and interpretable forecasts through hidden-state attribution. Built on this foundation, SSMCGM-Agent delivers risk-aware, natural-language decision support by translating forecasts, explanations, and counterfactuals into grounded recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. Evaluated on the T1DEXI cohort, SSMCGM-Stream achieves forecasting performance comparable to strong neural baselines while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling continuous on-device diabetes decision support.

Abstract

Continuous glucose monitoring supports diabetes management but requires forecasting models that are accurate, interpretable, and efficient enough for real-time deployment. We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space model that maintains a personalized hidden state updated with each incoming glucose reading to provide constant-time forecasting, physiologically structured counterfactual reasoning, and interpretable forecasts through hidden-state attribution. Built on this foundation, SSMCGM-Agent delivers risk-aware, natural-language decision support by translating forecasts, explanations, and counterfactuals into grounded recommendations through a guarded language-model interface. Evaluated on the T1DEXI cohort, SSMCGM-Stream achieves forecasting performance comparable to strong neural baselines while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling continuous on-device diabetes decision support.

## 1 Introduction

Managing type 1 diabetes involves a constant stream of decisions about meals, insulin, and physical activity [1]. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) provides real-time glucose measurements that support these decisions [2]. Despite advances in sensor technology and algorithmic control
[3, 4, 5], current systems provide limited insight into the factors driving an individual’s glucose dynamics.

Currently, glucose forecasting models can anticipate hypo- and hyperglycemic events 30-60 minutes ahead [6, 7]. These forecasts support proactive glucose management, such as maintaining time-in-range [8], lowering an individual’s risk for diabetic complications [9]. However, these models are typically optimized for predictive performance without revealing whether they learn physiologically meaningful insulin and meal effects on glucose. Moreover, emerging transformer-based glucose foundation models [10] introduce computational challenges for continuous deployment such as attention scaling quadratically with sequence length [11]. This is problematic when type 1 diabetes decision support requires efficient inference and training over continuously arriving data. Instead, state-space models (SSMs) can maintain a compact recurrent state with constant-time updates [12, 13], making them useful for streaming and on-device inference.

We present SSMCGM-Stream, a streaming state-space forecasting model for personalized type 1 diabetes decision support using the T1DEXI cohort [14].
SSMCGM-Stream maintains a constant-memory recurrent state paired with a scenario-conditioned horizon decoder. From a single running state, SSMCGM-Stream (i) forecasts impending hypo- and hyperglycemia events; (ii) attributes forecasts to individual-specific drivers; (iii) answers counterfactual ‘what-if’ questions about meals, exercise, and insulin; (iv) cold-starts from population priors while adapting to individuals over time; and lastly (v) integrates large-language models (LLM) as an advisory agent. Together, SSMCGM-Stream provides a framework for interpretable, personalized, real-time glucose decision support.

## 2 Methods

## 2.1 Dataset

Dataset and Preprocessing. We used 24-30 days of 5-minute multimodal data (3,915,944 observations) from $497$ participants with type 1 diabetes in T1DEXI [14], including CGM, insulin, meals, exercise, heart rate, steps, and static demographic characteristics (Table S1). All modalities were resampled onto a common 5-minute grid. For the CGM input, short gaps were imputed by linear interpolation ( $\leq$ 15 min) and forward-fill ( $\leq$ 30 min). Forecast windows spanning longer gaps were excluded, cutting the stream into valid segments. We split participants 70/15/15 into $338$ train, $73$ validation, and $73$ test participants. For fair, leakage-free benchmarking, the decoder observes only calendar time and the planned actions (e.g., meal, insulin, and exercise events) are masked at inference time.

## 2.2 SSMCGM-Stream Architecture

Figure 1: SSMCGM-Stream Architecture. Static and time-varying covariates update a streaming hidden state, $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ , while scenario conditioning enables forecasts under planned future actions.

Problem setup. SSMCGM-Stream enables multiple tasks from a single running state (Fig. 1). At each 5-minute step $t$ , SSMCGM-Stream forecasts glucose over horizon $H$ , $y_{t+1:t+H}$ , from the observed history of glucose and covariates, $\mathbf{x}_{1:t}$ , static features, $S$ , known-future calendar features, $T_{t+1:t+H}$ , and planned-scenario (action) paths, $A_{t+1:t+H}$ , indicated by an availability mask, $M$ :

 $\hat{y}_{t+1:t+H}=F_{\theta}\!\big(\mathbf{x}_{1:t},\,S,\,T_{t+1:t+H},\,A_{t+1:t+H},\,M\big).$ 

(1)

Participant state and conditioning. A static encoder maps $S$ to a participant embedding
 $\mathbf{e}_{s}=g_{\phi}(S)$ , which (i) initializes the state $\mathbf{s}_{0}=\psi(\mathbf{e}_{s})$ and (ii) modulates the history
features through a FiLM layer [15]. Per-variable features are merged by a grouped
linear fusion $\mathbf{z}_{t}$ , then conditioned: $\mathbf{u}_{t}=\gamma(\mathbf{e}_{s})\odot\mathbf{z}_{t}+\beta(\mathbf{e}_{s})$ .

Selective state-space recurrence. The history is encoded by a stack of selective
state-space Mamba-2 blocks [12, 16, 13]. Per channel, with an
input-dependent step size $\Delta_{t}=\mathrm{softplus}(w^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{t}+b)$ and selective parameters
 $B_{t},C_{t}$ , the discrete recurrence is

 $\mathbf{s}_{t}=\bar{A}_{t}\,\mathbf{s}_{t-1}+\bar{B}_{t}\,\mathbf{u}_{t},\qquad h_{t}=C_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{s}_{t}+D\,\mathbf{u}_{t},\qquad\bar{A}_{t}=\exp(\Delta_{t}A),\;\ \bar{B}_{t}=\Delta_{t}B_{t}.$ 

(2)

Here, $\mathbf{s}_{t}$ is the recurrent state of the SSM stack and $h_{t}$ is its readout. At deployment, the recurrent state $\mathbf{s}_{t}$ persists between observations, while $h_{t}$ is the streaming representation for forecasting and scenario decoding.
We use the interpretable multi-expand SSM (MES) Mamba-2 readout introduced for CGM forecasting [17], which attributes a forecast to a feature and a lag.

Scenario horizon decoder. A scenario horizon decoder initializes from $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ and rolls the SSM recurrence (Eq. (2)) over the forecast horizon, conditioned on calendar features $T$ , the gated scenario $A\odot M$ , and the availability mask $M$ :

 $\hat{y}_{t+1:t+H}=f_{\theta}\big(\mathbf{h}_{t},\ \mathbf{e}_{s},\ T,\ A\odot M,\ M\big).$ 

(3)

We decompose forecasts into a scenario-free baseline and an additive scenario effect:

 $\hat{y}=\underbrace{f^{\text{base}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{e}_{s},T)}_{\text{no scenario }(M{=}0)}\;+\;\Delta\hat{y}_{\text{sce}},\qquad\Delta\hat{y}_{\text{sce}}=f^{\text{eff}}_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{e}_{s},T,A\odot M,M).$ 

(4)

This isolates the effect of planned actions while holding the observed history encoded in $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ fixed.

Physiologic kinetic channel. Planned actions are convolved with learned physiological kernels before entering the decoder. For action $a$ , the kernel $\kappa_{a}(t)$ peaks at learned delay $\tau_{a}$ , allowing insulin and macronutrient effects to exhibit distinct temporal dynamics.

 $\kappa_{a}(t)\ =\ \frac{t}{\tau_{a}}\,\exp\!\Big(1-\frac{t}{\tau_{a}}\Big),\qquad t\geq 0,$ 

(5)

The decoder sees $g_{a}(\mathbf{e}_{s})\,(\kappa_{a}*a)$ : the kernel sets an action’s shape and timing, while the learned gain $g_{a}(\mathbf{e}_{s})=\mathrm{softplus}(\gamma_{a})\exp[(W_{g}\mathbf{e}_{s}+b_{g})_{a}]$ sets its amplitude and personalizes it through $\mathbf{e}_{s}$ . Both are shared between encoder and decoder.

## 2.3 SSMCGM-Stream Training and Benchmarking

Figure 2: Online/streaming formulation.
The recurrent state is updated per observation and forecasts are emitted from the streaming representation $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ at anchor points. Truncated BPTT is utilized over defined chunks to update gradients.

Training. We train SSMCGM-Stream over participant streams using truncated backpropagation through time (BPTT) [18]. The streaming hidden state is carried across chunks and detached at chunk boundaries, while forecasts are scored at anchors with fully observed horizons (Fig. 2, Alg. 1). Deployment follows the same state-update recurrence without gradient computations, updating the hidden state once per 5-minute observation. The full model configuration is given in Table S2.

Loss function.
The decoder predicts quantiles ( $\tau\in\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}$ ) at each horizon using the pinball loss,

 $\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{A}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{\tau}\rho_{\tau}\!\big(y_{t+h}-\hat{y}_{\tau,t+h}\big).$ 

(6)

The median ( $\tau{=}0.5$ ) provides the point forecast, while the $q_{0.1}$ / $q_{0.9}$ tails support risk-sensitive hypo- and hyperglycemia detection.

Benchmarking and clinical metrics.
We compared SSMCGM-Stream with persistence, ARIMA, LightGBM [19], LSTM [20], NHiTS [21], and TFT [22] under the same leakage-free forecast-only protocol and equivalent available inputs. Forecast accuracy was evaluated using MAE and RMSE at 1- and 3-hour horizons. Clinical evaluation included hypo- and hyperglycemia detection and Clarke [23] and Parkes [24] error grids. Hypoglycemia is defined as glucose $<$ 70 mg/dL and hyperglycemia as $>$ 180 mg/dL.

## 2.4 SSMCGM-Stream Inference

Interpretability. The multi-expand-state (MES) readout attributes each forecast to additive per-feature, per-lag contributions of the hidden state:

 $h_{t}=\sum_{k}\underbrace{C_{t}^{(k)\top}\mathbf{s}_{t}^{(k)}}_{\phi_{k}},\qquad\mathbf{s}_{t}^{(k)}=\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bar{A}_{t}^{\,\ell}\,\bar{B}\,u^{(k)}_{t-\ell}.$ 

(7)

A prediction traces to each figure k (glucose, insulin, carbohydrate, exercise, etc.) through its contribution $\phi_{k}$ , and unrolling the state exposes at which delay l it acted. Additionally, learned kinetic kernels (Equation 5) characterize the temporal effects of planned actions, while static conditioning captures participant-specific effects.

Counterfactuals.
The scenario decoder answers counterfactual (“what-if”) queries by re-decoding from the same streaming representation $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ under a modified future plan. The decoder receives the planned-action sequence $A$ and a reveal mask $M$ , specifying if the future action is set or unset. To evaluate setting action $a$ to a counterfactual value $a^{\prime}$ , we compare two decodes:

 $\Delta\hat{y}(a\!\to\!a^{\prime})=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{e}_{s},T,A^{\prime}\!\odot M^{\prime},M^{\prime})-f_{\theta}(\mathbf{h}_{t},\mathbf{e}_{s},T,A\odot M,M).$ 

(8)

Practically, we compute counterfactuals where the baseline reveals no actions ( $M$ masks all, a do-nothing forecast) and the edited decode reveals only $a^{\prime}$ . Both share $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ , so history is held fixed, and only the plan changes. We restrict counterfactual queries to in-support configurations of meal intake, insulin dosing, and exercise intensity.

Personalization.
Personalization is carried by the online state, where the learned initializer, $\mathbf{h}_{0}$ , cold-starts an unseen participant from population priors (i.e., static features), and the recurrence updates the state, $\mathbf{h}_{t}$ , as observations arrive. Forecast targets are residualized against the observed anchor $a_{t}$ , $r_{h}=(y_{t+h}-a_{t})/s_{h}$ with per-horizon scales fit on training participants only and $\hat{y}_{t+h}=a_{t}+s_{h}\hat{r}_{h}$ , so no per-participant center is learned and the transformation holds at cold start.

## 2.5 SSMCGM-Agent Integration

Figure 3: SSMCGM-Agent architecture. A large language model interfaces with SSMCGM-Stream
to provide on-device recommendations.

On-device decision-support agent. We interface SSMCGM-Stream with an on-device instruction-tuned language model (Qwen2.5-Instruct [25]) for natural-language decision support (Fig. 3). SSMCGM-Agent maps user queries to structured SSMCGM-Stream tools for forecasting, explanation, simulation, and recommendation, and narrates their returned outputs (Fig. 3). Physiological reasoning therefore remains grounded in SSMCGM-Stream rather than the language model. A perception boundary maps free text to typed model actions through deterministic resolvers over external databases (USDA FoodData Central [26]) and an empirical activity-curve library built from T1DEXI participants. An expression boundary narrates structured outputs and a deterministic guard rejects unsupported numerical or treatment claims (Fig. S6). We stress test the guard across Qwen2.5 sizes (0.5–7 B) with (i) a number-tracking test that perturbs the forecast minimum and checks whether the narration reports the edited value, and (ii) an adversarial red-team [27, 28] of fabrication, unsafe-action, and prompt-injection prompts, generated by Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic) [29] and human-reviewed (Table S8).

Accuracy. At the 3-hour horizon, SSMCGM-Stream achieved an MAE of 27.05 mg/dL, comparable to TFT (26.90) and LightGBM (27.22), while outperforming ARIMA, LSTM, and NHiTS (Table 1). Importantly, SSMCGM-Stream trained more efficiently, 27.4 s/epoch compared with 2594.5 s/epoch for TFT (Fig. 4). Similar accuracy trends were observed at the 1-hour horizon (Table S3).

Efficiency. SSMCGM-Stream maintained constant per-reading computation and memory as historical context increased, with 6.7 ms inference latency and 1.7 MB per-forecast memory. In contrast, TFT latency grew with context (10–48 $\times$ slower over 24–192 h) and its inference memory reached 112 MB at 192 h, approximately $66\times$ greater (Fig. 4). Together with its 0.85 M parameters, these results support efficient streaming deployment.

Personalization. Forecast error decreases as the streaming representation accumulates participant history after cold start, $\mathbf{h}_{0}$ , plateauing after approximately the first day (Fig. 4).

## 3.2 Clinical safety and early detection

Clinical Safety. Forecast accuracy alone does not capture clinically consequential errors; for example, predicting hyperglycemia when an individual becomes hypoglycemic may lead to inappropriate actions. We therefore evaluated forecasts using the Clarke and Parkes error grids [23, 24, 30], which classify prediction errors by clinical risk. At the 30-minute horizon, 98.2% (Clarke) and 99.3% (Parkes) of SSMCGM-Stream forecasts fell within clinically acceptable A/B zones, comparable to TFT (Tables 2, S4, S1 and S5).

Early Detection. Early detection of hypoglycemia ( $<70$ mg/dL) and hyperglycemia ( $>180$ mg/dL) can provide individuals time to respond before an adverse glycemic excursion. Using risk-sensitive quantile forecasts, SSMCGM-Stream detected hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia at 30 minutes with AUROC of 0.891 and 0.965, respectively, and hypoglycemia sensitivity of 0.735 at 95% specificity. Across the full 3-hour forecast, hypoglycemic events were anticipated with a median lead time of 25 min (Tables 2 and S6).

Detection and error-grid safety therefore match TFT to within overlapping 95% confidence intervals
(hypoglycemia AUROC 0.891 vs. 0.910; Clarke A+B 98.2% vs. 98.1%), from a state updated once per
reading rather than a re-encoded history.
