conclusion:
SSMCGM-Stream reformulates continuous glucose modeling around an evolving physiological representation that supports multiple decision-support tasks from a single streaming hidden state. Rather than repeatedly encoding historical context, SSMCGM-Stream updates a persistent hidden state from incoming multimodal observations with constant memory and per-reading computation. This formulation enables private, on-device inference [33, 34, 35].

This perspective complements recent CGM foundation models that learn population-level representations for prediction, transfer learning, and risk stratification [10]. Large-scale models may provide strong population priors, while streaming representations continuously adapt to the individual. Under this formulation, forecasting, explanation, simulation, and personalization become queries of a shared evolving representation rather than separate learning problems.

Diabetes decision support requires both accurate forecasting and explanations of the factors driving future glycemic excursions. SSMCGM-Stream addresses these needs through learned temporal response kernels, forecast attribution, and counterfactual simulation. Additionally, we integrate an on-device large language model, SSMCGM-Agent, that serves as an interface between users and SSMCGM-Stream. Existing work has largely focused on the reasoning ability of large language models applied to CGM data [36, 37]. In contrast, we separate physiological modeling from communication. SSMCGM-Stream generates structured forecasts, explanations, and counterfactual simulations, while the language model translates between natural language and structured model inputs and outputs under deterministic safety constraints.

Several limitations should be considered. SSMCGM-Stream was trained on observational data from T1DEXI [14], limiting causal interpretation of counterfactual simulations because recorded actions were observed rather than assigned under structured interventions. Important sources of confounding include the temporal coupling of meals and insulin boluses, which makes their individual effects difficult to disentangle, and the dependence of actions on glucose state. Conditioning on SSMCGM-Stream’s evolving representation of longitudinal context may reduce this confounding, but cannot guarantee that all factors influencing both actions and subsequent glucose trajectories are captured. title: From Weather to Enhanced Weathering: Weather Foundation Models for Carbon Dioxide Removal at Operational Scale
abstract: Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO$_2$ per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field's mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$$10^5$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. Few-shot prediction, blending the model with a few samples per field, is supported today: TerraNova-ERW recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields with two samples per field, roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field's mean removal, and can cut sampling on our densest fields by 28-98%.

body_start:
Abstract

Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a carbon removal solution with the potential to remove gigatons of CO2 per year, but quantifying that removal today requires dense soil sampling and laboratory analysis. We evaluate five weather Foundation Models (FMs) as frozen encoders feeding lightweight decoders, under a leave-one-field-out protocol on 5,192 chronosequences from 264 fields across Brazil and the US. To our knowledge, this is the first holistic evaluation of weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We find that across weather FMs, representations transfer to ERW: our best model, TerraNova-ERW, built on Aurora 1.5, positively orders measurements within fields it has never seen. Zero-shot prediction of a new field’s mean removal is not yet feasible, and we attribute this to data scale: the same architecture excels on $\sim$ $10^{5}$ natural-weathering sequences, anchoring the scale we expect ERW data must reach. Few-shot prediction, blending the model with a few samples per field, is supported today: TerraNova-ERW recovers over 60% of the highest-removal fields with two samples per field, roughly halves the samples needed to estimate a field’s mean removal, and can cut sampling on our densest fields by 28–98%.

## 1 Introduction

To avoid the most adverse effects of climate change, nearly every mitigation pathway requires Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) to balance hard-to-abate residual emissions, with $\sim$ 10 gigatons of CDR required annually by 2050 [1].

Enhanced Rock Weathering (ERW) is a promising CDR solution, which accelerates Earth’s natural weathering process that draws down carbon over geological timescales. By applying finely crushed silicate rocks, such as basalt, to agricultural soils, ERW accelerates this process to occur in years rather than millennia. Scaled globally, ERW has the potential to remove gigatons of CO2 per year while providing agronomic co-benefits such as improved crop yields and soil health [2].

The key obstacle to scaling up ERW today is the Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) required to quantify the CDR. Quantifying removal currently requires dense physical ground-truth samples, including soil samples, along with rigorous laboratory analysis at every site. Process-based models such as Reactive Transport Models (RTMs) have been used to model ERW, but they require explicitly defining and approximating all relevant processes, such as mineral kinetics, and can be challenging to parametrize and computationally expensive to scale. Meanwhile, deep learning is increasingly applied across climate and Earth system problems [3], and weather Foundation Models (FMs) pretrained on decades of reanalysis data offer rich representations of the atmospheric drivers, such as precipitation, temperature, and soil moisture, that govern weathering rates.

Previous work by [4], to our knowledge, the first application of deep learning to ERW, trained lightweight decoders on frozen representations from Microsoft’s Aurora [5] to show that atmospheric FM representations transfer to rock weathering. We build upon and advance this work by evaluating five weather FM backbones on our own operational ERW data spanning Brazil and the US, to our knowledge, the first holistic evaluation of multiple weather FMs for ERW and the largest evaluation on operational ERW data. We then show how our best model, TerraNova-ERW, can be used operationally to reduce the sampling MRV requires.

## 2 Methods

## 2.1 Task and Dataset

We formulate ERW modeling as a sequence regression task using atmospheric FM representations: given monthly historic atmospheric representations and site-specific features (static soil, dynamic site, amendment, spatial, temporal; see Appendix A2 for the full list of features) at $t_{i}$ , predict at $t_{i+1}$ the CDR rate in t CO2e/ha/yr.

Similar to [4], we assemble a dataset of natural weathering data using the same sources and process. We augment this with ERW data from our own deployments in the US and Brazil. The data is assembled as chronosequences, such that a given training example is a pair of measurements from two time points. In total, we have $192{,}511$ sequences of natural weathering data with global coverage and $5{,}192$ sequences of our
own operational ERW data spanning 264 agricultural fields. The two datasets play distinct roles: all main ERW results (Tables 1 and 5) are on the ERW
sequences. The natural-weathering data is used only in two separate
experiments: a joint-training experiment (Appendix A6) and a natural-only scale study (Appendix Table 7).

## 2.2 Model Architecture

The general architecture of TerraNova-ERW is summarized in Appendix A1; key elements follow.

## Weather FM Backbones:

We consider five leading weather FMs to generate latents: Aurora 1.5 [6], Pangu [7], SFNO [8], FCN3 [9], and GraphCast [10]. For each backbone, we precompute global monthly latent representations by running the pretrained, frozen model on primarily ERA5 [11], extracting the activations from the final encoder layer. At each site, we pool the latent field at three fixed spatial scales (local, regional, global) and concatenate them into a single $d_{m}$ -dimensional embedding per month, obtained for every month spanning $t_{i}$ to $t_{i+1}$ of a chronosequence; this keeps training lightweight. Full details on the pooling scales and per-backbone extraction are in Appendix A3.

## Temporal Aggregation:

The interval spanning a chronosequence can vary, and the $T$ monthly embeddings spanning $t_{i}$ to $t_{i+1}$ must be reduced to a fixed-size representation. We aggregate by trapezoidal integration of the latent trajectory, selected over supervised and self-supervised LTAE [12] alternatives (Appendix A4).

## Lightweight Decoders:

We build upon [13] and [4] to train lightweight decoders that fuse the aggregated weather representation with site features to predict the target. Considering the backbone latents are high-dimensional while labeled ERW data is scarce, decoder capacity is an important choice: we sweep the fusion mechanism and the per-backbone latent-projection width, favoring shallow decoders with wide hidden layers (“light wide”); the backbone latent is separately down-projected before fusion. Throughout, TerraNova-ERW denotes the Aurora 1.5 backbone paired with a light-wide decoder and a $d{=}64$ latent projection (“64d”), with two refinements to its inputs and training: the three location inputs enter without per-fold standardization, and early stopping monitors validation RMSE rather than MAE. This is the configuration selected in Section 3.

## 2.3 Training and Evaluation

## Leave-One-Field-Out (LOFO):

We train and evaluate all models by rotating the held-out field. Fields sharing a 2-decimal location key are merged into components (264 fields $\to$ 101), since splitting fields that are spatially close would leak. Each fold trains with field-disjoint ERW validation, and predicts the held-out component (full LOFO protocol details in Appendix A5). We favor this evaluation approach over a traditional held-out validation split given the dataset size.

## Point vs. Site protocol:

Point Level scores every held-out measurement, testing whether the model captures within-field structure: the capability model-and-measure (few-shot) MRV would use, where model predictions can help complement physical samples. Site Level compares the predicted field mean to the true field mean, testing whether the model can place an unseen field’s overall removal without any on-field measurement: the capability fully model-based (zero-shot) MRV would require.

## Metrics and Uncertainty:

We report MAE, RMSE, and Spearman rank correlation throughout; the row-shuffled ERA5 experiment serves as the pooled no-information reference. Uncertainty ( $\pm$ ) is a bootstrap over held-out fields: resampling the scored components (64 for treated-row metrics) with replacement 1000 times. At the point level, we also report “% best”, the share of the closable error a model removes:

 $\%\,\text{best}\;=\;100\times\frac{\text{constant}-\text{model}}{\text{constant}-\text{best}}$ 

where the constant is each fold’s treated training mean and the best is each field’s own measured median (MAE) or mean (RMSE), the best any single value per field can achieve. It is undefined at site level, where the best case is the exact field mean.

## Experimental Configurations:

All experiments use trapezoidal aggregation and vary a single design choice, so each contrast isolates one effect: one configuration per weather FM backbone (which backbone transfers best), raw ERA5 inputs in place of the latent (the contribution of the FM encoding), and row-shuffled ERA5 (isolating the value of weather information itself), plus natural-weathering co-training, input-group ablation, and tabular AutoML configurations detailed in Appendix A6.

## FM representations transfer to CDR prediction across architectures; Aurora performs best.

We see that the weather FM representations transfer to CDR across all backbones, while shuffling the weather away destroys ranking, showing weather information is necessary (all-ERW point MAE 3.06–3.26 and Spearman $+0.12$ to $+0.29$ across backbones and Aurora variants, vs. 3.32 and $-0.01$ shuffled; raw ERA5 3.21 and $+0.22$ ; Appendix Table 5). The FM encoding matches raw ERA5 on error size at the base configuration, while TerraNova-ERW more than doubles the share of closable error removed (41% of MAE and 54% of RMSE vs. 19% and 18% for raw ERA5; Table 1), and is more robust.
Raw ERA5 ranking collapses on one of three seeds (per-seed Spearman $-0.02$ to $+0.22$ ), whereas the Aurora (base, 64d, 512d), SFNO, FCN3, and GraphCast encodings hold $+0.16$ to $+0.28$ on every seed; only Pangu and the natural-weathering co-training variant share ERA5’s instability (Appendix Table 6). Aurora 1.5 with a light-wide decoder, a $d{=}64$ latent projection, unstandardized location inputs, and RMSE early stopping achieved the best value on every all-ERW metric (point MAE 3.06, RMSE 4.20, Spearman $+0.29$ ; site MAE 1.78, RMSE 2.57, Spearman $+0.26$ ) while being stable on every seed, so we adopt it as our best model, which we call TerraNova-ERW. It was selected among about a dozen decoder and training variants evaluated on the same 68 folds.

## Model-and-Measure MRV is supported; fully model-based MRV is not yet.

At the point level on treated rows, weather FMs positively order held-out measurements on fields they have never seen (Appendix Table 5) with TerraNova-ERW’s pooled Spearman $+0.29$ (Brazil $+0.40$ ), which is the capability model-and-measure MRV builds on. At the site level the model also orders unseen fields (pooled Spearman $+0.26$ ; US $+0.17$ , Brazil $+0.37$ ), but its error on an unseen field’s mean is only marginally below the no-information reference: pooled site MAE is 1.78 $\pm$ 0.18 vs. 1.96 for Shuffled ERA5, and on the US subset 1.50 $\pm$ 0.16 vs. 1.57 (Appendix Table 5). Single fields with few measurements are high-variance targets, so ranking is recoverable where absolute measurement is not. Fully model-based quantification of unseen fields is therefore not yet supportable.

## Natural Weathering Scale:

Trained and evaluated exclusively on natural weathering chronosequences, the same TerraNova-ERW architecture reaches validation MAE 0.014 and RMSE 0.017, roughly 90% lower error than the deployable constant predictor (Appendix Table 7). Given $\sim$ 105 diverse sequences, this model family excels at natural weathering prediction. This anchors our expectations for the needed data scale for fully model-based MRV for ERW. From our own scale-up and the growth of the ERW industry, we estimate this scale will be reached in a few years.

## 4 Operational Deployment of TerraNova-ERW

Figure 1: Sampling-budget simulation (Appendix A8). (a) Share of the ten truly highest-removal fields recovered when ranking 52 fields under a budget of $k$ measured points per field. (b) Median error of the estimated field mean vs. budget. (c) Percent of samples the hybrid saves on the three densest fields at two precision targets.

## Site Selection with Limited Features:

Site-specific features require physical samples taken at the field or, as a fallback, gridded products. We test whether a reduced-input variant of the model can operate before either is available, using only the weather FM latents, obtainable globally from a field’s coordinates alone, together with the planned amendment specification. This Aurora $+$ Amendment configuration matches the full-input model at the same decoder settings on point-level error and orders unseen fields better (site Spearman $+0.32$ vs. $+0.13$ for Aurora 1.5 (base); Appendix A7), and it remains competitive with TerraNova-ERW on site ranking ( $+0.26$ ) without any site characterization. The advantage lies in ranking, not error: this supports prioritizing sites rather than quantifying them, and lets sampling and site visits be deferred.

## Reducing Samples for MRV:

Since TerraNova-ERW supports model-and-measure MRV, we quantify what the model is worth in samples by simulating sparser campaigns on the LOFO out-of-fold predictions: each Monte-Carlo draw reveals $k$ random measured intervals per field, and a hybrid estimator blends the revealed points with the model prediction at weights fitted out-of-sample (Protocol and results in Appendix A8). Three results stand out (Figure 1). (1) When ranking candidate fields, the hybrid recovers on average 63% of the ten highest-removal fields with two samples per field, vs. 49% for sampling alone at the same budget; the model alone, with no samples, already finds 50%, as many as two samples per field (Figure 1a). (2) At every budget below ${\sim}10$ points per field, the hybrid estimates field means with lower median error than sampling alone (1.13 vs. 2.18 t CO2e/ha/yr at one point), and the hybrid at three points matches what sampling alone needs five to ten points to reach (Figure 1b). (3) On our three densest fields, which hold 32% of all treated measurements, the hybrid saves 28–98% of samples (Figure 1c): at the $\pm 1.0$  t target one sample replaces 6–11 samples on all three fields, and at $\pm 0.5$  t Fields B and C need a single sample (96% and 98% saved) because the model alone already places their means within 0.10 and 0.32 t, while Field A still needs 44 of 62 (28% saved).

## 5 Discussion

Pathway to climate impact: MRV accounts for a third to over half of the cost of ERW [14]. Since sampling and laboratory analysis dominate MRV spend, cutting samples by 28–98% attacks the largest term in a cost that can reach $275/tCO2 [15]. TerraNova-ERW complements rather than replaces physical sampling, enabling sparser, targeted sampling designs and helping prioritize site selection. As latents can be precomputed globally and the decoder is lightweight, the marginal cost of modeling a new site is near zero, supporting cost-effective MRV as ERW scales to gigaton removal.

Limitations and future work: Our deployment data covers only two countries and two feedstock types; temporal horizons are limited to monitoring to date; LOFO does not cover entirely new regions. Further validation across lithologies, climates, regions, and longer horizons along with training on more ERW data will enable models like TerraNova-ERW to be more robustly deployed.

We thank Prof. David Lobell and Prof. Scott Fendorf for their expert review and domain feedback, which significantly strengthened this work. We thank the anonymous reviewers for their constructive feedback. This work was supported by Terradot, which provided the operational ERW data. Finally, we thank the Microsoft AI for Good and Aurora teams for providing compute resources and for their generous support and responsiveness as we built on Aurora.

title: Unit-Aware Differentially Private Quantum Machine Learning for Clinical and Wearable Health Data
abstract: Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.

Abstract

Clinical registries and wearable sensors support early health-risk assessment, yet models trained on these records may leak sensitive information when released. Differential privacy (DP) bounds this leakage by injecting noise whose total magnitude grows with the number of trainable parameters, a cost especially severe for small health cohorts. This motivates parameter efficient models including quantum machine learning (QML), whose variational circuits can represent complex decision boundaries with few trainable parameters. It raises a question: at matched input dimensionality and privacy budget, does a quantum model retain more utility than a classical one? We investigate this question on three clinical cohorts and one wearable cohort, treating each clinical record or participant as a privacy unit. We compare capacity-matched quantum, multilayer perceptron, and logistic regression models across five privacy budgets and five seeds. The quantum model leads on three clinical cohorts by up to 0.104 ROC AUC averaged across budgets; however, trails on the wearable cohort, where the small number of participants requires substantial noise. No difference survives Holm correction across 24 tests, so these results indicate a trend rather than a quantum advantage. An analytic gradient bound shows that lower clipping thresholds can improve utility by reducing noise despite clipping bias. Finally, an experiment on IBM quantum computer (ibm_fez, a 156-qubit superconducting processor) using eight fixed test cases yields mean absolute probability errors of 0.046 (private) and 0.063 (non-private) relative to simulation, supporting the feasibility of inference on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. The code is available publicly at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/DP-QML-Health.

Index Terms: 
Quantum machine learning, differential privacy, health data, wearable sensing, quantum hardware

## I Introduction

Healthcare data collection now extends well beyond hospital walls. Clinical registries record diagnoses, laboratory values, and treatment outcomes, while wearable devices continuously capture vital signs and physiological signals, including heart rate, respiration, skin conductance, temperature, and motion. Together they support automated risk stratification and continuous monitoring, improving early screening [1]. Machine learning (ML) enables predictive models to be trained on these data; however, the resulting models introduce a privacy risk: released model parameters can reveal whether an individual contributed data and can retain patient-specific patterns [2]. A trustworthy healthcare model must therefore protect patient privacy while maintaining useful predictive accuracy.

Differential privacy (DP) addresses this risk by bounding how much the output distribution of a training algorithm can change between neighboring datasets, which differ only in the data contributed by a single privacy unit [3]. The privacy unit identifies whose data the guarantee protects: one patient record in the clinical datasets and one participant in the wearable dataset. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) enforces the guarantee by clipping per-unit gradients, adding Gaussian noise, and accounting for privacy loss [4]. Since DP is closed under post-processing, its guarantee remains valid when trained weights are analyzed, including by future attacks. This makes DP-SGD a suitable mechanism for protecting training data when models are released [5]. The protection is not free, and its cost is general rather than specific to healthcare: the excess risk of DP-SGD can grow with the number of trainable parameters and decrease with the number of privacy units [6]. Small health cohorts make this tradeoff difficult: a few hundred records or a few dozen participants may need substantial noise to meet a fixed privacy budget, while heavy clipping can distort useful gradient information. Wearables compound this: each participant contributes many correlated windows, so treating windows as separate units inflates the unit count and overstates participant-level protection. A defensible analysis protects each participant as one unit and accepts the resulting scarcity of units [7].

These privacy constraints motivate exploring models that can work with fewer trainable parameters. Parameterized quantum circuits are promising in this regard, as they can represent complex decision boundaries with relatively few parameters [8]. A quantum neural network (QNN) built from such a circuit provides bounded measurement outputs, while the parameter-shift rule enables analytic gradient evaluation [9]. Still, it remains unclear whether quantum machine learning (QML) can maintain predictive performance under privacy constraints. Hardware testing is also needed as gate errors, readout errors, and finite-shot uncertainty can cause predictions to differ from ideal simulation [10].

In this study, we investigate whether QNNs make more accurate predictions than classical models under DP. We define a unit-aware DP-SGD framework that protects each clinical record or all windows from one wearable participant as a single privacy unit. We evaluate the framework on three clinical datasets and one wearable dataset, comparing a QNN with a capacity-matched multilayer perceptron (MLP) and logistic regression (LR). Each model is evaluated across clipping thresholds and privacy budgets under different random seeds. We use Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [11] with Holm correction [12] to assess whether observed performance differences are statistically significant to establish a potential quantum benefit in this domain. Our contributions are threefold:

• 

We derive a QNN gradient bound to identify a threshold that avoids clipping and test whether lower thresholds improve predictive performance by reducing DP noise.

• 

We conduct an ablation study to assess how encoding, parameter count, and circuit depth affect QNN performance under DP and identify best settings on each dataset.

• 

We run selected trained QNNs on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware, ibm_fez to compare their predictions with exact statevector simulation.

The study addresses three research questions:

• 

RQ1: Does a capacity-matched QNN retain more utility than classical baselines under record-level and participant-level DP in this domain?

• 

RQ2: How do the clipping threshold, encoding gate, parameter count, and circuit depth affect predictive performance under DP?

• 

RQ3: Do predictions from NISQ hardware agree with exact statevector inference for the same trained circuits?

Paper Organization: Section II introduces the necessary background; Section III reviews related work; Section IV presents the methodology; Section V reports the results; and Section VI concludes the paper.

## II Background

This section introduces the concepts underlying our work.

## II-A Quantum Neural Networks

A QNN embeds a parameterized quantum circuit within a hybrid classical-quantum model. Measurement yields a value mapped to a prediction, and a classical optimizer updates the gate parameters from the training loss [13]. Deep circuits complicate optimization [14], and hardware compilation expands them into noisy native operations.

## II-B Differential Privacy

DP guarantees that no single unit substantially affects the released model [3]. DP-SGD enforces this by clipping each unit’s contribution to an update and adding calibrated noise [15], with a R‘enyi accountant tracking the cumulative privacy budget [4].

## II-C The Choice of Privacy Unit

DP’s protection depends on how a data unit is defined. Fig. 1 shows this choice at the unit-sampling stage, prior to clipping and noise addition. A clinical row typically represents one patient encounter, and thus one protected unit. In wearable data, however, one participant contributes many correlated windows. Protecting windows individually still leaks participant-specific physiology, device placement, and labeling patterns across a participant’s other windows. We therefore group the 438 windows in WESAD dataset [16] by participant into 15 privacy units, following user-level private learning [7], which requires more noise at any fixed privacy budget.

## III Literature Review

Privacy-preserving quantum learning has adopted several DP strategies: Gaussian-noise clipping in variational classifiers [17], private teacher aggregation with a student trained on noisy votes [18], federated learning that protects clients without exchanging raw records [19], DP-SGD on variational circuits for time-series forecasting [20], and analyses of clipping and calibrated noise in hybrid pipelines [21]. These studies demonstrate DP training of variational circuits, mainly on image, synthetic, or non-clinical benchmarks.

Fig. 1: Quantum risk prediction with privacy-preserving training.

Quantum gradients can disclose input structure under some circuit conditions: bounded outputs alone do not guarantee privacy, and training requires an explicit mechanism and accountant [22]. The parameter-shift rule can tighten sensitivity bounds and reduce the noise required [23]. These two studies examine gradient leakage and its mitigation yet didn’t adapt an analogous gradient bound to identify a clipping threshold that preserves all per-unit gradients.

Quantum kernels and variational classifiers have reached several clinical tasks, including classification on NISQ hardware [24], ischemic heart-disease prediction from electronic records [25], and heart-disease prediction benchmarked against classical baselines [26]. A systematic review reports methodological weaknesses, limited hardware validation, and insufficient evidence of quantum advantage [27]. These results demonstrate the feasibility of quantum models for clinical tasks, yet not establish hardware-validated quantum advantage.

A remaining gap in QML is the joint evaluation of a formal privacy mechanism with reported privacy expenditure, comparisons with capacity-matched classical baselines, and record- and participant-level protection of health data. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study includes all three and executes a model trained with DP on real quantum hardware. We address this gap by using capacity-matched models, keeping results across privacy budgets grouped by random seed so that evaluations on the same data split are not treated as independent, correcting statistical tests for multiple comparisons, and comparing quantum hardware predictions with exact statevector simulation.

## IV Methodology

This section describes the models, training process, datasets, and evaluation procedure. Table I summarizes the notation used throughout the paper.

## IV-A Models Used in This Study

Our circuit, shown in Fig. 2, uses $d=4$ qubits to encode the four input components and $L=2$ trainable layers with $P=8$ angles. Each qubit starts in $\lvert 0\rangle$ and encodes one transformed feature through an $R_{Y}$ rotation. Each layer then applies four trainable $R_{Y}$ rotations and a ring of controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates connecting qubits in the order $0\rightarrow 1\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 3\rightarrow 0$ . We obtain the positive-class probability $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ by rescaling the expectation of $Z_{0}$ , the Pauli $Z$ operator on the first qubit as:

 $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1+\left\langle\psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\right|Z_{0}\left|\psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle}{2},$ 

(1)

where $\left|\psi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x})\right\rangle$ is the quantum state produced by the circuit for input features $\mathbf{x}$ and trainable angles $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ . For classical models, we use a capacity-matched MLP and LR. Capacity matching means using the same input dimensionality: each model receives the same $d=4$ principal component analysis (PCA) components. The MLP has four inputs, two hyperbolic-tangent hidden units, one sigmoid output, totaling $4\times 2+2+2\times 1+1=13$ parameters. The differentiable LR model has $P=5$ parameters and provides a linear baseline. We use ROC AUC as the primary metric, with PR-AUC, accuracy, mean squared error (MSE), and Brier score as additional metrics.

## IV-B System Overview

Fig. 3 presentes of the proposed system, which contains six different stages. First, the setup stage splits each dataset into training, calibration, and test sets under repeated random seeds, performs preprocessing, and prepares the features and models. The privacy calibration stage fixes the gradient clipping norm and the noise level for each privacy budget. Then, the private training stage trains every model with DP-SGD on a simulator through multiple substages and saves the checkpoints. The evaluation stage is for performance evaluation and compares the trained models with paired statistical tests. Finally, the ablation stage isolates the effect of each QNN design choice, and the hardware stage runs the trained QNN on an IBM quantum processor; both serve as additional experiments.

## IV-C Unit-Aware Private Optimization

We apply the same unit-aware DP-SGD procedure to the QNN, MLP, and LR models. For clinical data, the loss of one record is $\ell_{u}=(p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{x}_{u})-y_{u})^{2}$ . For WESAD, $\ell_{u}$ is the mean loss across all windows from one participant. At each training step, we independently sample each unit with probability $q$ . We then clip its gradient so that its Euclidean norm does not exceed the threshold $C$ :

 $\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{u}=\mathbf{g}_{u}\,\min\!\left(1,\frac{C}{\lVert\mathbf{g}_{u}\rVert_{2}}\right),\qquad\mathbf{g}_{u}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{u}.$ 

(2)

For the sampled units $\mathcal{B}_{t}$ , we update the parameters using clipped gradients and Gaussian noise, normalized by the expected batch size $nq$ :

 $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t}-\frac{\eta}{nq}\left(\sum_{u\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\bar{\mathbf{g}}_{u}+\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}\right).$ 

(3)

Here, $\eta$ is the learning rate and $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}C^{2}\mathbf{I})$ is Gaussian noise with standard deviation $\sigma C$ per coordinate, where $\sigma$ is the noise multiplier and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity matrix. Opacus selects $\sigma$ for the target privacy budget using Rényi accounting for the sampled Gaussian mechanism [28]. Every run uses $\delta=10^{-5}$ , 25 epochs, and an expected batch size capped at 32 units.

Fig. 2: Architecture of the variational quantum classifier.

Fig. 3: Overview of the unit-aware DP-SGD framework, including setup, training, statistical evaluation, circuit ablations, and quantum hardware inference.

## IV-D Gradient Sensitivity Certificate

Let $z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\langle Z_{0}\rangle\in[-1,1]$ . The parameter-shift rule bounds the magnitude of its derivative with respect to each angle by one. Since $p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}},y\in[0,1]$ , each coordinate $\partial\ell_{u}/\partial\theta_{k}$ of the single-record MSE gradient satisfies:

 $\left|\frac{\partial\ell_{u}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right|=\left|(p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-y)\frac{\partial z_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}{\partial\theta_{k}}\right|\leq 1,\qquad\lVert\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{u}\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{P}.$ 

(4)

The norm bound applies to a participant’s mean loss since its gradient averages window-level gradients. For the primary QNN, $P=8$ gives the certified threshold $C=\sqrt{8}$ . Clipping is inactive at or above this threshold. For fixed $\sigma$ , a lower threshold reduces the noise scale $\sigma C$ in Eq. (3); however, it can introduce bias by shrinking gradients whose norms exceed $C$ in Eq. (2).

## IV-E Datasets and Calibration

We divide each clinical dataset into stratified 60/20/20 training, calibration, and test subsets as shown on Table II. For each seed, WESAD’s 15 wrist-sensor participants are split into nine for private training, three for calibration, and three for testing, with 438 one-minute windows in total. We use median imputation to fill missing values and standardization to put features on a common scale. PCA reduces the input to four components for the four-qubit circuit, and $[0,\pi]$ rescaling maps these components to encoding angles.

## IV-F Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate models on four datasets with five random seeds to assess variation across data splits and training randomness. Each seed defines shared training, calibration, and test splits for paired model comparisons. QNN simulation uses PennyLane lightning.qubit with adjoint differentiation. Table III summarizes the setup. Three nonprivate QNN runs repeat one configuration, providing a baseline for each clipping-threshold column. WESAD has seven input features, so eight-component configurations are excluded. We average results across five budgets within each seed.

limitations:
For RQ1, the QNN exceeds the capacity-matched MLP on clinical datasets by 0.104, 0.056, and 0.070 average AUC across budgets; however, it trails by 0.162 on WESAD. No corrected test is significant, and LR remains competitive; therefore, results remain descriptive. For RQ2, performance depends on privacy-unit count, clipping threshold, and circuit design. The certified threshold avoids clipping while increasing noise. Shallow four-component circuits perform well on clinical datasets, while WESAD benefits from six components. title: Black-Box Red-Teaming of Multi-Agent Systems via Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user. Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning-based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.

## Black-Box Red-Teaming of Multi-Agent Systems via Reinforcement Learning

Yuqi Jia†, Hangsheng Zhang∗, Chenxi Liu‡, Junjie Liang∗, Xun Chen∗

†Duke University  ∗ByteDance  ‡University of Maryland, College Park

yuqi.jia@duke.edu
headings: Black-Box Red-Teaming of Multi-Agent Systems via Reinforcement Learning
body_start:
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MAS) to accomplish complex tasks. Prior black-box red-teaming attacks mainly focus on single agents, but we find that these methods are far less effective in MAS, where multiple sub-agents may not directly interact with the user.
Therefore, we introduce ReMAS, the first reinforcement learning–based red-teaming framework tailored to MASs, which fine-tunes attacker LLMs to generate effective adversarial prompts for system prompt extraction. The framework follows a two-step process: first, a rewrite stage refines base attack prompts to increase extraction success, and second, a template generation stage constructs attack templates that improve the likelihood of invoking specific sub-agents and thus revealing their system prompts. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves attack success rates compared to existing black-box attacks, with transferability across different backend LLMs and MAS structures. These results underscore the vulnerabilities of multi-agent systems and the importance of developing stronger defenses against adaptive black-box adversaries.

## 1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems (MASs) [5, 6, 9, 32, 2, 33, 16], due to their strong capabilities in tool use and problem solving. Compared to one single agent, MASs leverage the coordination of multiple specialized agents to tackle more diverse and challenging tasks [30], offering enhanced capability and modularity. However, this collaborative setting also introduces new security concerns. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural way to improve agent behavior through interaction feedback and task-level rewards, but existing RL-based alignment methods are mostly developed for single-agent settings [27, 34, 17]. Interactions among agents create additional channels where adversarial instructions can propagate, exposing MASs to novel risks. For example, prompt injection attacks [23, 24, 19, 11, 29], where adversarial inputs coerce LLMs into overriding their original objectives, pose a significant but underexplored threat in MAS environments. Despite the growing deployment of MASs, their robustness against such attacks remains largely unexplored.

Existing black-box jailbreak and prompt injection attacks mainly target single LLMs [3, 20, 22, 18], while their effectiveness against MASs remains underexplored. A common MAS design adopts a vertical structure with a coordinator agent and multiple specialized sub-agents [6, 32, 2, 8]. In such systems, the coordinator agent selects the appropriate sub-agent and may rewrite the forwarded query to better match the sub-agent’s functionality. This creates new challenges for attacks: an adversary must both manipulate the routing decision to reach the target sub-agent and survive the coordinator agent’s rewriting process, which can weaken or remove adversarial intent. As a result, attacks effective against single-agent LLMs often fail in MASs.

To address the unique challenges of attacking MASs, we propose ReMAS (Red-teaming for Multi-Agent Systems), the first red-teaming framework tailored to MASs. ReMAS focuses on system prompt extraction. It builds on existing base attack prompts and learns, through interaction with the MAS, to generate adversarial inputs that reliably elicit hidden system prompts of sub-agents. The framework operates in two steps: i). Rewrite Attack Prompt and ii). Generate Attack Template. Step I trains an attacker policy LLM to transform a base attack prompt into a stronger variant capable of eliciting hidden system prompts from target sub-agents, using a strategy pool with randomized selection to ensure effective and diversity. Step II trains another attacker policy to produce a wrapping attack template that embeds the rewritten attack prompt in a form that bypasses the coordinator agent’s routing and rewriting, ensuring the target sub-agent receives an input close to the rewritten attack prompt. Both policies are optimized using carefully designed rewards under the DAPO algorithm [34]. Unlike prior black-box methods that rely on iterative refinement during evaluation, ReMAS trains attacker policies end-to-end and executes them in a single-pass pipeline at test time, achieving high attack success while greatly improving efficiency.

We evaluate ReMAS using a set of base attack prompts sourced from industry and test it in simulated MAS environments spanning 10 different coordinator agents and 7 distinct sub-agent types. Results show that our RL-based framework consistently outperforms strong black-box baselines. In particular, ReMAS achieves routing success rates above 0.98, ensuring the coordinator agent reliably invokes the target sub-agent, while maintaining high ASRs close to 0.80 across sub-agent types. Ablation studies further validate the importance of the strategy pool with randomized selection, which prevents collapse onto a small set of strategies and significantly enhances both diversity and success. Moreover, ReMAS exhibits strong transferability, sustaining high effectiveness when evaluated on unseen MAS backend LLMs and alternative MAS structures such as Horizontal structures and Vertical Solver&Reviewer structure [5]. These results highlight the necessity of incorporating adversarial robustness into the design and deployment of MASs.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

• 

We propose ReMAS, the first RL-based red-teaming framework for MASs that systematically investigates system prompt extraction attacks.

• 

We propose an RL training method for attacker LLMs that leverages a strategy pool with randomized selection to improve both diversity and effectiveness.

• 

We conduct extensive experiments across seven sub-agent types, multiple MAS backends, and different MAS structures to show the effectiveness of ReMAS.

## 2 Related Work

LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems: Recent advances in LLMs have driven the development of MAS, where multiple specialized agents collaborate to solve complex tasks [14, 15, 5, 6, 9, 32, 2, 33]. Existing works have explored various designs of MAS, including vertical structures with coordinator agents that delegate subtasks [6, 32, 2, 8], as well as horizontal collaborations where agents communicate and coordinate decisions [4, 9, 31, 10]. These systems rely on hidden system prompts to define agent roles and behaviors. However, the use of hidden prompts and inter-agent communication also introduces new security risks, such as exploiting routing mechanisms or extracting private sub-agent system prompts, which differ fundamentally from attacks on single-agent systems.

Security Threats to LLMs: LLMs face various security threats. One major threat is jailbreak attacks [35, 3, 20, 18, 13], where adversarial prompts bypass safety rules and induce harmful outputs. Recent methods use automated search [3, 20], optimization [18], or reinforcement learning [13] to improve attack effectiveness. Another important threat is prompt injection [23, 24, 19, 11, 29, 22], where malicious instructions embedded in user inputs or external content manipulate model behavior, causing task deviation or system prompt leakage [11, 22]. While prior work mainly studies single-agent systems, multi-agent systems introduce new challenges because sub-agents often do not directly interact with users, motivating our work.

## 3 Problem Setup

## 3.1 Multi-Agent System

Following prior works and industry implementations on MASs [6, 32, 2, 8], we study a vertical MAS structure consisting of a central coordinator agent and $N$ sub-agents $\mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},\dots,A_{N}\}$ . Each sub-agent $A_{i}$ is associated with a name or functionality label $I_{i}$ (e.g., coding or translation) and operates with a hidden system prompt $s_{i}$ . Given a user query $u$ , the coordinator agent selects a sub-agent according to its routing policy and may rewrite it before forwarding. We denote the forwarded input to $A_{i}$ as $x_{i}=\mathcal{T}(u)$ , where $\mathcal{T}$ represents the coordinator agent’s internal transformation. The selected sub-agent then generates the final response $y$ conditioned on $x_{i}$ and $s_{i}$ .

## 3.2 Threat Model

Attacker’s goal: 
The attacker aims to train attack LLMs that rewrite existing candidate attack prompts so as to extract the hidden system prompt of a specific target sub-agent. Concretely, the attack policy is optimized to (i) maximize the probability that the coordinator agent will invoke the chosen target sub-agent for a given attack query and (ii) maximize the likelihood that the resulting interaction with the invoked sub-agent reveals content from its hidden system prompt.

Attacker’s background knowledge and capability: 
We consider a black-box threat model for MASs. The attacker is assumed to know only the name or general functionality of the target sub-agent (e.g., search, coding, or translation), which is often exposed through documentation or user interfaces. During evaluation, the attacker can only submit queries $u$ and observe the final responses $y$ . The attacker has no access to the coordinator agent or sub-agent system prompts, nor to the underlying LLM parameters or architecture. To train the attacker LLMs, we use a shadow training dataset with limited internal signals, such as the invoked sub-agent or the forwarded input $x_{i}$ after coordinator agent processing. These signals are used solely to improve training efficiency and are never available at test time. All evaluations are conducted on a disjoint test set under a strict black-box setting.

## 4 Our ReMAS

## 4.1 Overview

Our framework consists of two main steps. Step I is called Rewrite Attack Prompt, where the attacker policy LLM rewrites a base attack prompt into a stronger variant $\hat{p}$ , guided by a reward that balances textual similarity and length regularization, with a strategy pool and randomized selection to ensure effectiveness and diversity. Step II is Generate Attack Template, where another attacker policy produces a template $\phi(\cdot)$ that wraps $\hat{p}$ , ensuring the coordinator agent correctly invokes the target sub-agent and forwards an input close to $\hat{p}$ to the target sub-agent. At test time, we deploy both policies in a single-pass pipeline for efficiency, while preserving high attack success.

## 4.2 Rewrite Attack Prompt

The goal of this step is to transform an existing candidate attack prompt into a more potent prompt that, when used as the forwarded input to a target sub-agent, is likely to bypass that sub-agent’s safety filter and elicit content from its hidden system prompt. Importantly, this step performs prompt rewriting rather than generating attacks from scratch. Given a base attack prompt $p_{0}$ and the name or the general function $I_{i}$ of the target sub-agent $A_{i}$ , we use an optimized attacker policy LLM $\pi_{\theta}^{\text{rewrite}}$ that produces a rewritten prompt $\hat{p}$ . The policy is trained with RL to maximize the downstream effectiveness of each rewritten prompt $\hat{p}$ when presented to the target sub-agent.
We employ a carefully designed reward function tailored for the system prompt leakage task, balancing semantic similarity and length regularization to capture faithful extractions.
During training, we further leverage a strategy pool with randomized selection to stabilize learning and preserve prompt diversity.
The overall procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1 in the Appendix.

Reward design: 
We design a reward to optimize the rewriting LLM $\pi_{\theta}^{\text{rewrite}}$ . Given the sub-agent response $y_{t}$ and the ground-truth system prompt $s_{i}$ , the reward balances textual similarity and length regularization. Since the goal of system prompt extraction is to recover the original prompt content rather than a paraphrased version, word-level edit distance provides a natural measure of similarity between $y_{t}$ and $s_{i}$ . However, raw edit distances scale with sequence length and can produce highly variable reward values, which may destabilize RL training. To address this issue, we adopt a normalized edit similarity that keeps rewards bounded and comparable across different sequence lengths, while also reducing variance in reward signals. Formally, we define

 $R_{\text{NES}}(y_{t},s_{i})=1-\frac{\text{Lev}(y_{t},s_{i})}{\max(|y_{t}|,|s_{i}|)},$ 

where $\text{Lev}(\cdot)$ denotes the word-level Levenshtein distance. In addition, while we prefer to extract the system prompt in its entirety,
small deviations such as missing a short phrase should not be penalized excessively.
We therefore introduce a Relative Length Penalty (RLP):

 $R_{\text{RLP}}(y_{t},s_{i})=\exp\!\Big(-\alpha\cdot\tfrac{|\,|y_{t}|-|s_{i}|\,|}{\max(|s_{i}|,1)}\Big),$ 

which lies in $(0,1]$ and discourages unnatural mismatches in length.
This term is convex and ensures that small length differences still yield relatively high rewards,
while large mismatches are penalized more strongly. The final reward is a convex combination of the two terms:

 $R_{\text{rewrite}}(y_{t},s_{i})=(1-\lambda)\cdot R_{\text{NES}}(y_{t},s_{i})+\lambda\cdot R_{\text{RLP}}(y_{t},s_{i}).$ 

where $\lambda$ controls the trade-off between semantic similarity and length regularization. Together, normalized edit similarity and the length penalty yield a bounded training objective with low variance that improves sample efficiency and convergence of the RL optimizer.

Strategy pool: 
Inspired by AutoDAN-Turbo [18], we maintain a strategy pool to gain knowledge from past rewriting attempts. The idea is to preserve promising rewritten cases as reusable strategies, so that the policy can leverage previously successful patterns during fine-tuning. This process consists of two stages: (i) building and updating the strategy pool, and (ii) retrieving strategies from the pool.

For stage (i),
we first evaluate each base attack prompt on the instrumented MAS to obtain an initial reward score before training begins.
Concretely, let $p_{0}$ be a base attack prompt and let $R_{0}$ denote its initial reward when used as the sub-agent input.
During training, suppose the rewrite policy produces a rewritten prompt $\hat{p}$ whose reward when used as input is $\hat{R}$ .
We call the tuple $(p_{0},R_{0},\hat{p},\hat{R})$ a promising rewriting case if $\hat{R}>R_{0}$ . For every promising rewriting case we create a strategy entry in the pool. To make these strategies easier for the policy to reuse, we also employ a summarizer LLM to generate a concise name and summarization that can be fed back into the policy as guidance during optimization.
Each entry contains the following five elements:

• 

Key: a dense embedding of the base prompt $p_{0}$ , computed with a sentence embedding model. The key enables efficient nearest-neighbor retrieval by semantic similarity.

• 

Name: a strategy name produced by the summarizer LLM for human-readable indexing.

• 

Summarization: a one-sentence description generated by the summarizer LLM that captures the rewriting pattern or attack intent.

• 

Score: the improvement in reward achieved by the rewrite, measured as $\Delta R=\hat{R}-R_{0}$ .

• 

Direction: the rewritten attack prompt $\hat{p}$ , which can be used to seed future generations.

At each training step, we update the pool with newly discovered high-quality entries, keeping only the top $M$ entries with the highest scores and discarding the rest.

During stage (ii), the strategy pool allows the policy to retrieve past successful cases that are semantically close to the current base prompt.
Given a base attack prompt $p_{0}$ , we first encode it into an embedding using the same sentence embedding model employed when building the pool. We retrieve a candidate set of strategies nearest to the query in the embedding space.
The strategies are then ranked by their aggregated scores.
If strategies with sufficiently high scores (e.g., $\Delta R\geq 0.5$ ) are available, we return the one with the highest score and provide it as an exemplar for the model to reference.
Otherwise, we fall back to returning up to $k$ strategies (set to $3$ in our experiments) with moderate scores (e.g., $0.2\leq\Delta R<0.5$ ), which are also given as references to guide rewriting.
If no effective strategies exist, we return up to $k$ strategies with low scores (e.g., $\Delta<0.2$ ), which are explicitly marked as negative exemplars to indicate that the policy should not imitate them. After retrieval, the selected strategies’ name, summarization, and direction are embedded into the training sample inputs, so that the policy can leverage them as guidance signals during optimization.
In this way, the retrieval stage adaptively supplies the rewriting policy with strategies that are both semantically relevant to the base attack prompt $p_{0}$ and empirically effective in past training steps.

At the beginning of training, the strategy pool is empty, so retrieval is disabled for the first $E_{wp}$ warm-up steps while the pool is populated with promising rewritten attack examples. After warm-up, the strategy pool is updated at each training step with newly discovered high-quality strategies and becomes active for retrieval, allowing the policy to leverage past successful rewriting patterns during subsequent training.

Randomized selection: 
Although the strategy pool is updated at every training step, retrieval may repeatedly selects a small set of high-scoring strategies across consecutive steps, causing the policy to over-rely on similar rewriting patterns. We refer to this phenomenon as mode collapse, analogous to mode collapse in RL. To improve diversity, we introduce a random pool alongside the main strategy pool. After pruning the strategy pool to retain the top $M$ strategies, we randomly sample up to $M_{r}$ entries to form the random pool. During retrieval, with a fixed
conclusion: In this work, we present ReMAS, the first RL-based red-teaming framework for MASs. The rewrite stage leverages a strategy pool with randomized selection to preserve effectiveness and diversity, while the template stage ensures that rewritten prompts are correctly routed to the target sub-agent. With the two components, ReMAS achieves high success in extracting hidden system prompts and consistently outperforms baselines. Experiments further show strong transferability across MAS backends and structures. Future work includes extending ReMAS to broader adversarial goals and studying robustness under advanced defenses.

title: Can Quantum Layers offer Performance and Security Advantages in Vision-Language Models?
abstract: As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. Quantum components are expected to extend the capabilities of existing AI systems, yet it remains unclear how such components will help within large multimodal models. In this study, we try to answer that question for vision-language models (VLMs) using classically simulated quantum layers. With LLaVA-OneVision as the backbone, we evaluate 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring and strongly entangling circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. Insertion adds quantum layers to the classical model, while replacement substitutes them for classical components. Using the same setup, we compare performance and computational cost between classical and quantum-classical hybrid models. On the Visual Spatial Reasoning dataset, inserting a quantum layer after the visual projector reaches 80.7% development accuracy, 2.28 percentage-points above classical full fine-tuning. Replacing the final decoder feed-forward sublayer retains 79.22% accuracy with 13.07 million fewer trainable parameters. Quantum insertion can thus improve accuracy, and selective replacement can reduce parameters. These benefits depend strongly on where the quantum layer is inserted or which classical component it replaces: earlier replacements lower accuracy, and fewer parameters do not reliably shorten training or reduce computation. To assess potential security benefits, we evaluated the robustness of quantum-classical hybrid models under six attack settings. Overall, our study maps where quantum layers help and hurt within VLMs, offering a starting point for hybrid VLM design; whether these gains generalize remains open. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

Abstract

As quantum computing moves from the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era toward early fault-tolerant quantum computing (EFTQC), quantum-enhanced AI is shifting from a conceptual idea to experimental research. The code is available at https://github.com/TITANS-Lab-Artifacts/QuantumVLM.

Index Terms: 
Quantum machine learning, vision-language models, adversarial robustness, variational quantum circuits

## I Introduction

Vision-language models (VLMs) are widely used for tasks involving images and text [1]. One such task is Visual Question Answering (VQA), answering natural-language questions about an image, with applications in education, finance, and healthcare. The privacy-sensitive and high-stakes nature of these domains requires VLMs to be highly reliable, accurate, and robust. Developing VLMs with these capabilities requires significant computational resources, as VQA is often considered an AI-complete problem [2]. Despite this complexity, VLMs remain vulnerable to attack families including privacy breaches, model extraction, data extraction, and reverse engineering [3]. These issues motivate research into making VLMs more cost-effective and robust.

Quantum machine learning (QML) is one possible direction for addressing complex learning problems, with the potential for quantum advantage [4]. Till now, early fault-tolerant quantum systems remain constrained by residual noise, limited logical qubits, and restricted circuit depth [5, 6]. Outputs from current machines contain noise, making practical quantum advantage difficult to achieve [7]. However, quantum simulators can simulate ideal circuits using classical resources [8]. A full state-vector simulation of $n$ qubits stores $2^{n}$ complex amplitudes, each requiring 16 bytes in double precision [9].

Despite these hardware limitations, the prospect of quantum-enhanced AI has motivated research into quantum methods for improving machine learning [4]. For language-model fine-tuning, quantum parameter adaptation (QPA) has reduced trainable parameters in methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) while maintaining comparable or better performance [10]. Quantum layers have also been combined with vision models for image classification [11], and quantum circuits have been applied to language-processing tasks [12]. These works motivate investigating whether quantum layers can improve VLM performance. Experimental quantum adversarial learning has also demonstrated vulnerabilities in quantum classifiers and explored adversarial training as a defense [13]. This motivates testing whether quantum integration improves VLM robustness rather than assuming such benefits.

In this work, we use classical simulations of quantum layers to investigate how they affect three aspects of a VLM: (i) predictive accuracy, (ii) computational cost, and (iii) adversarial robustness. We use the Large Language and Vision Assistant (LLaVA) OneVision model, with its Qwen2-0.5B single-image (SI) variant as the backbone [14]. We examine four quantum circuits: 4- and 8-qubit basic-ring (BR4, BR8) and strongly entangling (SE4, SE8) circuits. We test two approaches: insertion and replacement. For insertion, we add quantum layers at four positions within the VLM: (i) before the visual projector, (ii) after the visual projector, (iii) after an early decoder block, and (iv) after the final decoder normalization. These positions let us examine quantum processing of visual features, projected visual features, early multimodal representations, and final representations used for prediction, respectively. For replacement, we substitute quantum layers for the visual-to-language projector or the feed-forward sublayers in early, intermediate, and final decoder blocks. We evaluate six untargeted adversarial image-perturbation attacks, grouped by attacker access: (i) the fast gradient sign method (FGSM) [15], (ii) projected gradient descent with a cross-entropy objective (PGD-CE), and (iii) PGD with a margin objective (PGD-margin), all using target-model gradients [16, 17]; (iv) simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA), using target-model scores [18]; (v) HopSkipJump (HSJ), using predicted labels only [19]; and (vi) transfer PGD (T-PGD), using a surrogate model [20]. Each attack modifies the image to cause an incorrect prediction while keeping the text prompt and weights fixed. Our contributions are threefold:

• 

We train and evaluate quantum-layer configurations and classical baselines on the same dataset to assess how circuit design and placement affect predictive accuracy.

• 

We compare trainable parameters, training time, and memory usage to assess whether any accuracy gains justify the computational cost of quantum simulation.

• 

We test whether quantum layers improve robustness against these six attacks using a common protocol.

These experiments address three research questions (RQs):

• 

RQ1: How does inserting quantum layers at different locations within a VLM affect predictive performance and computational cost?

• 

RQ2: Can quantum layers effectively replace classical components while maintaining predictive performance and reducing computational cost?

• 

RQ3: How do VLMs with quantum-layer insertion or replacement compare with classical baselines in adversarial robustness under different levels of attacker access?

Paper Organization: Section II presents the background. Section III discusses related work. Section IV presents the framework. Section V outlines the methodology. Section VI reports the results, and Section VII concludes the paper.

## II Background

This section introduces the concepts underlying our work.

## II-A VLM Components

In LLaVA-OneVision [21], the vision encoder converts an image into features representing its visual content. The projector converts these features into the format expected by the language model. The text prompt is converted into token embeddings and combined with the projected image features. Decoder blocks then process this combined sequence: attention connects information across tokens, helping relate the text to the image, while feed-forward sublayers transform each token’s features. Normalization controls feature scales, and residual connections carry information across processing stages. Finally, the output head maps normalized decoder features to token scores for True or False prediction.

## II-B Attacks on VLMs

We compare classical and quantum VLMs under six attacks that modify image pixels, with different levels of attacker access, shown in Fig. 1. FGSM uses the target model’s gradients to increase prediction loss in one step [15]. PGD-CE and PGD-margin repeatedly modify the image within a fixed limit: PGD-CE increases cross-entropy loss, while PGD-margin raises the incorrect class score relative to the correct one [16, 17]. SPSA estimates how to modify the image from output scores without target gradients [18]. HSJ uses predicted labels to make an adversarial image closer to the original [19]. T-PGD creates perturbations on a separate surrogate model and tests whether they also fool the target VLM [20].

Fig. 1: Overview and access level of the attack methods used in this work.

## III Literature Review

Quantum approaches to vision and language tasks target model architecture or parameter-efficient adaptation. Cherrat et al. [22] introduced quantum vision transformers with quantum attention, and Unlu et al. [23] reported competitive classification performance with much longer training than classical models. Liu et al. [10] generated language-model adaptation parameters with quantum circuits and a classical mapping, keeping inference classical. Chen et al. [24] proposed QuanTA, a quantum-inspired classical method for high-rank fine-tuning. Kong et al. [25] replaced parts of language transformers with variational quantum circuits and reported comparable generation performance. These studies show promise for quantum architectures and compact adaptation; none tests whether they reduce overall computational cost in VLMs.

Several studies have applied quantum methods to multimodal learning. Mukesh et al. [26] combined a classical vision-language transformer with quantum image-text fusion. Zhao et al. [27] proposed a quantum adapter using category-based semantic anchors to refine visual features for few-shot VLM adaptation. Wang and Shang [28] applied parallel quantum circuits after image-text fusion, comparing against a classical MLP and testing missing modalities and simulated circuit noise. These studies demonstrate quantum adaptation and fusion without testing quantum layers replacing classical layers in the same VLM under common adversarial attacks.

Adversarial robustness complements accuracy and computational cost when evaluating quantum layers. Ren et al. [13] demonstrated adversarial vulnerability in quantum classifiers on superconducting hardware and tested adversarial training as a defense. Athalye et al. [29] showed that obfuscated gradients can falsely suggest robustness, motivating evaluation with gradient-based, query-based, and transfer attacks. These findings call for direct adversarial evaluation; how quantum circuit design and placement affect robustness within the same VLM remains unclear.

Prior studies leave three gaps: how inserting quantum layers, or replacing classical layers with them, affects VLM performance; whether accuracy gains justify computational cost; and how quantum-enabled VLMs perform under adversarial attacks. Using a shared LLaVA-OneVision backbone, we test four quantum circuits at four insertion and four replacement locations. We compare accuracy, trainable parameters, training time, and memory with classical baselines, then evaluate six attacks with shared perturbation budgets and gradient, score, label, or surrogate-model access. We jointly examine how circuit design and placement affect accuracy, computational cost, and adversarial robustness.

## IV Proposed Framework

Fig. 2 shows the proposed framework for quantum insertion and replacement in backbone VLM. The vision encoder uses Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training (SigLIP), and the decoder uses root mean square normalization (RMSNorm).

Fig. 2: Proposed framework showing the LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-0.5B-SI backbone and quantum-layer insertion and replacement locations.

## IV-A Quantum Insertion Locations

Insertion adds a quantum layer to the model without removing any existing component.

• 

Before the visual projector (q1): We place the quantum layer on vision-encoder features before they reach the projector, to test whether adjusting image features before entering model’s feature space improves prediction.

• 

After the visual projector (q2): We insert the quantum layer after the projector, before image features are combined with text embeddings. It tests whether this adjustment helps the model to fuse image and text information.

• 

After an early decoder block (q3): We apply the quantum layer to the final prompt token after decoder block 5, adjusting image-text information early in decoding improves prediction.

• 

After final decoder normalization (q4): We position the quantum layer between the final normalization and the output head, acting on the final prompt token, to test whether adjusting the fully processed representation just before prediction improves accuracy.

## IV-B Quantum Replacement Positions

Unlike insertion, replacement swaps one classical component for a quantum module. We use linear input and output projections around the module to ensure that it receives and returns features of the same dimension as the original component. Thus, the rest of the model is unchanged. When replacing a decoder MLP, only the MLP is swapped; the block’s attention, normalization, and residual connections remain in place.

• 

Complete visual projector (r1): Here, we replace the entire projector with a quantum module. This tests whether visual features can be mapped into the language model’s feature space.

• 

Early decoder MLP (r2): We substitute a quantum module for the MLP in decoder block 0 to examine whether it can transform features at the start of decoding.

• 

Intermediate decoder MLP (r3): We swap the MLP in decoder block 11 for a quantum module. This assesses whether it can transform features after several stages of image-text interaction.

• 

Final decoder MLP (r4): We replace the MLP in decoder block 23 with a quantum module to determine whether it can perform the final feature transformation before normalization and prediction.

## V Methodology

This section describes our technical framework, details of used quantum circuits, training and attack setup, and the metrics used for evaluation. Table I defines the notation.

## V-A Quantum Circuits

We test two circuit families, each with 4 and 8 qubits, giving the four configurations shown in Fig. 3. The basic-ring circuit is the simpler design: each layer applies a trainable Y-axis rotation to every qubit, then links neighboring qubits in a closed ring with controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates. The strongly entangling circuit is more expressive: each layer applies a trainable Rot gate, a sequence of Z-, Y-, and Z-axis rotations, to every qubit, then uses CNOT gates whose connection range changes from layer to layer.

Fig. 3: Four quantum circuits used in this study.

## V-B Technical Framework

We use the same image preprocessing, prompt, and binary task for classical and quantum models to isolate differences arising from the quantum component. Given an image $x$ and a statement $t$ , the model predicts True or False, trained with $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}=-\log p_{y}$ , where $p_{y}$ is the probability of the correct label $y$ . For each selected token feature $h\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , we map the normalized feature to $n_{q}$ rotation angles $z=\pi\tanh(W_{\mathrm{in}}\mathcal{N}(h)+b_{\mathrm{in}})$ . We encode $z$ once with Y-axis rotations $V(z)$ , apply $L$ trainable layers $U_{\theta}$ to obtain $\lvert\psi\rangle=U_{\theta}V(z)\lvert 0\rangle^{\otimes n_{q}}$ , and measure each qubit’s Pauli-Z expectation $m_{j}=\langle\psi\rvert Z_{j}\lvert\psi\rangle$ .

An output projection gives $g_{\theta}(h)=W_{\mathrm{out}}m+b_{\mathrm{out}}$ . For insertion, we use $h^{\prime}=h+\gamma g_{\theta}(h)$ , with trainable $\gamma$ initialized to 0.1 to limit early changes to pretrained features. For replacement, the $d_{\mathrm{out}}$ -dimensional $g_{\theta}(h)$ is the component’s output; the module adds no residual, decoder residuals remain.

Insertion updates all retained visual tokens at q1 and q2, and only the final prompt token at q3 and q4. Replacement processes all visual tokens at r1 and all tokens entering the selected MLP at r2–r4. Insertion and projector replacement use layer normalization without learnable scale and shift; decoder replacements reuse the decoder’s normalized features. We simulate circuits exactly with a differentiable PyTorch state-vector simulator, without shot sampling or hardware noise.

conclusion:
The results answer our three research questions. For RQ1, insertion benefits depend on placement and training mode, with selected configurations improving accuracy without consistent resource savings. For RQ2, the final decoder feed-forward sublayer can be replaced while preserving accuracy in this run, whereas projector and early decoder replacements perform poorly. For RQ3, neither insertion nor replacement provides consistent robustness gains under the evaluated attacks.
These findings are limited to one backbone, one dataset, and one seed. The development split supports both checkpoint selection and reporting, and the best configuration is selected from many candidates. Held-out evaluation, multiple seeds, and parameter-matched classical controls are needed to confirm gains and isolate the circuit’s contribution. Unequal stopping budgets limit runtime comparisons, while the 40-example attack subset and unresolved gradient diagnostics limit robustness conclusions. The study covers image perturbations under classical simulation, not privacy attacks or quantum-hardware performance.

title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
abstract: Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints. Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats. Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space. In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge. Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources. To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness. The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm. Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B-14B planners to 70.5-76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85-26.41 W of average power. Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
