body_start:
Abstract

Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints.
Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can
provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats.
Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space.
In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge.
Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources.
To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness.
The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment.
We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.
Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B–14B planners to 70.5–76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85–26.41 W of average power.
Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.

## I Introduction

Robotic task planning converts a high-level goal into an executable sequence of actions [1].
In safety-critical settings, reaching the goal is not enough: every intermediate state must also satisfy requirements such as ordering, mutual exclusion, and resource constraints [2, 3].
A plan that eventually places an object correctly can still be unacceptable if it enters a restricted region, manipulates a fragile object in the wrong order, or violates a required inspection step.
We therefore study safety-constrained task planning: generating plans that are executable and goal-reaching while satisfying explicit trajectory-level constraints.

Classical planners offer a principled solution when a correct symbolic task specification is available.
Systems such as Fast Downward and OPTIC search over states defined by action preconditions and effects [4, 5]; PDDL3 expresses trajectory constraints, and tools such as VAL check a candidate plan against the formal specification [6, 7].
This formal structure provides an auditable safety criterion, but it comes with two practical costs.
First, tasks in complicated environments can induce exponentially growing search spaces as the number of objects and planning horizon increase, making symbolic search difficult to scale [8].
Second, users must provide rigid symbolic inputs and carefully engineered domain specifications.
Imitation and reinforcement learning can amortize planning into compact policies [9, 10, 11, 12].
However, learned policies are commonly tied to particular task distributions, and their outputs do not inherit a formal guarantee without an explicit specification and verifier.

LLM planners offer a complementary strength: they can interpret high-level
task descriptions and directly generate candidate action
sequences [13, 14].
Recent systems ground language into symbolic specifications or integrate LLMs
with planners and formal verifiers [15, 16, 17].
An inference-time verifier can reject an invalid plan
and prompt the model to revise it [18, 19].
However, this process leaves the base planner unchanged, so repeated failures
increase token usage, latency, and computation.
Moreover, general-purpose LLMs can be too large for memory- and power-limited
robot computers.
These limitations motivate a planner that combines safety-aware plan
generation, compact local inference, and flexible task interfaces.

We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework for this combination.
Rather than keeping the verifier only in the inference loop, SLoSa uses formal feedback to change the compact planner itself.
First, SLoSa constructs behavior-changing safety-aware training data by retaining planning instances in which the supplied constraint rejects the baseline plan while a verified alternative remains feasible.
Second, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts compact, quantized LLMs using the verified plans.
Third, verifier-guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the planner with a reward hierarchy that separates unparseable outputs, precondition violations, safety violations, goal failures, and successful plans.
At inference, SLoSa combines local plan generation with verifier feedback to enforce the supplied safety constraints while reducing the tokens spent on iterative repair.

We evaluate SLoSa using three compact open-source LLM backbones across four PDDL domains that cover manipulation, transportation, object transfer, and tool use, together with separately trained planners for safety-adapted VirtualHome and ALFWorld to evaluate the applicability of the same post-training pipeline beyond PDDL-based planning.
The results show consistent improvements from safety-aware post-training
across model sizes, task domains, and input representations.
We further evaluate local inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4080 and a Jetson Orin,
and demonstrate the complete vision-grounded planning pipeline on a desktop
6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) robotic arm.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

• 

We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework that
improves compact LLM planners through behavior-changing safety-aware data
construction, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning, and
verifier-guided GRPO.

• 

We construct safety-constrained evaluation tasks spanning four PDDL planning domains and two adapted household simulation benchmarks, with formally verified plans and task-specific trajectory constraints.

• 

We conduct extensive experiments across multiple model sizes, task
domains, and input representations, showing consistent improvements from
safety-aware post-training. We further validate local edge deployment,
verifier-guided inference, and physical robotic-arm execution.

## II Related Work

Classical, learned, and neuro-symbolic task planning.
Classical planners search over explicit task representations and can validate a plan against its goals and constraints [4, 5, 6, 7].
Their explicit semantics make failures interpretable, but formal specification construction is labor-intensive, and tasks in complicated environments can induce exponentially growing search spaces as the number of objects and the planning horizon increase [8].
Imitation learning and reinforcement learning instead learn policies or search guidance from demonstrations and interaction [9, 10, 11, 12].
But they are generally optimized for a specific training distribution.
SLoSa adopts this general direction but uses symbolic planners and validators primarily as sources of training supervision, while a compact neural model generates the initial plan at deployment.

LLM planning with formal grounding and runtime assurance.
LLMs have been used to generate actions, select skills, and translate natural-language requests into planning specifications [13, 14].
LIMP grounds open-ended robot instructions into symbolic representations from which verifiable behaviors can be synthesized [15], while
[16, 17] translate language into syntactically valid temporal logic for downstream motion planning.
Other systems retain a verifier in the inference loop: ISR-LLM translates natural-language tasks into PDDL and iteratively refines long-horizon plans, while the Safety Chip enforces LTL constraints around an LLM-driven agent [18, 19].
These approaches provide important assurance at the interface between language and execution, but a weak base planner can still require repeated generation and verification.
SLoSa instead uses formal validation during post-training to improve the first-pass plan quality of the compact planner itself.
At deployment, the resulting planner can still be paired with an ISR-style verifier and repair loop, retaining formal guarantees for validator-accepted plans while reducing regeneration tokens.

Safety post-training and compact deployment.
Quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduce the memory and adaptation cost of LLMs [20, 21, 22, 23], but compression alone does not optimize satisfaction of task-level safety constraints.
SafeGen-LLM uses verified PDDL supervision to improve safety generalization across properties, domains, and input formats [24].
SLoSa studies a complementary question: whether verifier knowledge can be transferred into small, low-power LLM planners that improve safe plan generation with lower memory use and less dependence on repeated repair.

## III Preliminaries

Safety-constrained robotic task planning.
We consider a high-level robotic planning problem
 $P=(S,A,s_{0},G,C)$ ,
where $S$ is the symbolic state space, $A$ is the action set, $s_{0}$ is the
initial state, $G$ is the goal, and $C$ is the set of safety constraints.
Each action $a\in A$ has preconditions $\mathrm{Pre}(a)$ and effects
 $\mathrm{Eff}(a)$ , and represents a high-level robot skill such as pick,
move, or place.

A plan is a finite action sequence $\tau=[a_{1},\ldots,a_{T}]$ .
A plan is executable, denoted by $\mathrm{Exec}(\tau)$ , if
 $s_{i-1}\models\mathrm{Pre}(a_{i})$ for all $i=1,\ldots,T$ .
If $\mathrm{Exec}(\tau)$ holds, applying the action effects induces a complete
trajectory
 $\rho(\tau)=(s_{0},s_{1},\ldots,s_{T})$ .
For an executable plan, goal achievement and safety are defined as
 $\mathrm{Goal}(\tau)\iff s_{T}\models G,\mathrm{Safe}(\tau)\iff\rho(\tau)\models C.$ 

PDDL3 constraints and plan verification.
We represent symbolic planning problems using PDDL and encode hard safety
requirements as PDDL3 trajectory constraints.
A PDDL3 domain defines predicates and actions, whereas a problem specifies
objects, the initial state, the goal, and trajectory constraints.

Given a generated output, the verifier applies its checks in a fixed order,
and the first failed check determines the outcome.
An output that cannot be parsed or contains undefined actions or objects is a
format error.
A parsed plan that violates an action precondition is a
precondition violation.
Only after obtaining a complete executable trajectory does the verifier
evaluate $C$ ; an executable plan that violates $C$ is a
safety violation.
A safe and executable plan is a goal failure if it does not reach $G$ ,
and a success otherwise.
This ordered procedure assigns exactly one category to every output and is
used for training data filtering, reward design, and evaluation.

SLoSa objective.
SLoSa stands for Small size, Low power demand, and Safety awareness.
Here, safety awareness means compliance with the formal task specification defined above, while low-power operation is an empirical deployment objective rather than an assumed property.
The goal of SLoSa robotic task planning is to train a compact LLM planner that generates safety-compliant plans with low deployment and inference cost.

## IV SLoSa

SLoSa is a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for safety-constrained robotic task planning.
It trains compact, quantized LLM planners using formally verified supervision and reward signals.
As shown in Figure 1, SLoSa has three stages.
First, it constructs safety-aware training data using classical planners, teacher models, and formal validators.
Only plans that pass formal validation are used as positive training targets.
Second, it applies SFT to compact and quantized LLMs using verified plans.
The model takes PDDL, structured text, or natural language as input and outputs a grounded action sequence.
Third, it applies verifier-guided GRPO, where formal verification gives error categories and classical planning gives progress signals for dense reward design.
Together, these stages use symbolic planning and verification to guide neural model compression and fine-tuning, so the final planner is easier to deploy and more likely to generate safety-compliant plans.

Fig. 1: 
Overview of SLoSa.
Classical planners, teacher models, and a formal verifier construct safety-aware data.
Student LLMs are trained by SFT and then refined by GRPO with verifier-based rewards.

## IV-A Safety-Aware Training Data Construction

The first stage of SLoSa constructs behavior-changing, safety-constrained
training instances for SFT and GRPO.
We use four robotics-inspired PDDL domains: Blocksworld, Ferry, Grippers, and
Spanner, covering manipulation, transportation, object transfer, and tool use.

For each base problem $P_{0}$ , a classical planner generates a baseline plan
 $\tau_{0}$ , which is verified as executable and goal reaching.
We then introduce a domain-grounded PDDL3 constraint $c$ to obtain a
constrained problem $P_{c}$ .
The constraint is derived from the domain semantics and the actions and objects
appearing in the task, following one of the four patterns summarized in
Table I.
For example, in Spanner, an ordering constraint requiring nut1
to be tightened before nut2 is encoded as
(sometime-before (tightened nut2) (tightened nut1)).
A plan that tightens both nuts in the reverse order may still reach the
task goal, but violates the inserted trajectory constraint.

TABLE I: Safety patterns used to construct behavior-changing constraints.

Pattern

PDDL3 construct

Robotic interpretation

Ordering safety

sometime-before

A required event must precede another event.

Staging safety

sometime, sometime-before

The robot must pass through a safe intermediate state.

Resource restriction

always, not

Unsafe, reserved, or faulty resources cannot be used.

Mandatory inspection

sometime

The robot must visit a checkpoint or complete an inspection.

A planner then solves $P_{c}$ to obtain an alternative plan $\tau_{c}$ .
Let $V(P,\tau)$ denote the verifier outcome for plan $\tau$ under problem $P$ .
We retain an instance only if 
 $V(P_{0},\tau_{0})=V(P_{c},\tau_{c})=\mathrm{success}$ 
and
 $V(P_{c},\tau_{0})=\mathrm{safety\ violation}$ .
Thus, the added constraint invalidates the baseline plan while preserving a
verified alternative, ensuring that the constraint changes the required
planning behavior rather than acting as a decorative condition.
We therefore refer to the retained instances as behavior-changing.
This definition is relative to the selected baseline plan $\tau_{0}$ and does
not imply that the formal specification captures every real-world hazard.

We assign each constrained problem a difficulty level solely according to the length of its verified plan, denoted by $d(P_{c})=\operatorname{bin}(|\tau_{c}|)$ .
The Easy, Medium, and Hard levels therefore differ only in planning-horizon length.

This measure represents the effective planning horizon under the safety
constraint rather than difficulty inferred from problem-size parameters.

Each constrained problem $P_{c}$ is converted into task prompts using PDDL or template-generated natural language.
The prompt is paired with the verified constrained plan $\tau_{c}$ as a positive
SFT example and is used without a target plan during GRPO.
For 20% of the constrained problems, a teacher model (GPT-5.4-mini) generates additional
candidate plans to increase demonstration diversity.
These plans are retained only if they receive a success label from the same
formal verifier.

Across the dataset, we use three input formats: PDDL, structured natural language, and narrative natural language.
Each constrained problem contributes one PDDL prompt and one natural-language prompt rendered in either structured or narrative form.
These representations preserve the same underlying symbolic problem while exposing the planner to different task interfaces.

## IV-B Compression-Aware Supervised Fine-Tuning

The safety-aware dataset provides verified plans, but the pretrained compact models do not know the required planning format, action semantics, or safety-constrained behavior.
We therefore use SFT as the first training stage.
The goal is to give the compact planner a strong initialization before GRPO, so that it can generate parseable and executable plans that are close to the verified constrained plans.

Given a positive training set
 $\mathcal{D}_{+}=\{(x_{i},\tau_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}$ ,
where $x_{i}$ is a task prompt constructed from a constrained planning problem

title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20x faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.

body_start:
Abstract

We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than $20\times$ faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.

Project Page:
https://hyperdrone.dev

Video:
https://youtu.be/rc3E-GuLqDw

Code:
https://github.com/rl-tools/hyperdrone

Figure 1: HyperDrone Output Modalities.

Keywords: Quadrotor, Simulator, Sim2Real

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, imitation learning from human demonstrations has become a dominant method for advanced learning-based control of robots. This is particularly the case in the field of manipulation [1, 2, 3] and locomotion [4, 5]. Conversely, for aerial vehicle autonomy, imitation learning from human demonstrations has not experienced comparable widespread adoption. In the case of quadrotors, in particular, two major trends have been imitation learning from (privileged) expert policies [6, 7, 8] and using pre-trained models as vision encoders [9, 10]. The latter promise to bring broader generalization by virtue of having been pre-trained on massive amounts of real-world images collected from the internet.

Imitation learning from human demonstrations and pre-trained vision models are motivated and driven by scaling laws that were first observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) [11]. Early indications hint that similar scaling laws might exist in robot imitation learning [12]. The potential that scaling robot imitation data could bear similarly large returns as LLM scaling, has led to the formation of a large number of commercial robot imitation data creation/curation companies. These companies also bet on monopolizing forces known as the “data flywheels” [13] limiting accessibility while the capital expenditure (CAPEX) requirement for large-scale robot data collection is by itself already a major hurdle for reproducibility and progress in the community.

The alternative is training robot control policies entirely in simulation without requiring real-world data. Not only are methods fully trained on synthetic data more accessible to fellow researchers, but they are also more introspectable. Due to the lack of interpretability of deep neural networks, in general we cannot get strong guarantees for learned end-to-end controllers. The best way to reason about the behavior of the trained control policy is through introspection of the data that went into training it. For vision foundation models [14, 15, 16, 17] this data is usually proprietary, hampering reproducibility, interpretability of the resulting behavior and the opportunity for independent researchers to study effects of modifying the data distribution.

To accelerate the research of vision-based aerial vehicle control we present the following contributions:

1. 

HyperDrone: An extremely fast simulator for training end-to-end visual control policies. HyperDrone consists of:

• 

HyperLux: A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception

• 

Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation

2. 

Sim2Real Transfer of a yaw-control policy trained entirely in simulation

Table 1: Comparison of quadrotor simulators and rendering backends.

In the recent past, several quadrotor simulators have been proposed and optimized for different purposes. We focus on simulating cameras and quadrotor dynamics to support visual control policies, and the main related simulators are listed in Table 1.

A very popular simulator for this purpose has been Flightmare [18]. However, it does not support batch rendering and hence is comparatively slow. It has been measured to yield $\approx 230$ Frames Per Second (FPS) in [19] which is prohibitively slow for reinforcement learning which usually requires millions or even billions of samples. Furthermore, it requires proprietary, licensed software to replace the default scenes.

To overcome the low rendering throughput, multiple batch-rendering-based simulators have been proposed. These cluster into Nvidia Isaac-based and Habitat-based simulators. VisFly [19] is based on a custom version of Habitat [23] for batch rendering. Habitat in turn uses OpenGL through the Magnum engine. It is the only other simulator that supports quadrotor dynamics, batch rendering and is compatible with the latest generation GPUs (Nvidia Blackwell/5000-series, released in early 2025). However, it falls short of HyperDrone when it comes to fidelity features like motion blur and anti-aliasing. Note that we leave an exhaustive performance comparison for later and only focus on qualitative features in this section.

Aerial Gym [20] is based on Isaac Gym and implements a batch raytracer mainly for depth perception and semantic segmentation. While depth perception and semantic segmentation is also supported in HyperDrone, our main focus is on RGB observations which are not supported for general 3D mesh scenes (only for simple geometric objects) by Aerial Gym. Furthermore, due to Nvidia Warp limitations, Aerial Gym does not take advantage of ray-tracing cores in modern GPUs. Additionally, Isaac Gym, which Aerial Gym builds upon, was deprecated in mid-2024 and hence Aerial Gym does not support Nvidia Blackwell GPUs (5000 series).

OmniDrones [21] follows a similar strategy by building onto Isaac Sim. Compared to Aerial Gym it does not implement its own rendering pipeline and relies on Isaac Sim for camera simulation. OmniDrones is built on Isaac Sim 4.1.0 which was released in mid-2024 and hence does not support Blackwell/5000-series GPUs, either. Since the project is not maintained anymore we do not expect this to change.

Initially, when conceptualizing HyperDrone we were planning to build it on top of Madrona [22], an open-source batch raytracer and rasterizer that has shown promising performance. However, while investigating Madrona we found that it does not take advantage of ray-tracing hardware in RTX-series cards and that the codebase is relatively complex.

Hence, we concluded that there is a need for a new simulator that focuses on rendering performance while supporting the needs of realistic visual quadrotor simulation like motion blur, anti-aliasing and reflections. While designing HyperDrone we also keep in mind that in the future we should support rolling-shutter simulation as well, even though for now we focus on global shutter cameras.

## 3 Method

In the following we describe the architecture of HyperDrone and then the control problem formulation, platform and general setup for the simulation-to-reality transfer of a visual policy trained from scratch in HyperDrone.

## 3.1 Architecture

Figure 2: HyperDrone Architecture.

A main premise guiding the architecture of HyperDrone is that we want to avoid CPU $\leftrightarrow$ GPU memory transfers that commonly occur when quadrotor dynamics simulation is being run on the CPU while a batch renderer is run on the GPU. With OptiX, both run on the GPU. Another premise motivated in Section 2 is the ability to take advantage of the ray-tracing cores in modern hardware.

The first component of HyperDrone is HyperLux, our ray-tracing renderer. Ray-tracing cores are fixed-function hardware that accelerate finding intersections of 3D rays with a 3D mesh. Compared to rasterization, which maps 3D geometry from a 3D mesh onto the camera plane, ray-tracing takes the more physically motivated approach of tracing rays of light. In practice, we shoot a ray from each pixel towards the 3D mesh and find the first point of intersection (this is what the ray-tracing fixed-function hardware supports). Once we identify the intersection, we can use the information from the mesh to e.g. look up the appropriate color for that particular intersection point from a texture map.
To make this tractable the 3D mesh first needs to be processed into an accelerated data-structure. This acceleration structure and using ray-tracing cores to intersect rays with it is not accessible via compute APIs like CUDA. HyperLux therefore uses Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan or Apple Metal, which handle the acceleration structure and return intersection points for the rays we supply, and falls back to software ray traversal on WebGPU, which does not expose ray-tracing hardware.

The second component of HyperDrone is the quadrotor dynamics simulator. The quadrotor dynamics simulation is based on the implementation introduced in [24] combined with years of continuous development, refactoring and improvements.
Due to rendering not being the bottleneck anymore (cf. rendering performance benchmarks in Section 4), we can just render every frame from scratch. This basically rules out overfitting to any particular dataset in the traditional sense. We might still overfit to the data-distribution that the simulator generates (e.g. in terms of visual fidelity, artifacts etc.) but overfitting to particular samples is virtually ruled out by never using a sample twice.

For the proof-of-concept of the simulation-to-reality transfer, we use RAPTOR [8] as a teacher policy and train a student policy to estimate the yaw between a target frame and the current frame (more in the next Section 3.2). We run both the teacher and the student on the GPU as well. Please refer to Figure 2 for a graphical overview of the HyperDrone architecture.

## 3.2 Visual Simulation-to-Reality Transfer

Figure 3: Control Architecture Overview.

Figure 4: ProcTHOR [25] Train-1 Scene.

Figure 5: Probe Rays.

To show that HyperDrone actually allows simulation-to-reality transfer after training from scratch on synthetic images, we propose a simple task, a training pipeline and a hardware platform to deploy it on and an experimental setup to test the trained network.

We choose a simple task to disentangle the visual simulation-to-reality transfer from control challenges. As can be seen in Figure 3, we abstract most of the high-frequency control problem by using the RAPTOR [8] foundation policy for low-level and position control and only leave yaw control to the network trained in simulation and deployed on a real camera. The task of the student policy is to provide the relative yaw offset between a target frame and the current frame. Hence, we use a convolutional network on the channel-wise stack of both frames, followed by a dense head that predicts the relative yaw.

Figure 6: Rendering Fidelity Comparison with Four Secondary Drones.

We want to support a large diversity of 3D scenes to avoid overfitting to a specific scene. Hence, we use the procedurally generated indoor scenes from the ProcTHOR [25] dataset. This dataset includes $10000$ diverse indoor scenes with randomized room layouts and object placements (cf. Figure 5). It also strikes a good balance between realism and performance (cf. Figures 6 and 7). However, HyperDrone is not limited to ProcTHOR, it can load general binary glTF 2.0 (.glb) files. And glTF is a widely used open standard, also known as the “JPEG of 3D” [26]. Supporting open and widely used formats is a large advantage for the community accessibility of HyperDrone over other simulators like Flightmare which rely on proprietary formats.

Given a 3D scene mesh, we need to find random positions that can be used as initial states for our training pipeline. Since the room layouts are irregularly shaped (cf. Figure 5) and also because there are random obstacles and walls in the scenes, we cannot use simple uniform position sampling. Hence, we implement a probe-ray-based rejection sampling mechanism that allows us to specify the minimum distance to any object. As depicted in Figure 5, we use 64 probe rays that are shot out from the ego-camera position in all directions using a deterministic Fibonacci sphere distribution. These probe rays use the same ray-tracing hardware acceleration as the rays used to retrieve pixel colors and hence the performance overhead is minimal (roughly $\frac{64}{64\times 64}\approx 1.6\%$ for $64\times 64$ frames, even lower for higher resolutions). In the future, these probe rays can also be used for collision detection with the actual 3D mesh, not some simplified collision mesh as in most other simulators/engines.

For control, RAPTOR [8] outputs direct motor commands at $500$ Hz, based on position observations from a motion capture system as well as roll/pitch, linear velocity and angular velocity observations from the on-board Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) on the Crazyflie platform.
We mount an OpenMV AE3 camera board on the Crazyflie and run the trained neural network on a Neural Processing Unit (NPU) on the camera board. We develop a Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter (UART)-based protocol to transfer the yaw commands to the Crazyflie microcontroller to be consumed by RAPTOR.

The protocol also allows for a backchannel that allows instructing the inference code to take the current image as a target image. The “Logic” corresponds to a simple state machine that first instructs the capturing of two target frames with a yaw offset between them. After that, the packet contains another bit that can select between two target frames which leads to the back-and-forth yaw control that you can see in the complementary video and in Figure 8. This demonstrates the successful simulation-to-real transfer of a visual control policy that has been only trained on synthetic images from HyperDrone.

## 4 Results

Figure 7: Motion Blur Parameters.

In this section, we first investigate the visual results, analyzing the effects of different parameters in the HyperDrone raytracer. Then we analyze the performance, and finally we discuss results from the simulation-to-reality transfer.

## 4.1 Visual Results

In Figure 6, we compare rendering modes, resolutions and anti-aliasing. The comparison includes three ray-tracing modes (more details in Appendix B):

1. 

High: Supports complex reflections like the reflection of the picture on the wall in the table surface in Figure 6. It also supports more complex lighting (cf. desk lamp in Figure 6) and higher fidelity material appearance.

2. 

Medium: Still supports complex materials but has more limited support for reflections and lighting.

3. 

Low: No textures, pre-baked colors, optimized for performance.

Additionally, due to the popularity in the robot learning community [6, 27, 28, 29], we also support depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception. Figure : Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second shows these outputs alongside RGB rendered at high fidelity (cf. Appendix B). In Figure 6, we show different resolutions from $2048\times 2048$ to $64\times 64$ with anti-aliasing on and off. Particularly when comparing the lower resolution cases like in $64\times 64$ , we can see that there are strong aliasing effects. These effects happen because our ray is infinitesimally narrow and either hits an object or not, hence e.g. the edge of the table being hit in some pixels while others hit the ground. Naturally, this does not occur because each pixel collects photons from a frustum (a rectangular cone), densely sensing all the surfaces in the frustum and then averaging them. We implement anti-aliasing by simulating this natural process with $2\times 2$ rays per pixel that are averaged, leading to vastly reduced aliasing. While more apparent for us at lower resolutions, even at higher resolutions aliasing is an unnatural effect that the neural networks could overfit to.

For fast-moving robots, particularly robots with agile rotational dynamics like quadrotors, it is important to take into account motion blur. Motion blur appears because the assumption that the camera takes a snapshot at a particular instant in time is not true. Cameras need to accumulate photons over time to build an accurate picture. While the shutter is open and the camera sensor is accumulating photons, the robot can move, leading to different objects contributing to any particular pixel over time. In Figure 7, we show motion blur for different shutter durations. In contrast to game engines, where approximations are more common, we implement motion blur by simulating the actual physical process i.e. by subsampling $N$ rays throughout the shutter period and then averaging them for the final frame. limitations:
While providing a step change in performance and demonstrating simulation-to-reality transfer, HyperDrone still has a few limitations:

1. 

Rolling shutter simulation not supported, yet. The focus is on global shutter cameras but in the future we plan to support rolling shutter as well.

2. 

Collision detection. While probe rays are implemented, we have neither implemented a proper collision avoidance interface nor tested them for collision avoidance, yet.

3. 

Simple, low-frequency control problem. We only show a proof-of-concept simulation-to-reality transfer that still relies on an external position reference and RAPTOR as an end-to-end low-level controller.

Unlike related works, we built HyperDrone to be durable, maintainable and long-term stable. We plan to address the mentioned limitations and more in future research and development.
conclusion:
In this work, we presented HyperDrone, a fast and efficient simulator for synthesizing and training vision-based quadrotor control policies.
By handing this powerful simulator over to the community we expect qualitatively new results, enabling researchers and practitioners to iterate much faster and with minimal hardware requirements compared to the predominant alternatives. This lowers the barrier to do research on learned, vision-based control policies and helps to democratize this area of research. In collaboration with the community, we hope to overcome many of the limitations mentioned above and advance toward an autonomy stack that enables fully synthetic training of vision-based policies for advanced robotic autonomy. Our goal is to make such capabilities accessible on consumer-grade hardware while maintaining an open and extensible framework that can be readily explored, modified, and improved by researchers, developers, and hobbyists alike.
